# Boundary behaviour of stable Allen-Cahn limit-interfaces in Riemannian manifolds

**Authors:** Martin Man-chun Li Address: Department of Mathematics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shatin, N.T., Hong Kong Email address: martin.li@cuhk.edu.hk , Davide Parise Address: Department of Mathematics, Zeeman Building, University of Warwick, Gibbet Hill Road, Coventry CV4 7AL, UK Email address: Davide.Parise@warwick.ac.uk and Lorenzo Sarnataro Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Toronto, 40 St George St., Toronto, Ontario M5S 2E4, Canada Email address: lorenzo.sarnataro@utoronto.ca

## Abstract

This is the second paper in our series of works to develop the min-max theory for free boundary minimal hypersurfaces in Riemannian manifolds with boundary via the Allen-Cahn equation. Building on our previous work for general critical points, we study the boundary behaviour of limit-interface integral varifolds arising from stable (or finite Morse index) solutions to the Allen-Cahn equation with Neumann boundary condition. More precisely, we prove that the limit-interface is a curvature varifold with boundary in the sense of Mantegazza satisfying a generalized stability inequality. Furthermore, we rule out classical tangent cones at the boundary and show that the first variation of the limit-interface varifold is singular with respect to its weight measure. In particular, our result confirms a folklore conjecture that the boundary concentration examples of Malchiodi, Ni and Wei have unbounded Morse index. As will be evident in our forthcoming work, the results obtained in this paper are crucial ingredients towards the optimal boundary regularity in the Allen-Cahn free boundary min-max theory.

## 1. Introduction and Main Results

Let $(M^{n},g)$ be an $n$ -dimensional smooth compact Riemannian manifold with boundary. We consider the following (elliptic) Allen-Cahn equation with Neumann boundary condition:

$$ \left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}-\varepsilon^{2}\Delta_{g}u+W^{\prime}(u)=0&\text{in $M$}\\
\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=0&\text{on $\partial M$}\end{array}\right. $$

where $\Delta_{g}$ is the Laplace-Beltrami operator on $(M,g)$ , $\nu$ is the unit outward normal of $\partial M$ and $W:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a smooth double well potential such as $W(t)=\frac{1}{4}(1-t^{2})^{2}$ . Here, $\varepsilon>0$ is a small parameter. A solution $u\in C^{\infty}(M)$ to (1.1) is said to be stable if it satisfies in addition the stability inequality, i.e.

$$ \int_{M}\varepsilon|\nabla\psi|^{2}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}W^{\prime\prime}(u)\psi^{2}\;d\mathrm{vol}_{g}\geq 0\quad\text{for all $\psi\in C^{\infty}(M)$.} $$

The main goal of this paper is to study the (local) boundary behaviour of the limit-interface varifold arising from a sequence of stable solutions $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ to (1.1) with $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ .

### 1.1. Background and motivations

We begin with a discussion on the background and some recent development in the field which motivates our study here.

#### 1.1.1. Bernstein problems and De Giorgi Conjecture

The parabolic counterpart of the Allen-Cahn equation (1.1) is a reaction-diffusion equation first proposed in phase transition theory to describe the process of phase separation in multi-component alloy systems. In the sharp interface limit as $\varepsilon\to 0$ , heuristically the limit-interface separating stable phases would be evolving under mean curvature flow whose stationary solutions are given by minimal surfaces. Since the 1970s, the theory of $\Gamma$ -convergence [48, 49, 36] pioneered by De Giorgi showed a deep connection between the Allen-Cahn equation and minimal surface theory. Motivated by the classical Bernstein problem in minimal surface theory, De Giorgi made several famous conjectures about similar rigidity results for entire solutions to the Allen-Cahn equation. Progress made around De Giorgi’s conjectures have driven some of the major developments for semi-linear partial differential equations (see [15] for an excellent survey up to 2018) in the past few decades.

In recent years, we have witnessed significant breakthroughs on the stable Bernstein problem for minimal hypersurfaces [17, 16, 47, 9, 32]. As a result, we now know that stable two-sided complete minimal hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are flat for $n\leq 7$ while non-flat examples exist for $n\geq 8$ . Nevertheless, the analogous De Giorgi conjecture for stable entire solutions to the Allen-Cahn equation remains unsolved in its full generality (see, however, [26, 27, 42, 14] for some remarkable recent progress). On the other hand, variants of the stable De Giorgi conjecture have been confirmed affirmatively in certain low dimensional settings (c.f. [11, 25, 12, 13]).

#### 1.1.2. Min-max theory via Allen-Cahn equation

The compactness and regularity of stable (or finite Morse index) solutions to the Allen-Cahn equation is closely related to the existence theory of minimal hypersurfaces by global Morse-theoretic min-max constructions. Building on the fundamental work of [33, 58], Guaraco [29] pioneered a PDE approach via Allen-Cahn equation to construct closed embedded minimal hypersurfaces in closed Riemannian manifolds, as an alternative to the classical Almgren-Pitts approach based on geometric measure theory. This new PDE-based approach has proven powerful especially in low dimensions (e.g. [18, 19]) by exploiting novel curvature estimates first discovered by Wang-Wei [61]. See also the recent work [22] of the second and third-named author with their collaborators in the free boundary setting.

#### 1.1.3. Free boundary minimal hypersurfaces

This paper constitutes part of the broader program initiated by the same authors in [39] to develop a PDE-based min-max theory for free boundary minimal hypersurfaces via the Allen-Cahn equation on Riemannian manifolds with boundary. In the free boundary setting, the Almgren-Pitts min-max theory in the geometric measure theoretic framework was developed by the first-named author with X. Zhou in [40]. In contrast to the boundaryless situation, a technically subtle but major difficulty is to understand the boundary concentration phenomena known as touching or improperness as observed in [41]. In the context of Allen-Cahn equations, such boundary concentrating solutions have been constructed rigorously by Malchiodi, Ni and Wei [43] inside the unit ball and by Malchiodi-Wei [44] inside any strictly mean convex domain in Euclidean space. More precisely, for any given $N\in\mathbb{N}$ , [43] established the existence of a sequence of radially symmetric solutions $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\}$ to (1.1) for $M=\mathbb{B}^{n}$ and $W(t)=\frac{1}{4}(1-t^{2})^{2}$ such that the zero level sets $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}=0\}$ converge as $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ to the boundary sphere $\partial\mathbb{B}^{n}$ with multiplicity $N$ . Moreover, each solution $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ has Morse index equal to $N$ within the class of radially symmetric functions. Nonetheless, it is a folklore conjecture that if we consider the bigger class of functions which are not necessarily radially symmetric, the Morse index should become unbounded in these examples.

#### Conjecture 1.1.

The solutions $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ constructed by Malchiodi, Ni and Wei in [43] and [44] have unbounded Morse index as $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ .

Heuristically, the boundary mean-convexity suggests that the limit-interface should be unstable in the direction along the inward normal of the domain boundary. By imposing oscillatory Fourier modes along the direction tangential to the domain boundary, this would then create infinitely many independent directions for the second variation. However, it is very difficult to make this quantitative as a-priori the level sets $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}=0\}$ only converges to the domain boundary in a very weak topology; and it is ambiguous to make sense of the Morse index of the limit-interface (in our case here is simply the domain boundary) as it is not a genuine minimal surface in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . To the best of our knowledge, the exact Morse index of the examples in [43] and [44] has yet to be computed.

### 1.2. Main results

By our previous work [39], for any sequence of solutions $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\}$ to (1.1) satisfying natural uniform energy and $L^{\infty}$ bounds (see Assumptions 4.2), we can associate to each $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ a codimension-one varifold $V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}$ in $M$ such that, after passing to a subsequence as $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ , $V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}$ converges as varifolds to a limit varifold $V$ , known as a limit-interface11 1 Note that the limit-interface $V$ may depend on the choice of the subsequence of $\varepsilon_{i}$ .. Moreover, we know from [39] that $V$ is integer-rectifiable up to the boundary and is free boundary stationary as a varifold in $M$ (we refer the readers to Section 3 for the precise definitions).

We now describe the main results obtained in this paper which establish further analytic and geometric properties of $V$ under the additional assumptions that each $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ is stable (see Assumptions 4.6). See Theorem 4.8 and 4.18 for more precise statements.

#### Theorem 1.2.

Let $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ and suppose $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\}$ is a sequence of stable solutions to the Allen-Cahn equation (1.1) with $E_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})\leq E_{0}$ and $\|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\|_{L^{\infty}(M)}\leq C_{0}$ for some constants $E_{0},C_{0}>0$ . Then, for any limit-interface $V$ obtained from a subsequential limit of $V^{\varepsilon_{i}}$ as above, the following hold:

- (1) $V$ is a curvature varifold with boundary in the sense of Mantegazza (c.f. Definition 3.33)

- (2) $V$ satisfies a stability-type inequality: for any $\psi\in C^{1}_{c}(M)$ , we have

$$ \int|\mathbf{B}_{V}|^{2}\psi^{2}\,d\|V\|\leq\int|\nabla\psi|^{2}\,d\|V\|+C_{M}\int\psi^{2}\,d\|V\|+C_{M}\int\psi^{2}\,d\|\delta V\|_{sing}, $$

where $\mathbf{B}_{V}$ is the generalized second fundamental form of $V$ (c.f. Definition 3.33) and $C_{M}\geq 0$ is a geometric constant depending only on $M$ .

- (3) $V$ is stationary across the “touching set”, i.e. the first variation of $V$ is given by

$$ \delta V(X)=\int X\cdot\nu\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing} $$

where $X$ is any $C^{1}$ vector field on $M$ which is not necessarily tangential to $\partial M$ .

- (4) $V$ admits no classical tangent cones except possibly on an $\mathcal{H}^{n-2}$ -null set of $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ .

#### Remark 1.3.

To understand (3), note that if $V$ is the unit-density varifold corresponding to the domain boundary $\partial M$ , then it is automatically a free boundary stationary varifold with free boundary in $\partial M$ (c.f. Definition 3.4). However, it will satisfy (3) only when $\partial M$ is itself a minimal hypersurface (since in this case $\|\delta V\|_{sing}=0$ as $\partial M$ itself has no boundary). Therefore, (3) is saying in a weak sense (which can be made precise by (3.7)) the limit-interface $V$ must be “minimal” on the part where it leans onto $\partial M$ (c.f. Remark 4.11).

Because of Remark 1.3, boundary concentration for stable limit-interface cannot happen on the non-minimal part of $\partial M$ . Combining with a standard trick due to R. Schoen (c.f. [54]) by considering disjoint small open balls, boundary concentration can happen only at at most $N$ non-minimal points on $\partial M$ if a limit-interface arises from solutions $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\}$ of the Allen-Cahn equation (1.1) with Morse index uniformly bounded above by $N$ . Note that the examples considered in [43, 44] have strictly mean-convex domain boundary, as an immediate consequence of Theorem 1.2 (3) we have:

#### Corollary 1.4.

Conjecture 1.1 is true.

#### Remark 1.5.

(4) is the free boundary analogue of a fundamental result of Tonegawa-Wickramasekera [58, Proposition 3.2] for the interior case in the Euclidean setting. Here, we extend their result up to the boundary and in the Riemannian setting. In another paper [8] of the same authors with Bellettini, we established the compactness and regularity theory for stable free boundary minimal hypersurfaces under an a-priori smallness assumption on the singular set in the spirit of Schoen-Simon (c.f. [53] and [9]). In our forthcoming work, where we develop the full free boundary optimal regularity of Wickramasekera’s far-reaching interior compactness and regularity theory [63], (3) is the key variational hypothesis and (4) will be used to verify the main structural hypothesis on the absence of classical singularities.

### 1.3. Main ideas and key challenges

We now give a more detailed discussion on the major difficulties and some of the novel ideas in proving our main result Theorem 1.2 above (see also Theorem 4.8 and 4.18 for more precise statements).

#### 1.3.1. Complications due to boundary interaction

While the overall strategy to prove Theorem 1.2 is similar to the one laid out in the foundational work of Tonegawa and Wickramasekera in [60, 58] which established the same results in the interior Euclidean setting (see also [29] for an extension to the Riemannian setting), the extra Neumann boundary condition in (1.1) interacts in a highly non-trivial way with the semi-linear Allen-Cahn equation in the interior. To better understand the new challenges due to such boundary interaction, let us first recall the main steps of [60, 58] in establishing the optimal regularity of stable Allen-Cahn limit-interfaces in the interior setting (we shall restrict to the Euclidean setting for now and leave the discussions about the Riemannian setting until Section 1.3.2).

- Step 1: The first step is to study the limit-interface $V$ obtained as the limit of varifolds associated to general critical points $u_{\varepsilon}$ of the Allen-Cahn energy functional with uniform energy and $L^{\infty}$ bounds. It was shown in [33] that $V$ must be an integer-rectifiable stationary varifold. The key element here is an almost monotonicity formula at the $\varepsilon$ -level which relies on a pointwise upper bound on the discrepancy function.

- Step 2: The second step is to analyse stable solutions to the Allen-Cahn equation (1.1) at the $\varepsilon$ -level. This was done in [51]. Here an $\varepsilon$ -stability inequality satisfied by the enhanced second fundamental form of $u_{\varepsilon}$ is obtained.

- Step 3: The next step is to pass $\varepsilon\to 0$ in the $\varepsilon$ -stability inequality to infer that the limit-interface $V$ is a curvature varifold in the sense of Hutchinson [34]. This allows the generalized second fundamental form of $V$ to be defined and a stability inequality holds by passing $\varepsilon\to 0$ the $\varepsilon$ -stability inequality from Step 3. This was done in [60].

- Step 4: As an intermediate step towards the regularity of the stable limit-interface $V$ , one needs to analyse in detail the top two strata of the singular set according to the Almgren-Federer stratification. In particular, one needs to rule out the existence of classical tangent cones on a generic subset of singular points. This is done in [58] by a blow-up and contradiction argument, using the stability inequality from Step 3 together with some fine analysis in [33].

- Step 5: The final step is to apply the far-reaching Schoen-Simon-Wickramasekera’s compactness and regularity theory [53, 63] to conclude that the support of the limit-interface $V$ is smooth except possibly on a small singular set of codimension $7$ .

We now highlight some of the major new challenges in the presence of boundary interaction. Due to the boundary concentration examples in [44, 43], the study of general critical points in Step 1 has to be robust enough to cover these situations. This was done in our previous paper [39]. Unlike the interior Euclidean case treated in [33], the discrepancy function only satisfies a weaker pointwise upper bound $\xi_{\varepsilon}\leq\varepsilon^{-4/5}$ (as opposed to $\xi_{\varepsilon}\leq C$ in [33]) near the domain boundary. Using this weaker pointwise bound, the almost monotonicity formula is only effective down to the scale of order $\varepsilon^{4/5}$ . In order to improve it down to the scale of order $\varepsilon$ , we utilize in [39] careful covering arguments to derive the desired variational and regularity properties of the limit-interface up to the domain boundary based on integral estimates. In particular, the limit-interface is free boundary stationary and integer-rectifiable up to the boundary. Among other things, we also established that the discrepancy function $\xi_{\varepsilon}$ converges to zero in the strong $L^{1}$ -sense up to the domain boundary, which implies “equi-partition of energy” as in [33]. This finishes Step 1 in the setting with boundary.

Steps 2-4 are treated in this paper. For Step 2, we proceed as in [51] to obtain an $\varepsilon$ -stability inequality for the enhanced second fundamental form of $u_{\varepsilon}$ with an additional boundary term involving the second fundamental form of the domain boundary, which arises from integrating by parts of the Bochner formula. For Step 3, the notion of curvature varifolds in [34] is insufficient for our purpose here, as the limit-interface is supposed to contain a free boundary in our setting. Therefore, we need to adopt instead the concept of curvature varifold with boundary by Mantegazza [45] to describe the limit-interface. One technical difference to the interior setting of [60] is that we do not know whether the restriction of the discrepancy function $\xi_{\varepsilon}$ to the domain boundary still converges to zero strongly in $L^{1}$ with respect to the domain boundary. As a result, we do not have equi-partition of energy when restricted to the domain boundary and thus several naturally defined Radon measures on the domain boundary may be inequivalent. To overcome this difficulty, we employed a local $L^{1}$ -trace inequality for the energy density in [39] to control the extra boundary term in the $\varepsilon$ -stability inequality in order to obtain uniform $L^{2}$ -bounds on the enhanced second fundamental form of $u_{\varepsilon}$ to carry out the compactness arguments. When passing $\varepsilon\to 0$ the $\varepsilon$ -stability inequality, the singular part can be identified with appropriate quantities from the first variation of $V$ . This relies on some fine boundary properties of curvature varifold with boundary established in [45]. From this we also infer a novel conclusion that the limit-interface $V$ must be stationary across the part where it leans on the domain boundary.

For Step 4, we introduce the definition of boundary classical tangent cones and classify them into two types, depending on whether the spine of the cone is contained in or perpendicular to the domain boundary. While the second type can be treated in a similar way to the interior setting, the first type depicts boundary concentration phenomenon which has to be studied separately. We carry out in detail here the blow-up and contradiction arguments as in [58], but using the ideas to treat boundary concentration as developed in [39]. In the final contradiction argument, we need to argue that the planar curves obtained from generic slices of level sets of $u_{\varepsilon}$ have to turn by a definite positive amount (depending solely on the boundary classical tangent cone). In contrast to the boundaryless setting in [58], besides closing up or having their ends going to infinity, such a planar curve may also end on the domain boundary. This is the place where we need to make use of the Neumann boundary condition, which translates to the geometric fact that such a planar curve has to hit the domain boundary orthogonally. By carefully exhausting all possible cases on the “ends” of such planar curves, we can derive the same contradiction as in [58].

One technical point in the above arguments is that one requires up-to-the-boundary Hausdorff convergence of the intermediate level sets of $u_{\varepsilon}$ to the support of the limit-interface $V$ . This was not established in [39] since the almost monotonicity formula only holds for balls that are either centred at a boundary point or are completely disjoint from the boundary. This is the case because we chose to give a much streamlined approach to avoid the use of reflected balls in [39]. In our current paper, we also supply the arguments using reflected balls in Appendix A and show the full Hausdorff convergence of the intermediate level sets up to the boundary. Moreover, in Appendix B we give an alternative proof on the integer-rectifiability of stable limit-interfaces based on the approach in [21]. The advantage is that it is much shorter than [39] but it relies heavily on stability.

#### 1.3.2. Intrinsic approach on varifolds in Riemannian manifolds

For our purpose of developing an Allen-Cahn min-max construction of free-boundary minimal hypersurfaces in Riemannian manifolds, as in [39] we established all the results in this paper in the setting of Riemannian manifolds. There are two existing mainstream approaches in the literature to generalize the theory of varifolds in Euclidean spaces to the Riemannian setting. One is via Nash’s isometric embedding as was done in [4, 50]; another one is via an intrinsic approach as was done in [53, 52]. We adopt the second approach in this paper for two reasons. The first is concerning the required regularity assumption on the Riemannian metric. The existence of isometric embedding requires at least $C^{2,\alpha}$ regularity of the Riemannian metric while one only requires $C^{2}$ regularity for the intrinsic approach. The second is that the boundary value problem for isometric embedding is not canonically well-posed. One can get around by first extending our Riemannian manifold $M^{n}$ with boundary into a closed Riemannian manifold $\widetilde{M}^{n}$ of the same dimension, and then apply Nash’s isometric embedding theorem to the extended Riemannian manifold (c.f. [40]). Although the same conclusions can be drawn as far as regularity is concerned, much of the geometric information of the original Riemannian manifold $M$ is obscured due to the arbitrary choice of the extension $\widetilde{M}$ and the rather obscure isometric embedding. For example, it would be difficult to obtain effective quantitative estimates in terms of geometric quantities such as curvatures or second fundamental form of $M$ .

In the first part of this paper, we systematically develop the foundational theory of varifolds in the intrinsic setting. For example, we derive the monotonicity formula, the existence and properties of tangent cones, the stratification of the singular set, as well as the notion of free-boundary varifolds and curvature varifolds with boundary in the intrinsic Riemannian setting. Apart from identifying the natural coordinate-free definitions, a new significant difficulty arises in the intrinsic approach due to the fact that a varifold in the Riemannian manifold $M$ which has locally bounded first variation (or even stationary), when written as a varifold in the tangent space under geodesic normal coordinates, may not even have locally bounded first variation (with respect to the flat metric)! Therefore, a-priori one cannot apply any of the classical results like the compactness theorem of integral varifolds in [4] to such varifolds expressed in a geodesic normal coordinate chart. This is because the Riemannian metric $g$ only agrees with the flat metric at origin up to first order in geodesic normal coordinates. The variational information (such as stationarity) is lost once we move slightly away from the origin. This obstruction was first observed in [53] and some of the related results have been established in their setting. However, they made use of some additional assumptions such as stability or sheeting (c.f. [53, Section 5, Remark 12]) to derive their results. Here in this paper, we establish all the results such as integrality of tangent cones, under merely first-order assumption such as locally bounded first variation in the original Riemannian manifold $(M^{n},g)$ . We believe that these fundamental results, that are shown to hold in such generality, will be useful in other geometric contexts (c.f. for example, [57] for some recent breakthrough on the singular set of minimal hypersurfaces in the Rimemannian setting).

### 1.4. Organization of the paper

The rest of the paper is organized into three sections. In Section 2, we describe our geometric setup and state various definitions, notations and concepts that will be used in this paper. In Section 3, we systematically develop the theory of varifolds in Riemannian manifold using an intrinsic approach. We also treat in detail the boundary behaviour in the context of free-boundary varifolds and curvature varifolds with boundary. In Section 4, we prove all the main results (Theorem 1.2 in local form) concerning properties of the stable limit-interfaces arising from Allen-Cahn equation. Finally, we collect in the appendix various results that supplement the content of this paper.
