## 2. Definitions, Notations and Preliminaries

In this section, we state various basic definitions, introduce some notations and recall certain preliminary concepts that will be used throughout the rest of this paper.

### 2.1. Ambient geometry

Let $(\widetilde{M}^{n},g)$ be a smooth22 2 In fact all the results in this paper are valid provided that the metric $g$ is $C^{2}$ and $M$ is a manifold of class $C^{3}$ . For the sake of readability, we will assume that $g$ is $C^{\infty}$ throughout this paper. complete $n$ -dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary, and let $\nabla^{g}$ denote the Levi-Civita connection on $\widetilde{M}$ induced by $g$ . We shall sometimes use $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{g}$ to denote the inner product $g$ on the tangent spaces of $\widetilde{M}$ or simply use $\cdot$ when there is no ambiguity. We use $B^{g}_{r}(x)$ to denote the geodesic ball in $(\widetilde{M},g)$ of radius $r$ centred at $x$ . For any $0\leq k\leq n$ , the $k$ -dimensional Hausdorff measure on $(\widetilde{M},g)$ is denoted by $\mathcal{H}^{k}$ . Note that $\mathcal{H}^{n}$ agrees with the volume measure $d\mathrm{vol}_{g}$ on $(\widetilde{M},g)$ . As in [39], we will always assume $(\widetilde{M},g)$ has positive injectivity radius lower bound

$$ \operatorname{inj}_{g}(\widetilde{M})\geq i_{0}\quad\text{for some constant $i_{0}>0$.} $$

and a two-sided sectional curvature bound

$$ |\sec_{(\widetilde{M},g)}|\leq k_{0}\quad\text{for some constant $k_{0}\geq 0$.} $$

We shall omit the subscripts or superscripts $g$ if the metric is clear from the context.

Let $\Omega\subset\widetilde{M}$ be an open and connected domain with smooth33 3 Again, $C^{2}$ regularity of $\partial\Omega$ would suffice for our purposes. non-empty boundary $\partial\Omega$ , whose outward unit normal is denoted by $\nu$ . As in [39], we will always assume that $\Omega$ has bounded ball curvatures (c.f. [39, Section 2.2])

$$ \max\{|\overline{Z}_{\Omega}|,|\underline{Z}_{\Omega}|\}\leq\kappa_{0}\quad\text{for some constant $\kappa_{0}\geq 0$.} $$

Under this assumption, the signed boundary distance function $d(\cdot):=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\cdot,\partial\Omega)$ , with $d>0$ in $\Omega$ , is smooth in the tubular neighbourhood $U_{\frac{1}{2\kappa_{0}}}(\partial\Omega)$ of size $\frac{1}{2\kappa_{0}}$ around $\partial\Omega$ and satisfies the following:

$$ |\nabla d|_{g}=1,\quad(\operatorname{Hess}_{g}d)\,(\nabla d,\cdot)=0\quad\text{ and }\quad\|\operatorname{Hess}_{g}d\,\|\leq C_{1}(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0}). $$

Moreover, for any boundary point $x\in\partial\Omega$ , the distance function $r(\cdot):=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\cdot,x)$ satisfies

$$ |r\nabla r\cdot\nu|(y)\leq\frac{\kappa_{0}}{2}r^{2}(y)\quad\text{for all $y\in\partial\Omega\cap B_{\frac{i_{0}}{2}}(x)$.} $$

### 2.2. Functions, vector fields and measures

Since our arguments will be local, we let $U\subset\widetilde{M}$ be an open subset (sometimes of the Grassmannian manifold). We will use the following notations to denote various vector spaces of functions and vector fields:

$$ \begin{array}[]{cl}C_{c}(U)&\text{real-valued continuous functions on $U$ with compact support}\\
C^{k}_{c}(U)&\text{real-valued $C^{k}$ functions on $U$ with compact support}\\
L^{p}(U;\mu)&\text{real-valued $L^{p}$ functions on $U$ with respect to a measure $\mu$}\\
L^{p}_{loc}(U;\mu)&\text{real-valued locally $L^{p}$ functions on $U$ with respect to a measure $\mu$}\\
\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)&\text{$C^{1}$ vector fields on $U$ with compact support}\\
\mathfrak{X}^{tan}_{c}(U)&\text{$X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ such that $X\cdot\nu=0$ along $\partial\Omega\cap U$}\end{array} $$

### 2.3. Euclidean geometry

We will use $(\mathbb{R}^{n},\delta)$ to denote the standard $n$ -dimensional Euclidean space with the flat metric $\delta$ and the flat covariant derivative $D$ . For any $p\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $r>0$ , we denote the homothety map $\eta_{p,r}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}$ by

$$ \eta_{p,r}(q):=\frac{q-p}{r}. $$

In particular, $\eta_{p,1}$ is the translation which takes $p$ to the origin, and $\eta_{0,r}$ is the dilation by a factor $r^{-1}$ with respect to the origin. Given any unit vector $v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , we use $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}(v):=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\;|\;u\cdot v\geq 0\}$ to denote the closed half-space and $\theta_{v}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to denote the reflection about $v$ defined by

$$ \theta_{v}(p):=p-2(p\cdot v)v. $$

We shall omit the dependence on $v$ when there is no ambiguity. For the purpose of this paper, the most important case we have in mind is the flat Euclidean space $(T_{x}\widetilde{M},g_{x})$ for $x\in\partial\Omega$ with $v=-\nu(x)$ . We will denote the $k$ -dimensional Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^{k}$ by $\mathcal{L}^{k}$ .

### 2.4. Cutoffs and constants

Throughout this paper, we will use $\chi:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)$ to denote any $C^{3}$ even (i.e. $\chi(t)=\chi(-t)$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$ ) cut-off function satisfying the following requirements:

$$ \chi(t)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}1&\text{ for $0\leq t\leq\frac{1}{2}$}\\
0&\text{ for $t\geq 1$}\end{array}\right.\;\text{ and }\chi^{\prime}(t)\leq 0\text{ for every $t>0$.} $$

We shall use the convention that $C(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\cdots)$ denotes a non-negative constant that depends only on the parameters $\alpha$ , $\beta$ , $\gamma$ , $\cdots$ .

## 3. Intrinsic varifolds in Riemannian manifolds

We recall some definitions from geometric measure theory and refer the readers to the standard references [4, 55] for more details. Most of the existing literature on varifolds is considered in the framework of Euclidean ambient space. One common way to extend these to the Riemannian setting is via Nash isometric embedding as in [4], which requires at least $C^{2,\alpha}$ regularity of the metric with $\alpha>0$ [35, Section 8]. Another way is to develop the whole theory from the intrinsic point of view as, for example, in [52], which only requires the metric to be $C^{2}$ . The latter also has the advantage that we can obtain estimates with constants depending explicitly on geometric quantities such as curvatures and injectivity radius bounds.

Let $\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,k)$ be the space of unoriented $k$ -dimensional subspaces of $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ . For $T\in\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,k)$ , we identify $T$ with the corresponding orthogonal projection (with respect to $g_{x}$ ) of $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ onto $T$ . The orthogonal complement of $T\in\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,k)$ and its corresponding orthogonal projection will be denoted by $T^{\perp}\in\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-k)$ . In the case of $k=n-1$ , we also identify $T\in\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ with the unit vector $\pm N_{T}\in T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ which is perpendicular to $T$ . Note that we may express the relation by $T=I-N_{T}\otimes N_{T}$ where $I$ is the identity map on $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ . We shall mainly consider codimension-one varifolds in this paper but many of our discussions can be carried over to the case of general dimension and codimension.

For any open set $U\subset\widetilde{M}$ , let $G(U):=\cup_{x\in U}\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ be the Grassmannian bundle over $U$ which is a locally compact separable metric space. An $(n-1)$ -dimensional varifold in $U$ is simply a Radon measure on $G(U)$ . We denote the set of all $(n-1)$ -dimensional varifolds in $U$ by $\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ , equipped with the usual weak topology. For $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ , let $\|V\|$ be the weight of $V$ , which is the Radon measure on $U$ defined by

$$ \|V\|(\phi):=\int_{G(U)}\phi(x)\;dV(x,T),\qquad\forall\phi\in C_{c}(U). $$

We say $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ is rectifiable if there exists an $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$ -measurable, countably $(n-1)$ -rectifiable subset $\Sigma\subset U$ and a locally $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$ -integrable non-negative function $\Theta_{V}$ defined on $\Sigma$ such that

$$ V(\phi)=\int_{\Sigma}\phi(x,T_{x}\Sigma)\;\Theta_{V}(x)d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(x),\qquad\forall\phi\in C_{c}(G(U)). $$

Here $T_{x}\Sigma\in\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ is the unique approximate tangent space of $\Sigma$ at $x$ which exists $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$ -a.e. on $\Sigma$ . A rectifiable varifold $V$ is uniquely determined by its weight $\|V\|=\Theta_{V}\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\Sigma$ through the formula above. For this reason, we naturally say a Radon measure $\mu$ on $U$ is rectifiable when one can associate a rectifiable varifold $V$ such that $\|V\|=\mu$ . If $\Theta_{V}(x)\in\mathbb{N}$ for $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$ -a.e. $x\in\Sigma$ , we say $V$ is integer rectifiable or an integral varifold. The set of all $(n-1)$ -dimensional rectifiable varifolds and integral varifolds in $U$ is denoted respectively by $\mathbf{RV}_{n-1}(U)$ and $\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ . We say that $V$ is a unit-density varifold if $\Theta_{V}(x)=1$ for $\|V\|$ -a.e. $x$ . For any $C^{1}$ embedded hypersurface $\Sigma\subset U$ with (possibly empty) boundary, we will denote $|\Sigma|\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ the integral varifold associated to $\Sigma$ with multiplicity one.

#### Remark 3.1.

Note that the definition of a varifold does not really require the Riemannian metric $g$ . In fact, the notion of rectifiability and integer-rectifiability is independent of the choice of $g$ . The reason is that (integer) rectifiability is bi-Lipschitz invariant and any Riemannian metric is infinitesimally isometric to the flat Euclidean space. In particular, if $F:U\to\widetilde{U}$ is a $C^{1}$ proper map between two open sets of Riemannian manifolds, then the pushforward map $F_{\sharp}:\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)\to\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(\widetilde{U})$ , as defined in [55, Section 39], satisfies $F_{\sharp}(\mathbf{RV}_{n-1}(U))\subset\mathbf{RV}_{n-1}(U)$ and $F_{\sharp}(\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U))\subset\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ (c.f. [4, 3.5(3)] in the context of isometric embedding or [6, I.1 (13)]).

For $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ let $\delta V$ be the first variation of $V$ , namely,

$$ \delta V(X):=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\|(F_{t})_{\sharp}V\|(U)=\int_{G(U)}\operatorname{div}_{T}X(x)\;dV(x,T),\qquad\forall X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U) $$

where $\operatorname{div}_{T}X(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\nabla_{e_{i}}X(x)\cdot e_{i}$ for any orthonormal basis $\{e_{1},\cdots,e_{n-1}\}$ of $T\in\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ with respect to the Riemannian metric $g$ , and $\{F_{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$ is the flow generated by $X$ . We also denote the total variation measure (see [55, (39.3)]) of $\delta V$ by $\|\delta V\|$ . If $\|\delta V\|$ is a Radon measure on $U$ (i.e. $V$ has locally bounded first variation in $U$ ), by Riesz representation and the Radon-Nikodym theorem there exists a $\|V\|$ -measurable vector field $H_{V}$ , a $\|\delta V\|$ -measurable vector field $\eta_{V}$ with $|\eta_{V}|=1$ $\|\delta V\|$ -a.e., and a Borel set $Z_{V}\subset U$ such that $\|V\|(Z_{V})=0$ and

$$ \delta V(X)=-\int_{U}X(x)\cdot H_{V}(x)\;d\|V\|(x)+\int_{Z_{V}}X(x)\cdot\eta_{V}(x)\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing}(x) $$

for all $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ , where by $\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ we denote the singular part of $\|\delta V\|$ with respect to $\|V\|$ . We call $H_{V}$ the generalised mean curvature vector, $\eta_{V}$ the generalized outward co-normal, $\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ the generalized boundary measure, and $Z_{V}$ the generalized boundary of $V$ . Note that in general we have $H_{V}\in L^{1}_{loc}(U;\|V\|)$ and $\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ is a Radon measure on $U$ . We may omit the subscript $V$ when there is no ambiguity.

#### Remark 3.2.

In contrast to Remark 3.1, the notion of first variation $\delta V$ is a geometric quantity that depends on the Riemannian metric $g$ . This is intuitively clear as the first variation represents in a generalized sense the mean curvature vector and the boundary with its outward unit normal which are both geometric quantities. In particular, the notion of locally bounded first variation is not a diffeomorphism invariant. This is more evident when there is a singular part of the first variation. For example, consider the one-dimensional rectifiable varifold in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ in [2, Example 2, p.256] which is stationary in a ball centred at the origin, if we apply a diffeomorphism to this ball which preserves the origin but distorts the angles at all the triple junctions, we will end up with a rectifiable varifold with unbounded first variation near the origin.

We next describe the concept of tangent varifolds in the Riemannian setting from the intrinsic point of view. Given $x\in U$ and $0<\rho<\frac{1}{2}\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}}\}$ , the exponential map $\exp_{x}$ is a diffeomorphism44 4 The exponential map is a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism if the metric $g$ is of class $C^{2}$ . from the Euclidean ball $B^{\delta}_{\rho}(0)\subset(T_{x}\widetilde{M},g_{x})$ onto the geodesic ball55 5 Because of (2.3), we know that $B_{\rho}(x)\cap\partial\Omega$ is a connected, embedded hypersurface diffeomorphic to an $(n-1)$ -dimensional ball which separates $B_{\rho}(x)$ into two connected components, one of which is contained in $\Omega$ . $B_{\rho}(x)\subset(\widetilde{M},g)$ . Let $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ . We can consider the pushforward varifold $\overline{V}:=(\exp_{x}^{-1}|_{B_{\rho}(x)})_{\sharp}V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ inside the Euclidean space $(T_{x}\widetilde{M},g_{x})$ . If (recall (2.6))

$$ C=\lim_{i\to\infty}(\eta_{0,r_{i}})_{\sharp}\overline{V}\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M}) $$

is a weak limit for a sequence of positive numbers $r_{i}\to 0$ , then we say that $C$ is a varifold tangent to $V$ at $x$ , and write $C\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)\subset\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ , where $\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ denotes the set of all possible varifold tangents to $V$ at $x$ . Note that $(T_{x}\widetilde{M},g_{x})$ can be identified with the Euclidean space $(\mathbb{R}^{n},\delta)$ for which the usual theory of varifolds applies.

#### Remark 3.3.

Note that one can also define the set of tangent varifolds via isometric embedding as in [4]. If the metric $g$ is regular enough (say $C^{2,\alpha}$ regularity), the two notions of tangent varifolds are equivalent. Since we chose to avoid using Nash’s isometric embeddeding in this paper, we adopt the above intrinsic definition instead. Another formulation is to consider the rescaling of the metric $r_{i}^{-2}g$ as done in [39] which is again equivalent as $d\exp_{x}|_{0}$ is the identity map of $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ .

### 3.1. Free boundary varifolds

To study the fine properties close to the boundary, we shall also need the notion of free boundary varifolds defined in [23, Section 3] (see also [20, Definition 2.4]). Since both [23] and [20] are stated in the Euclidean setting, we will recall several useful results concerning this sub-class of varifolds and point out the differences (if any) in the Riemannian setting.

#### Definition 3.4 (Free boundary varifolds).

Given a smoothly66 6 It is sufficient to assume $C^{2}$ regularity of $S$ . embedded hypersurface $S\subset U$ oriented by the (outward) unit normal $\nu_{S}$ , a varifold $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ is said to have free boundary in $S$ 77 7 As in [23, 20], this definition implicitly assumes that $\delta V$ has locally bounded first variation with $\|\delta V\|_{sing}=0$ away from the support hypersurface $S$ . if there exists a $\|V\|$ -measurable vector field $H^{tan}_{V}\in L^{1}_{loc}(U;\|V\|)$ and $H^{tan}_{V}(x)\cdot\nu_{S}(x)=0$ for $\|V\|$ -a.e. $x\in S$ , satisfying

$$ \delta V(X)=-\int_{U}X(x)\cdot H^{tan}_{V}(x)\;d\|V\|(x)\qquad\text{$\forall$ $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ such that $X\cdot\nu_{S}=0$ on $S$.} $$

If $\delta V(X)=0$ for all $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ such that $X\cdot\nu_{S}=0$ on $S$ (in other words, $H^{tan}_{V}=0$ $\|V\|$ -a.e.), we say that $V$ is free boundary stationary with free boundary in $S$ .

Note that we use the notation $H^{tan}_{V}$ to distinguish it from the generalised mean curvature vector $H_{V}$ defined in (3.2). In fact, if such an $H_{V}$ exists as in (3.2) with $\|\delta V\|_{sing}=0$ , then $H^{tan}_{V}$ is indeed the tangential projection of $H_{V}$ along $S$ (see [23, Definition 3.0.3]). We also remark that $H^{tan}_{V}$ in Definition 3.4 is uniquely defined $\|V\|$ -a.e. with the condition $H^{tan}_{V}(x)\cdot\nu_{S}(x)=0$ for $\|V\|$ -a.e. $x\in S$ (c.f. [20, Remark 2.5]).

#### Remark 3.5.

Unlike in [20] (and implicitly in [23]), according to our Definition 3.4, the varifold $V$ is not required to lie on one side (determined by the unit normal $\nu_{S}$ ) of the support hypersurface $S$ . Although most of the time we will only consider $S=\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ with $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ , having this extra flexibility is convenient for us in certain rescaling arguments in the Riemannian setting as will be evident in the next subsection.

The following elementary but fundamental result was obtained by [20, Corollary 4.7] (and [23, Proposition 3.2] for integral varifolds) in the Euclidean setting. Roughly speaking, it says that free-boundary varifolds are varifolds with locally bounded first variation together with certain prescribed Neumann boundary condition along the singular part $\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ of the first variation measure.

#### Proposition 3.6 (Characterization of free boundary varifolds).

Let $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ . Then $V$ has free boundary in $S$ if and only if $V$ has locally bounded first variation in $U$ with $\operatorname{spt}\|\delta V\|_{sing}\subset S$ and $\eta_{V}(x)=\pm\nu_{S}(x)$ for $\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ -a.e. $x\in S$ .

#### Proof.

First, note that the same constancy lemma [20, Lemma 3.1] and the main theorem [20, Theorem 1.1] hold in the Riemannian setting by (2.4). Therefore, the proposition follows immediately as in [20, Corollary 4.7] from the following formula:

$$ \delta V(X)=-\int_{U}X(x)\cdot(H^{tan}_{V}(x)+H_{S}(x))\;d\|V\|(x)+\int_{S}X(x)\cdot\eta_{V}(x)\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing}(x), $$

for all $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ , where $H_{S}$ is the mean curvature vector of $S$ (which by convention vanishes outside $S$ ) and $\eta_{V}(x)=\pm\nu_{S}(x)$ for $\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ -a.e. $x$ . Note that $H^{tan}_{V}$ and $H_{S}$ are mutually orthogonal for $\|V\|$ -a.e. $x$ . We want to remark that we have $\eta_{V}=\nu_{S}$ only when $V$ is assumed to be supported on one side of $S$ (c.f. the last paragraph in Step 4 of the proof of Theorem 1.1 in [20]). In general, we only have $\eta_{V}=\pm\nu_{S}$ . ∎

#### Remark 3.7.

Given the main results in [39] (see Theorem 4.3), we shall only be concerned with free boundary varifolds that are also integral, we shall from now on implicitly make that assumption, even though it is not strictly necessary for some of the general results in this section. We shall refer to [20] for a more general treatment for free boundary varifolds which are not necessarily integral (or even rectifiable).

From now on, we will mainly focus on the case that $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ has free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ with $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ . Although we do not have a monotonicity formula for $\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ , by [20, Theorem 1.1] the following one-sided local bound holds:

$$ \|\delta V\|_{sing}(B_{r/2}(x))\leq\frac{C_{2}(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0})}{r}\|V\|(B_{r}(x))+\int_{B_{r}(x)}|H^{tan}_{V}|\;d\|V\|, $$

for all $x\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $0<r<\min\left\{\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial U),\frac{1}{2\kappa_{0}}\right\}$ .

We will mostly be interested in varifolds that are free boundary stationary with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ , i.e. varifolds $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ with the additional property that $\delta V(X)=0$ for all $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}^{tan}(U)$ . For such free boundary stationary varifolds $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ with $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ , (3.5) becomes

$$ \delta V(X)=-\int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}X(x)\cdot H_{\partial\Omega}(x)\;d\|V\|(x)+\int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}X(x)\cdot\nu(x)\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing}(x) $$

for all $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ . Note that both terms on the right hand side are supported along $\partial\Omega\cap U$ . Similarly, (3.6) simplifies to

$$ \|\delta V\|_{sing}(B_{r/2}(x))\leq\frac{C_{2}(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0})}{r}\|V\|(B_{r}(x)). $$

For general free boundary varifolds that are not necessarily stationary, we can still obtain the following weighted version of (3.6).

#### Lemma 3.8 ( $L^{1}$ -trace inequality for free boundary varifolds).

Let $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ be a varifold with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ . For any nonnegative $f\in C_{c}^{1}(U)$ , we have

$$ \int f\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing}\leq C_{3}\int\left((1+|H^{tan}_{V}|)f+|\nabla f|\right)\;d\|V\| $$

where $C_{3}=C_{3}(n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0})>0$ .

#### Proof.

We will basically follow the arguments in [20, Subsection 3.2] adapted to the local Riemannian setting. Fix $f\in C^{1}_{c}(U)$ . Since $f$ has compact support in $U$ , a straightforward covering argument shows that it suffices to establish (3.9) locally around any $x_{0}\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ . Let $r=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\cdot,x_{0})$ and $d=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\cdot,\partial\Omega)$ . We test (3.5) with the compactly-supported vector field

$$ X(x)=-f(x)\chi\left(\frac{r(x)}{R}\right)\nabla d(x) $$

where $\chi$ is the cut-off function defined in Section 2.4, and $R=\frac{1}{2}\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{2\kappa_{0}}\}$ . Thus, we have the following

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\int_{B_{R/2}(x_{0})}f(x)\;&d\|\delta V\|_{sing}(x)\leq\int f(x)\chi\left(\frac{r(x)}{R}\right)\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing}(x)=\int X(x)\cdot\nu(x)\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing}(x)\\
&=\int\mathrm{div}_{S}X(x)\;dV(x,S)+\int X(x)\cdot\left(H^{tan}_{V}(x)+H_{\partial\Omega}(x)\right)\;d\|V\|(x).\end{split} $$

On the other hand, a direct computation shows $\mathrm{div}_{S}X(x)$ is equal to

$$ -f(x)\chi^{\prime}\left(\frac{r(x)}{R}\right)\frac{1}{R}\left(S(\nabla r)\cdot\nabla d\right)(x)-f(x)\chi\left(\frac{r(x)}{R}\right)\mathrm{div}_{S}\nabla d(x)-\chi\left(\frac{r(x)}{R}\right)\left(\nabla d\cdot S(\nabla f)\right)(x). $$

Note that $|\mathrm{div}_{S}\nabla d|\leq(n-1)C_{1}(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0})$ in $B_{R}(x_{0})$ by (2.4). Furthermore, $|H_{\partial\Omega}|\leq(n-1)\kappa_{0}$ by (2.3). Therefore, we can bound

$$ \displaystyle-\int f(x)\chi\left(\frac{r(x)}{R}\right) \displaystyle\mathrm{div}_{S}\nabla d(x)\;dV(x,S)-\int f(x)\chi\left(\frac{r(x)}{R}\right)\nabla d(x)\cdot\left(H^{tan}_{V}(x)+H_{\partial\Omega}(x)\right)d\|V\|(x) \displaystyle\leq C(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0})\int_{B_{R}(x_{0})}\left(1+|H^{tan}_{V}(x)|\right)f(x)\;d\|V\|(x). $$

The other terms appearing in $\mathrm{div}_{S}X(x)$ can be controlled by fixing a cutoff function such that $\|\chi^{\prime}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq 3$ and the observation that $|\nabla r|=|\nabla d|=1$ . This concludes the proof. ∎

Taking $f=\psi^{2}$ in (3.9) and applying Cauchy’s inequality, we have the following simple but important consequence of Lemma 3.8.

#### Corollary 3.9.

For every $\eta>0$ , there exists $C_{4}(\eta,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0})>0$ such that the following holds: let $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ be a varifold with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ , for any $\psi\in C^{1}_{c}(U)$ , we have

$$ \int\psi^{2}\,d\|\delta V\|_{sing}\leq(1+\eta)\int|\nabla\psi|^{2}\,d\|V\|+C_{4}\int\left(1+|H^{tan}_{V}|\right)\psi^{2}\,d\|V\|. $$

We also recall a useful reflection principle and constancy lemma for free boundary stationary varifolds from [40] and [20], adapted to our setup and terminology. We will mostly apply the lemma below at the level of tangent cones, hence we can take $\mathbb{R}^{n}=T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ and $v=-\nu$ (recall the notations from (2.7) for the lemma below).

#### Lemma 3.10 ([40, Lemma 2.2]).

For any $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ with $\operatorname{spt}V\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ , define the doubled-varifold

$$ \overline{V}:=V+(\theta_{v})_{\sharp}V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}). $$

If $V$ is free boundary stationary with free boundary in $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ , then $\overline{V}$ is stationary in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ .

#### Lemma 3.11 ([20, Lemma 3.1 and Corollary 4.3]).

Let $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ be a varifold with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ . Then, for any $\phi\in C_{c}(G(U))$ , we have

$$ \int_{G(U)}\phi(x,S)\;dV(x,S)=\int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}\phi(x,T_{x}\partial\Omega)\Theta^{n-1}(\|V\|,x)\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(x)+\int_{G(U\setminus\partial\Omega)}\phi(x,S)\;dV(x,S). $$

In particular, $\|V\|\,\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}_{\partial\Omega}=\Theta^{n-1}(\|V\|,\cdot)\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\,\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}_{\partial\Omega}$ and $V$ is rectifiable along $\partial\Omega\cap U$ with

$$ V\left(\{(x,S)\in G(U)\,|\,x\in\partial\Omega\cap U,S\neq T_{x}\partial\Omega\}\right)=0. $$

We shall use Lemma 3.10 and Lemma 3.11 to prove the following technical result.

#### Lemma 3.12.

Using the same notation as in Lemma 3.10, and suppose $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ is free boundary stationary with free boundary in $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . Assume, in addition, that $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . Then $V$ is stationary in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and thus $V=m|\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}|$ for some real constant $m>0$ .

#### Proof.

By the classical constancy theorem [55, 41.1], it suffices to show that $V$ is stationary in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . We claim that $(\theta_{v})_{\sharp}V=V$ . Once the claim is established, we see from Lemma 3.10 that the doubled varifold $\overline{V}=V+(\theta_{v})_{\sharp}V=2V$ is stationary in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . This of course implies stationarity of $V=\frac{1}{2}\overline{V}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ .

It remains to establish the claim that $(\theta_{v})_{\sharp}V=V$ . Since $v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\,|\,u\cdot v=0\}$ , for all $x\in\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ we have $\theta_{v}(x)=x$ and $D_{x}\theta_{v}$ acts as the identity map on $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . Moreover, notice that for any $(y,S)\in G(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ , the Jacobian (see [55, §39]) is given by $J_{S}\theta_{v}(y)=1$ . Therefore, by the definition of pushforward of a varifold (see again [55, §39]), we have for all $f\in C^{0}_{c}(G(\mathbb{R}^{n}))$

$$ \begin{split}\int_{G(\mathbb{R}^{n})}f(z,T)\;d((\theta_{v})_{\sharp}V)(z,T)&=\int_{G(\mathbb{R}^{n})}f(\theta_{v}(y),D_{y}\theta_{v}(S))J_{S}\theta_{v}(S)\;dV(y,S)\\
&=\int_{\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\times\mathbf{G}(n,n-1)}f(\theta_{v}(y),D_{y}\theta_{v}(S))\;dV(y,S)\\
&\qquad+\int_{G(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+})}f(\theta_{v}(y),D_{y}\theta_{v}(S))\;dV(y,S).\end{split} $$

Using (3.11), $\theta_{v}(y)=y$ for $y\in\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ and the fact that $D_{y}\theta_{v}(S)\neq\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ for all $y\in\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ , $S\neq\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ , we see that

$$ \int_{\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\times\mathbf{G}(n,n-1)}f(\theta_{v}(y),D_{y}\theta_{v}(S))\;dV(y,S)=\int_{\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\times\{\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\}}f(y,\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+})\;dV(y,S). $$

On the other hand, since $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ by assumption, we have

$$ \int_{G(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+})}f(\theta_{v}(y),D_{y}\theta_{v}(S))\;dV(y,S)=0. $$

Combining all these and Lemma 3.11, we have established the claim that $(\theta_{v})_{\sharp}V=V$ . ∎

#### Remark 3.13.

In fact, the above result is local and the same statement holds when $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ (and respectively $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ ) is replaced by any open set $U\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ (and respectively $U\cap\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ ) which is invariant under the reflection $\theta_{v}$ .

### 3.2. Monotonicity formula and tangent cones

We will assume mostly in this section that $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ is a free boundary stationary (integral) varifold with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ . The goal is to recall various monotonicity formulae and look at their immediate consequences, especially regarding the basic properties of the varifold tangents $C\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ .

We first recall the following (almost) monotonicity formula for geodesic balls for free boundary varifolds with an $L^{\infty}$ bound on $H^{tan}_{V}$ . Note that we do not need to assume $V$ is integral.

#### Lemma 3.14 (Monotonicity formula).

For every $\Lambda\geq 0$ , there exists $C_{5}(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0},\Lambda)>0$ such that for any varifold $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ , $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ and $\|H^{tan}_{V}\|_{L^{\infty}(U)}\leq\Lambda$ , the function

$$ \rho\mapsto e^{C_{5}\rho}\frac{\|V\|(B_{\rho}(x))}{\rho^{n-1}} $$

is monotone increasing for $0<\rho<\frac{1}{2}\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{k_{0}}},2\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial U)\}$ when $x\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ ; and for $0<\rho<\frac{1}{2}\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{\sqrt{k_{0}}},2\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial\Omega\cup\partial U)\}$ when $x\in U\setminus\partial\Omega$ . In particular, the $(n-1)$ -dimensional density

$$ \Theta_{V}(x):=\lim_{\rho\to 0}\frac{\|V\|(B_{\rho}(x))}{\omega_{n-1}\rho^{n-1}} $$

exists for all $x\in U$ (and vanishes outside $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ ).

#### Proof.

The proof (in the Euclidean setting) is essentially contained in [20, Section 4.5]. We include the main steps here for our readers’ convenience and to adapt the calculations in the Riemannian setting. We will only focus on the case $x\in\partial\Omega$ as the interior case can be found for example in [52]. The key idea is to test (3.5) with suitable test vector fields. In what follows, we denote as in Section 2.1 that $r(\cdot)=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\cdot,x)$ and $d(\cdot)=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\cdot,\partial\Omega)$ be the intrinsic distance function from $x$ and $\partial\Omega$ respectively. Recall the cutoff function $\chi$ defined in section 2.4.

Fix $x\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ and let $\rho$ be as in the lemma, so that $\overline{B_{\rho}(x)}\subset U$ . Set

$$ I(\rho):=\int\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)\,d\|V\|,\qquad I^{\prime}(\rho)=\int-\frac{r}{\rho^{2}}\chi^{\prime}\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)\,d\|V\|\geq 0, $$

and let

$$ A:=\Lambda+(n-1)(\kappa_{0}+\sqrt{k_{0}}),\qquad B:=\Lambda+(n-1)(\kappa_{0}+C_{1}), $$

where $C_{1}=C_{1}(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0})$ is as in (2.4). First consider

$$ X=\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)r\nabla r\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U). $$

By Hessian comparison (c.f. [39, (2.1)]),

$$ \left|\operatorname{div}_{S}X-(n-1)\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)-\frac{r}{\rho}\chi^{\prime}\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)|S(\nabla r)|^{2}\right|\leq(n-1)\sqrt{k_{0}}\,r\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right). $$

Thus (3.5), (2.5), and $|H_{\partial\Omega}|\leq(n-1)\kappa_{0}$ give

$$ \begin{split}&\int\left((n-1)\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)+\frac{r}{\rho}\chi^{\prime}\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)|S(\nabla r)|^{2}\right)\,dV(y,S)\\
&\hskip 56.9055pt\leq A\rho I(\rho)+\frac{\kappa_{0}}{2}\int r^{2}\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)\,d\|\delta V\|_{sing}.\end{split} $$

To estimate the boundary term while retaining its quadratic factor, use

$$ \tilde{X}=-r^{2}\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)\nabla d\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U). $$

Since $-\nabla d=\nu$ on $\partial\Omega$ , and the support of $V$ lies in $\overline{\Omega}$ , the boundary term in (3.5) is now exactly $\int r^{2}\chi(r/\rho)\,d\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ . Moreover, (2.4) gives

$$ |\operatorname{div}_{S}\tilde{X}|\leq(n-1)C_{1}r^{2}\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)+2r\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)-\frac{r^{2}}{\rho}\chi^{\prime}\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right). $$

Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle\int r^{2}\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)\,d\|\delta V\|_{sing} \displaystyle\leq\int(Br^{2}+2r)\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)\,d\|V\|+\int-\frac{r^{2}}{\rho}\chi^{\prime}\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)\,d\|V\| \displaystyle\leq(B\rho^{2}+2\rho)I(\rho)+\rho^{2}I^{\prime}(\rho). $$

Here the term $\Lambda$ in $B$ controls $\tilde{X}\cdot H^{tan}_{V}$ .

Since $\chi^{\prime}\leq 0$ and $|S(\nabla r)|\leq 1$ , the left-hand side of (3.17) is at least $(n-1)I(\rho)-\rho I^{\prime}(\rho)$ . Combining the two estimates gives

$$ \rho\left(1+\frac{\kappa_{0}\rho}{2}\right)I^{\prime}(\rho)\geq\left(n-1-(A+\kappa_{0})\rho-\frac{\kappa_{0}B}{2}\rho^{2}\right)I(\rho). $$

In particular,

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\left(\frac{I(\rho)}{\rho^{n-1}}\right)\geq-\frac{A+\frac{n+1}{2}\kappa_{0}+\frac{\kappa_{0}B}{2}\rho}{1+\frac{\kappa_{0}\rho}{2}}\frac{I(\rho)}{\rho^{n-1}}\geq-C_{5}\frac{I(\rho)}{\rho^{n-1}}, $$

where we may choose any $C_{5}>0$ with

$$ C_{5}\geq\max\left\{A+\frac{n+1}{2}\kappa_{0},\,B\right\}. $$

Hence $e^{C_{5}\rho}I(\rho)/\rho^{n-1}$ is nondecreasing. For centres away from $\partial\Omega$ , the radial test field alone gives the interior assertion with the same $C_{5}$ . ∎

#### Remark 3.15.

We would like to point out that the monotonicity formula above holds only for ambient geodesic balls that are either centred at a boundary point on $\partial\Omega$ or is completely disjoint from the boundary $\partial\Omega$ . A standard argument (c.f. [55, Corollary 17.8]) then shows that the density function $\Theta_{V}$ is “partially” upper semi-continuous at the boundary in the sense that $\limsup_{x_{i}\to x}\Theta_{V}(x_{i})\leq\Theta_{V}(x)$ in general holds for $x\in\partial\Omega$ only when $x_{i}\in\partial\Omega$ for all $i$ . A free boundary half-plane contained in the half-space of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ illustrates this point as the boundary points have density $\frac{1}{2}$ and the interior points have density $1$ . However, as already observed in the proof of [39, Theorem 5.7], one can also use the arguments of reflected balls as in [28, Corollary 3.2] (c.f. Appendix A) to conclude that the reflected density defined by

$$ \overline{\Theta}_{V}(x):=\left\{\begin{matrix}\begin{aligned} &\Theta_{V}(x)&\text{if }x\notin\partial\Omega\cap U\\
&2\Theta_{V}(x)&\text{if }x\in\partial\Omega\cap U\end{aligned}\end{matrix}\right. $$

is actually an upper semi-continuous function in $x$ . In particular, if $V$ is further assumed to be integral, i.e. $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ , then we have the following uniform density lower bound88 8 In fact, $\Theta_{V}(x)\geq 1$ for all $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\Omega$ . For boundary points $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\partial\Omega$ which are in the closure of $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\Omega$ , it follows from upper semi-continuity of the reflected density. For boundary points $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\partial\Omega$ which are not in the closure of $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\Omega$ , by the free boundary assumption and Lemma 3.11, $V=\Theta_{V}|\partial\Omega|$ in a small ball $B_{r}(x)$ and the conclusion follows once again from integrality of $V$ and upper semi-continuity of the reflected density.

$$ \Theta_{V}(x)\geq\frac{1}{2}\quad\text{for every $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$.} $$

By the monotonicity formula, this implies the following uniform density ratio bounds

$$ \frac{1}{C_{6}}\leq\frac{\|V\|(B_{\rho}(x))}{\rho^{n-1}}\leq C_{6}\frac{\|V\|(B_{R_{x}}(x))}{R_{x}^{n-1}} $$

for any $0<\rho<R_{x}=\min\{R_{6},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial U)\}$ when $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\partial\Omega$ ; and $0<\rho<R_{x}=\min\{R_{6},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial\Omega\cup\partial U)\}$ when $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\setminus\partial\Omega$ . Here, $C_{6}=C_{6}(n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\Lambda)>0$ and $R_{6}=R_{6}(n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0})>0$ are positive constants.

#### Remark 3.16.

The same test fields give a weighted version of (3.18). Let $h\in C^{1}_{c}(U)$ be nonnegative and set

$$ I_{h}(\rho):=\int h\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)\,d\|V\|,\qquad G_{h}(\rho):=\int r\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)|S(\nabla h)|\,dV. $$

At a boundary centre, test (3.5) with $hX$ and $h\tilde{X}$ , where $X$ and $\tilde{X}$ are the fields in the proof above. The additional derivative terms are bounded by $G_{h}(\rho)$ and $\rho G_{h}(\rho)$ , respectively. With the same constants $A,B$ , this yields

$$ \begin{split}\rho\left(1+\frac{\kappa_{0}\rho}{2}\right)I_{h}^{\prime}(\rho)\geq{}&\left(n-1-(A+\kappa_{0})\rho-\frac{\kappa_{0}B}{2}\rho^{2}\right)I_{h}(\rho)\\
&-\left(1+\frac{\kappa_{0}\rho}{2}\right)G_{h}(\rho).\end{split} $$

Thus, for the same choice of $C_{5}$ ,

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\left(\frac{e^{C_{5}\rho}}{\rho^{n-1}}\int h\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)\,d\|V\|\right)\geq-\frac{e^{C_{5}\rho}}{\rho^{n}}\int r\chi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)|S(\nabla h)|\,dV. $$

At an interior centre the same inequality follows using $hX$ alone. Integrating in $\rho$ and then letting the cutoffs increase to the characteristic function of $[0,1)$ gives

$$ \begin{split}&\frac{e^{C_{5}R_{2}}}{R_{2}^{n-1}}\int_{B_{R_{2}}(x)}h\,d\|V\|-\frac{e^{C_{5}R_{1}}}{R_{1}^{n-1}}\int_{B_{R_{1}}(x)}h\,d\|V\|\\
&\qquad\geq-\int_{R_{1}}^{R_{2}}\frac{e^{C_{5}t}}{t^{n}}\left(\int_{G(B_{t}(x))}r\,|S(\nabla h)|\,dV\right)dt\end{split} $$

for $0<R_{1}<R_{2}$ in the corresponding range of Lemma 3.14.

The monotonicity formula in Lemma 3.14 is fundamental in the singularity analysis of free boundary varifolds as this allow us to perform blow-up arguments to reduce some of the problems to the study of tangent varifolds. The following proposition in the Euclidean setting is contained in [20, Lemma 5.4]. The proof turns out to be technically rather subtle in the Riemannian setting so we have decided to give complete details. We would like to point out that the analysis here is somewhat similar to that in [53, Section 5]. Besides the fact that we are not assuming (almost) stability nor a-priori sheeting, we have to deal with the new difficulty coming from the singular part of the first variation which is not present in [53].

#### Proposition 3.17 (Existence and properties of tangent cones).

Let $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ be a varifold with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ , $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ and $\|H^{tan}_{V}\|_{L^{\infty}(U)}\leq\Lambda$ . Then for any $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\partial\Omega$ , the space $\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ of varifold tangents at $x$ is non-empty and compact (in the weak topology). Moreover, for any $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ the following holds:

- (i) $\mathbf{C}$ is free boundary stationary with free boundary on $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\subset T_{x}^{+}\widetilde{M}$ , i.e.

$$ \delta\mathbf{C}(X)=0\quad\text{for all $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ such that $X\cdot\nu(x)=0$ along $T_{x}\partial\Omega$}; $$

- (ii) $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(0)=\Theta_{V}(x)$ and $\|\mathbf{C}\|$ is a cone with vertex at the origin of $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ , i.e.

$$ (\eta_{0,r})_{*}\|\mathbf{C}\|=r^{n-1}\|\mathbf{C}\|\quad\text{for all $r>0$}; $$

- (iii) The generalized boundary measure $\|\delta\mathbf{C}\|_{sing}$ in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ is scale-invariant (with dimension $n-2$ ), i.e.

$$ (\eta_{0,r})_{*}\|\delta\mathbf{C}\|_{sing}=r^{n-2}\|\delta\mathbf{C}\|_{sing}\quad\text{for all $r>0$.} $$

Here, we identify $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ with $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and denote $T_{x}^{+}\widetilde{M}:=\{v\in T_{x}\widetilde{M}:v\cdot\nu(x)\leq 0\}$ the tangent half-space that points into $\Omega$ , and the homothety maps $\eta_{p,r}:T_{x}\widetilde{M}\to T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ defined by $\eta_{p,r}(q):=r^{-1}(q-p)$ (c.f. Section 2.3).

If we assume, furthermore, that $V$ is rectifiable, i.e. $V\in\mathbf{RV}_{n-1}(U)$ , and the density of $V$ satisfies a uniform positive lower bound, i.e.

$$ \Theta_{V}(x)\geq 1\text{ for $\|V\|$-a.e. $x\in U$.} $$

then for any $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ , we have $\mathbf{C}\in\mathbf{RV}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ is a varifold cone with vertex at the origin of $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ , i.e.

$$ (\eta_{0,r})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}\quad\text{for all $r>0$}. $$

If $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ (in which case (3.24) is trivially satisfied), then $C\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ .

#### Proof.

We provide again the key steps of the proof of [20] adapted to the Riemannian setting. Consider a sequence of positive numbers $r_{i}\to 0$ , and the sequence of varifolds99 9 More precisely, for any fixed $R>0$ , $V_{i}$ is an integral varifold in $B^{\delta}_{R}(0)$ for all sufficiently large $i$ .

$$ V_{i}:=(\eta_{0,r_{i}}\circ\exp_{x}^{-1})_{\sharp}V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M}). $$

Since we are working with geodesic normal coordinates of $(\widetilde{M},g)$ centred at $x$ , we have the standard estimates from (2.1) and (2.2)

$$ |g_{ij}(q)-\delta_{ij}|\leq C(n,k_{0})|q|^{2} $$

for sufficiently small $|q|$ depending only on $n,k_{0}$ and $i_{0}$ . This implies the following estimate on the exponential map and its Jacobian factor (recall [55, (39.1)]):

$$ \max\{\|d(\exp^{-1}_{x})|_{y}\|,\|d(\exp_{x})|_{\exp_{x}^{-1}(y)}\|\}\leq 1+C(n,k_{0})\operatorname{dist}_{g}(y,x), $$

$$ |J_{S}(\exp^{-1}_{x})(y)-1|\leq C(n,k_{0})\operatorname{dist}_{g}(y,x), $$

From (3.26) and (3.27), by the monotonicity formula Lemma 3.14 and the fact that the rescaled pushforward metrics $r_{i}^{-2}(\exp_{x}^{-1})_{*}g$ converges in $C^{2}_{loc}$ to the flat Euclidean metric $\delta$ on $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ , $V_{i}$ has locally uniformly bounded mass in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ as varifolds in $(T_{x}\widetilde{M},\delta)$ . Therefore, standard compactness theorem for Radon measures implies that, after passing to a subsequence, we have $V_{i}$ converging weakly to some $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ . This implies $\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)\neq\emptyset$ and it follows from the same argument and the definition that $\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ is compact in the weak topology.

Suppose now $\mathbf{C}=\lim_{i\to\infty}V_{i}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ . We now compute its first variation as varifolds in Euclidean space $(T_{x}\widetilde{M},\delta)$ using (3.1) as follows: suppose $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ with $\operatorname{spt}X\subset B^{\delta}_{R}(0)$ , then for all sufficiently large $i$ we have

$$ \delta V_{i}(X)=\int_{G(B^{\delta}_{R}(0))}(\operatorname{div}_{T}^{\delta}X)(p)\;dV_{i}(p,T)=\frac{1}{r_{i}^{n-1}}\int_{G(B^{\delta}_{Rr_{i}}(0))}(\operatorname{div}^{\delta}_{T}X)(r_{i}^{-1}q)\;d\overline{V}(q,T) $$

$$ =\frac{1}{r_{i}^{n-2}}\int_{G(B^{\delta}_{Rr_{i}}(0))}\operatorname{div}^{g}_{T}\left(X(r_{i}^{-1}q)\right)\;d\overline{V}(q,T)-\frac{1}{r_{i}^{n-2}}\int_{G(B^{\delta}_{Rr_{i}}(0))}(\operatorname{div}^{g}_{T}-\operatorname{div}^{\delta}_{T})\left(X(r_{i}^{-1}q)\right)\;d\overline{V}(q,T) $$

where $\overline{V}:=(\exp^{-1}_{x})_{\sharp}V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ 1010 10 Again, $\overline{V}$ is more precisely a varifold in some open neighbourhood of $0$ .. By the definition of pushforward of varifolds, we have $d\overline{V}(q,T)=J_{S}(\exp^{-1}_{x})(y)\;dV(y,S)$ where $q=\exp^{-1}_{x}(y)$ , $T=(d\exp^{-1}_{x})|_{y}(S)$ , and $J_{S}(\exp^{-1}_{x})(y):=\sqrt{\det\left((d\exp^{-1}_{x}|_{S})^{*}\circ(d\exp^{-1}_{x}|_{S})\right)}(y)$ is the Jacobian factor of $\exp_{x}^{-1}$ relative to $S$ . It then follows from (3.25) that for all $i$ sufficiently large

$$ \left|\operatorname{div}^{g}_{T}\left(X(r_{i}^{-1}q)\right)\right|\leq 2\left(|q||X(r_{i}^{-1}q)|+r_{i}^{-1}|DX(r_{i}^{-1}q)|\right), $$

$$ \left|(\operatorname{div}^{g}_{T}-\operatorname{div}^{\delta}_{T})\left(X(r_{i}^{-1}q)\right)\right|\leq C(n,k_{0})\left(|q||X(r_{i}^{-1}q)|+|q|^{2}r_{i}^{-1}|DX(r_{i}^{-1}q)|\right). $$

Combining these estimate with (3.27), we see that

$$ |\delta V_{i}(X)-r_{i}^{-(n-2)}\delta V(X_{i})|\leq C(n,k_{0})r_{i}\int\left(r_{i}|p||X(p)|+|p||DX(p)|\right)\;d\|V_{i}\|(p) $$

where $X_{i}:=d(\exp_{x})(X\circ\eta_{0,r_{i}})\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ is supported inside $B_{Rr_{i}}(x)=\exp_{x}(B^{\delta}_{Rr_{i}}(0))$ for all large $i$ . Note that $V_{i}$ may not have locally bounded first variation in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ due to the term involving $DX$ . On the other hand, using (3.5), we have

$$ r_{i}^{-(n-2)}\delta V(X_{i})=-\frac{1}{r_{i}^{n-1}}\int_{\partial\Omega}X_{i}\cdot(r_{i}H^{tan}_{V}+r_{i}H_{\partial\Omega})\;d\|V\|+\frac{1}{r_{i}^{n-2}}\int_{\partial\Omega}X_{i}\cdot\nu\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing}. $$

By (2.3) and (3.27), we have for all sufficiently large $i$ the following estimate for the first term on the right hand side above:

$$ \left|\frac{1}{r_{i}^{n-1}}\int_{\partial\Omega}X_{i}\cdot(r_{i}H^{tan}_{V}+r_{i}H_{\partial\Omega})\;d\|V\|\right|\leq C(n,\kappa_{0},\Lambda)r_{i}\int|X(p)|\;d\|V_{i}\|(p). $$

For the second term, if we further assume that $X$ is tangential to $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , by (3.25) and (2.3), we have the estimate

$$ \|X_{i}\cdot\nu\|_{L^{\infty}(B_{Rr_{i}}(x))}\leq C(\kappa_{0})Rr_{i}\left(R\|DX\|_{L^{\infty}(U_{C(\kappa_{0})R^{2}r_{i}}(T_{x}\partial\Omega))}+\|X\|_{L^{\infty}(U_{C(\kappa_{0})R^{2}r_{i}}(T_{x}\partial\Omega))}\right) $$

where $U_{h}(T_{x}\partial\Omega):=\{p\in T_{x}\widetilde{M}:\operatorname{dist}^{\delta}(p,T_{x}\partial\Omega)<h\}$ denotes the parallel slab of width $h$ around the hyperplane $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . Combining this with (3.8), we can estimate the second term as follow:

$$ \left|\frac{1}{r_{i}^{n-2}}\int_{\partial\Omega}X_{i}\cdot\nu\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing}\right|\leq C(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0},\Theta_{V}(x))R^{n-1}r_{i}\left(R\|DX\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|X\|_{L^{\infty}}\right). $$

Putting all these estimates together, (3.28) can be written as: for all sufficiently large $i$ , and $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ with $X$ is tangential to $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , $\operatorname{spt}X\subset B^{\delta}_{R}(0)$ , we have

$$ |\delta V_{i}(X)|\leq C(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0},\Lambda)r_{i}\int\left((1+r_{i}|p|)|X(p)|+|p||DX(p)|\right)\;d\|V_{i}\|(p) $$

$$ \hskip 56.9055pt+C(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0},\Theta_{V}(x))R^{n-1}r_{i}\left(R\|DX\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|X\|_{L^{\infty}}\right) $$

where the $L^{\infty}$ norms on the right hand side are taken in the slab $U_{C(\kappa_{0})R^{2}r_{i}}(T_{x}\partial\Omega)$ as before.

The estimate (3.29) on the first variation of $V_{i}$ implies that

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\delta V_{i}(X)=0\quad\text{$\forall X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ tangential to $T_{x}\partial\Omega$.} $$

By the continuity of first variation with respect to varifold convergence, we conclude that $\mathbf{C}$ is free boundary stationary with free boundary on $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . Moreover, as $\operatorname{spt}\|\overline{V}\|\subset\exp_{x}^{-1}(\overline{\Omega})$ and $\eta_{0,r_{i}}(\exp^{-1}_{x}(\Omega))$ converges locally in Hausdorff topology to $T^{+}_{x}\widetilde{M}$ , it is clear that $\operatorname{spt}\|C\|\subset T^{+}_{x}\widetilde{M}$ .

Next, we move on to the assertions in (ii) and (iii). Because of (3.27), $\Theta_{\overline{V}}(0)$ exists and is equal to $\Theta_{V}(x)$ . As $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(\overline{V},0)$ , standard arguments (c.f. [55, Section 42]) shows that

$$ \frac{\|\mathbf{C}\|(B_{R}(0))}{\omega_{n-1}R^{n-1}}\equiv\Theta_{V}(x)\quad\text{for all $R>0$}. $$

Recall that $\mathbf{C}$ is free boundary stationary in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ with free boundary on the hyperplane $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , we therefore conclude from the monotonicity formula that $\|\mathbf{C}\|$ is a cone centred at $0$ . This proves (ii). Finally, (iii) is a direct consequence of (i) and (ii) because of the scaling of first variation [4, Remark 4.12(1)] and $\|\delta\mathbf{C}\|=\|\delta\mathbf{C}\|_{sing}$ .

To establish the other assertions in the proposition, it remains to show that $\mathbf{C}$ is rectifiable (resp. integral) under the assumption that $V$ is rectifiable (resp. integral) satisfying (3.24). First of all, notice that we cannot apply the standard compactness theorem for rectifiable or integral varifolds as $V_{i}$ does not have locally bounded variation due to the terms involving $DX$ on the right hand side of (3.29). To get around this difficulty, we first note that since $V\in\mathbf{RV}_{n-1}(U)$ is free boundary stationary with uniform density lower bound (3.24), by Remark 3.15 and (3.21) therein, we have the following uniform density ratio bounds at the geometric level:

$$ \frac{1}{C_{6}}\leq\frac{\|V\|(B_{\rho}(y))}{\rho^{n-1}}\leq C_{6}\frac{\|V\|(B_{R_{y}}(y))}{R_{y}^{n-1}} $$

for all $y\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap B_{d_{x}/2}(x)$ provided that $0<\rho<R_{y}:=\min\{R_{6},d_{x}/2\}$ when $y\in\partial\Omega$ ; and $0<\rho<R_{y}:=\min\{R_{6},d_{x}/2,\operatorname{dist}_{g}(y,\partial\Omega)\}$ when $y\in\Omega$ . Here, $d_{x}:=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial U)>0$ . It is important to keep in mind that $C_{6},R_{6}$ are positive constants depending only on the ambient geometric quantities $n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0}$ and $\Lambda$ but not on $V$ and $y$ . These estimates pass to the level of geodesic normal coordinates (due to (3.26), (3.27) and the fact that uniform density ratio bounds are bi-Lipschitz invariant) to yield for any fixed $R>0$ and all sufficiently large $i$ ,

$$ \frac{1}{2C_{6}}\leq\frac{\|V_{i}\|(B^{\delta}_{\rho}(p_{i}))}{\rho^{n-1}}\leq 2C_{6}\frac{\|V_{i}\|(B^{\delta}_{R_{p_{i}}}(p_{i}))}{R_{p_{i}}^{n-1}} $$

for all $p_{i}\in\operatorname{spt}\|V_{i}\|\cap B^{\delta}_{R}(0)$ provided that $0<\rho<R_{p_{i}}:=R$ when $p_{i}\in\eta_{0,r_{i}}(\exp_{x}^{-1}(\partial\Omega))$ ; and $0<\rho<R_{p_{i}}:=\min\{R,\operatorname{dist}_{\delta}(p_{i},\eta_{0,r_{i}}(\exp_{x}^{-1}(\partial\Omega)))\}$ when $p_{i}\in\eta_{0,r_{i}}(\exp_{x}^{-1}\Omega)$ . Recall the elementary observation that density is preserved under $C^{1}$ -diffeomorphism, we have $\Theta_{V_{i}}$ exists everywhere in $B^{\delta}_{R}(0)$ and $\Theta_{V_{i}}(p_{i})\geq\frac{1}{2}$ for every $p_{i}\in\operatorname{spt}\|V_{i}\|\cap B^{\delta}_{R}(0)$ because of (3.20).

We now argue that the uniform density ratio bounds (with slightly different constants) pass on to the tangent varifold $\mathbf{C}=\lim_{i\to\infty}\|V_{i}\|$ . Let $p\in\operatorname{spt}\|C\|$ , it is clear from definition that there exists $p_{i}\in\operatorname{spt}\|V_{i}\|$ such that $p_{i}\to p$ . Since $\operatorname{spt}\|C\|\subset T^{+}_{x}\widetilde{M}$ , either $p$ is an interior point, i.e. $p\notin T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , or $p$ is a boundary point, i.e. $p\in T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . For an interior point $p\notin T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , the approximating sequence $p_{i}\in\operatorname{spt}\|V_{i}\|$ will also be interior points for all sufficiently large $i$ . Applying the interior case of (3.31), we have for such $p$ the following density ratio lower bound

$$ \frac{\|\mathbf{C}\|(B_{\rho}^{\delta}(p))}{\rho^{n-1}}\geq\frac{1}{4^{n}C_{6}}>0 $$

provided that $0<\rho<\min\{R,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{dist}_{\delta}(p,T_{x}\partial\Omega)\}$ . Since $\mathbf{C}$ is free boundary stationary, the density $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}$ exists everywhere and letting $\rho\to 0$ in the above inequality implies that $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)\geq\frac{1}{4^{n}\omega_{n-1}C_{6}}>0$ for all interior points $p\in\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\setminus T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . Suppose now $p\in\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\cap T_{x}\partial\Omega$ is a boundary point. If there are infinitely many $p_{i}$ in the approximating sequence that lies on the boundary $\eta_{0,r_{i}}(\exp_{x}^{-1}\Omega)$ , then the same argument as above gives the same density lower bound for such $p$ . It remains to treat the remaining case for those $p\in\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\cap T_{x}\partial\Omega$ but there exists some $r>0$ with $\operatorname{spt}\|V_{i}\|\cap B^{\delta}_{r}(p)$ contained in the interior $\exp_{x}^{-1}(\Omega)$ for all sufficiently large $i$ . Going back to the geometric setting, it means that $V$ indeed has empty free boundary and hence we are once again reduced to the interior situation which has been treated before1111 11 More precisely, in this case although $\operatorname{dist}_{\delta}(p_{i},\eta_{0,r_{i}}(\exp_{x}^{-1}\Omega))\to 0$ , we can still obtain (3.31) with $R_{p_{i}}$ replaced by a fixed $R_{0}>0$ independent of $i$ .. Finally, since $\mathbf{C}\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ is free boundary stationary with free boundary in $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ (hence $\mathbf{C}$ has locally bounded first variation in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ ) and its density exists and has a fixed positive lower bound everywhere in $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|$ , we can apply Allard’s Rectifiability Theorem [4, 5.5(1)] to conclude that $\mathbf{C}\in\mathbf{RV}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ . Once we know that $\mathbf{C}$ is rectifiable and is free boundary stationary in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ with free boundary on the hyperplane $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , standard arguments (c.f. [55, Section 42]) show that $\mathbf{C}$ is a varifold cone centred at $0$ .

We now show that $\mathbf{C}$ is integral, i.e. $\mathbf{C}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ , if $V$ is integral. In other words, we need to show that $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)\in\mathbb{N}$ for $\|\mathbf{C}\|$ -a.e. $p\in\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|$ . First we address the interior points, i.e. $p\in\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\setminus T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . Since we already know that $\mathbf{C}$ is rectifiable, we can assume without loss of generality that $\|\mathbf{C}\|$ has an approximate tangent space $T_{p}\mathbf{C}\in\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ at $p$ in the sense that

$$ \lim_{s\to 0}s^{-(n-1)}(\eta_{p,s})_{\sharp}\|\mathbf{C}\|=\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}T_{p}\mathbf{C} $$

as Radon measures in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ . Our goal is to show that $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)\in\mathbb{N}$ .

Since $\lim_{i\to\infty}V_{i}=\mathbf{C}$ as varifolds, we also have $\lim_{i\to\infty}\|V_{i}\|=\|\mathbf{C}\|$ and therefore we can fix some sequence $s_{i}\to 0$ and then, after passing to a subsequence, assume that

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}r_{i}s_{i}^{-1}=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lim_{i\to\infty}(\eta_{p,s_{i}})_{\sharp}V_{i}=\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)|T_{p}\mathbf{C}| $$

as varifolds in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ . Again, although each $W_{i}:=(\eta_{p,s_{i}})_{\sharp}V_{i}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ , we cannot apply the compactness theorem for integral varifolds in [4, Theorem 6.4] to conclude that the limit is integral since $(\eta_{p,s_{i}})_{\sharp}V_{i}$ a-priori do not have locally bounded first variation. Instead, we will proceed as in the proof of [4, Theorem 6.4]. Since all the $W_{i}$ satisfy uniform density ratio bounds as in (3.31), we have $\operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|$ converges to $T_{p}\mathbf{C}$ locally in Hausdorff topology (c.f. [53, Remark 10]). Let $\pi:T_{x}\widetilde{M}\to T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ denote the orthogonal projection onto $T_{p}\mathbf{C}$ . Then, we have from (3.32) and the rectifiability of $W_{i}$ that after projecting $W_{i}$ inside the slab $U_{\epsilon}(T_{p}\mathbf{C}):=\{q\in T_{x}\widetilde{M}:|q-\pi(q)|<\epsilon\}$ of width $\epsilon>0$ (to be fixed later) we have

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\pi_{\sharp}(W_{i}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}G(U_{\epsilon}(T_{p}\mathbf{C})))=\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)|T_{p}\mathbf{C}|. $$

Since $W_{i}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ , after possibly re-defining on a set of $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$ -measure zero, we consider the $L^{1}_{loc}$ function $\psi^{\epsilon}_{i}:T_{p}\mathbf{C}\to\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$ defined by

$$ \psi^{\epsilon}_{i}(q)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\tilde{q}\in\operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|\cap U_{\epsilon}(T_{p}\mathbf{C})\\
\pi(\tilde{q})=q\end{subarray}}\Theta_{W_{i}}(\tilde{q}) $$

converges weakly in $L^{1}_{loc}(T_{p}\mathbf{C};\mathcal{H}^{n-1})$ to the constant function $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)$ . However, weak $L^{1}$ -convergence is not sufficient to conclude convergence almost everywhere. We need to upgrade it (after suitable truncation) to strong $L^{1}$ -convergence. This will be achieved by the following (c.f. [55, Lemma 42.9])

Claim: For any $\gamma\in(0,1)$ , there exists $\epsilon=\epsilon(\gamma)>0$ such that for any sufficiently large $i$ , there exists $A_{i}\subset B^{\delta}_{1}(0)\cap T_{p}\mathbf{C}$ with $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(A_{i})<\gamma$ such that for every $q\in(B^{\delta}_{1}(0)\cap T_{p}\mathbf{C})\setminus A_{i}$ , we have

$$ \psi^{\epsilon}_{i}(q)\leq(1+\gamma)\frac{\|W_{i}\|(B^{\delta}_{2}(q))}{\omega_{n-1}2^{n}}+\gamma. $$

We first see how the claim implies $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)\in\mathbb{N}$ . Choose any sequence $\gamma_{i}\to 0$ , there exists $\epsilon_{i}\to 0$ and, after passing to a subsequence, there exists $A_{i}\subset B^{\delta}_{1}(0)\cap T_{p}\mathbf{C}$ with $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(A_{i})\to 0$ such that by (3.32)

$$ \psi^{\epsilon_{i}}_{i}(q)\leq\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)+\frac{1}{i}\quad\text{for all $q\in(B^{\delta}_{1}(0)\cap T_{p}\mathbf{C})\setminus A_{i}$.} $$

Hence, for any positive integer $N>\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)$ , the integer-valued function $\max\{\psi^{\epsilon_{i}}_{i},N\}$ converges strongly in $L^{1}(B^{\delta}_{1}(0)\cap T_{p}\mathbf{C};\mathcal{H}^{n-1})$ to $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)$ . By taking a subsequence that converges $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$ -a.e. in $B^{\delta}_{1}(0)\cap T_{p}\mathbf{C}$ , we conclude that $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)\in\mathbb{N}$ .

It remains to establish the claim above. Fix $\gamma\in(0,1)$ . We will follow the arguments in [55, Lemma 42.9] with the caveat that $W_{i}$ does not have locally bounded first variation. First of all, we observe that by (3.32), for all sufficiently large $i$ we have

$$ \|W_{i}\|(B^{\delta}_{4}(0))\leq 5^{n-1}\omega_{n-1}\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p). $$

Therefore, $W_{i}$ have uniformly bounded mass in $B^{\delta}_{4}(0)$ . Moreover, (3.32) also implies the $L^{1}$ -tilt excess for $W_{i}$ in $B^{\delta}_{4}(0)$ converges to zero, i.e.

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\int_{G(B^{\delta}_{4}(0))}\|S-T_{p}\mathbf{C}\|\;dW_{i}(q,S)=0. $$

For any $\tau>0$ , we now define the subset $A^{\tau}_{i}:=\pi(\tilde{A}^{\tau}_{i})\subset B^{\delta}_{1}(0)\cap T_{p}\mathbf{C}$ where

$$ \tilde{A}^{\tau}_{i}:=\left\{\tilde{q}\in\operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|\cap B^{\delta}_{2}(0)\;:\;\exists\rho\in(0,2)\text{ such that }\int_{G(B^{\delta}_{\rho}(q))}\|S-T_{p}\mathbf{C}\|\;dW_{i}(\tilde{q},S)>\tau\rho^{n-1}\right\}. $$

Since $W_{i}$ satisfies uniform density ratio bounds, by Besicovitch covering lemma [55, Lemma 4.6], we have the following estimate on the measure of $\tilde{A}^{\tau}_{i}$ :

$$ \|W_{i}\|(\tilde{A}^{\tau}_{i})\leq C(n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\Lambda)\tau^{-1}\int_{G(B^{\delta}_{4}(0))}\|S-T_{p}\mathbf{C}\|\;dW_{i}(q,S). $$

Since $W_{i}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ , this implies

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(A^{\tau}_{i})=0\quad\text{for any fixed $\tau>0$.} $$

Next, by the (interior) weighted monotonicity formula (3.23) applied to the original free boundary varifold $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ , together with (3.26), (3.27) and some scaling arguments as before, we see that for all sufficiently large $i$ , and any $q\in B^{\delta}_{1}(0)\setminus\tilde{A}^{\tau}_{i}$ (note that $q$ need not be in $\operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|$ ) and any $h>0$ ,

$$ \frac{\|W_{i}\|(U^{h}_{R_{1}}(q))}{\omega_{n-1}R_{1}^{n-1}}\leq(1+C(n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\Lambda)r_{i}s_{i}R_{2})\frac{\|W_{i}\|(U^{2h}_{R_{2}}(q))}{\omega_{n-1}R_{2}^{n-1}}+\frac{4}{3}\tau\left(\frac{R_{2}}{h}\right)^{n-1} $$

for any $0<R_{1}\leq R_{2}\leq 2$ . Here, we denote $U^{h}_{R}(q):=B^{\delta}_{R}(q)\cap\{p\in T_{x}\widetilde{M}:|N_{T_{p}\mathbf{C}}\cdot(p-q)|<h\}$ where $N_{T_{p}\mathbf{C}}$ is a unit vector orthogonal to $T_{p}\mathbf{C}$ . If furthermore $q\in\operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|$ , by letting $R_{1}\to 0$ and $R_{2}=h=2$ in (3.35), we obtain (note that $U^{2h}_{2}(q)\subset B^{\delta}_{2}(q)$ for any $h>0$ )

$$ \Theta_{W_{i}}(q)\leq(1+\gamma)\frac{\|W_{i}\|(B_{2}^{\delta}(q))}{\omega_{n-1}2^{n-1}}+\gamma $$

for all sufficiently large $i$ and sufficiently small $\tau$ (both depending on $\gamma$ besides the ambient constants $n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0}$ and $\Lambda$ but independent of $q$ ). This proves the claim in case there is only one $\tilde{q}\in\operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|\cap U_{\epsilon}(T_{p}\mathbf{C})$ such that $\pi(\tilde{q})=q\in(B^{\delta}_{1}(0)\cap T_{p}\mathbf{C})\setminus A_{i}$ (note that all such $\tilde{q}\in B^{\delta}_{2}(0)$ ) with $A_{i}=A_{i}^{\tau}$ .

We assert that for all sufficiently large $i$ (depending on $\tau$ and $n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\Lambda$ ), with $\epsilon=\tau^{\frac{1}{2(n-1)}}/2$ for any $\tau\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\|W_{i}\|(U^{h}_{R}(\tilde{q}_{j}))}{\omega_{n-1}R^{n-1}}\leq(1+C(n,N)\tau^{\frac{1}{2(n-1)}})\frac{\|W_{i}\|(B_{2}^{\delta}(0))}{\omega_{n-1}2^{n-1}}+C(n,N)\tau^{1/2} $$

provided that $h\leq\frac{1}{4}\min_{j\neq k}|\tilde{q}_{j}-\tilde{q}_{k}|$ and $R<\min\{2,\tau^{-\frac{1}{2(n-1)}}C(N)h\}$ .

To establish (3.36), we first note that by the interior monotonicity formula (Lemma 3.14), the same argument as before shows for any $q\in B^{\delta}_{1}(0)$ (again not necessarily inside $\operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|$ ), $0<R_{1}\leq R_{2}\leq 2$ , and all sufficiently large $i$ ,

$$ \frac{\|W_{i}\|(B^{\delta}_{R_{1}}(q))}{\omega_{n-1}R_{1}^{n-1}}\leq(1+C(n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\Lambda)r_{i}s_{i}R_{2})\frac{\|W_{i}\|(B^{\delta}_{R_{2}}(q))}{\omega_{n-1}R_{2}^{n-1}} $$

For the purpose of induction on $N$ in (3.36), note that when $N=1$ , it follows directly from (3.35) by setting $R_{1}=R_{2}=R$ , $C(1)=2$ , $\epsilon=1$ and using (3.37). Suppose now (3.36) holds up to $N-1$ . Consider now $N$ distinct $\tilde{q}_{1},\cdots,\tilde{q}_{N}\in\operatorname{spt}\|W_{i}\|\cap U_{\epsilon}(T_{p}\mathbf{C})$ such that $\pi(\tilde{q}_{j})=q\in(B^{\delta}_{1}(0)\cap T_{p}\mathbf{C})\setminus A^{\tau}_{i}$ for $j=1,\cdots,N$ . Set

$$ \hat{h}:=\min_{1\leq j\neq k\leq N}|\tilde{q}_{j}-\tilde{q}_{k}|\leq\frac{2\epsilon}{N-1}. $$
