#### Remark 3.18.

By (3.7), if $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\Omega\cap U$ (i.e. $x$ is an interior point), then the varifold $V$ is stationary in a neighbourhood of $x$ away from $\partial\Omega$ , and we can proceed with the same arguments above (cf. e.g. [55, §42]), so in particular $\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)\neq\emptyset$ and any $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ is an integer-rectifiable cone in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ , which is stationary in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ provided that $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ .

Let us record here a simple consequence of Proposition 3.17 and Lemma 3.12.

#### Corollary 3.19.

Let $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ be a varifold with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ , $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ and $\|H^{tan}_{V}\|_{L^{\infty}(U)}\leq\Lambda$ . Suppose $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ , where $x\in\partial\Omega$ , satisfies $\operatorname{spt}\|C\|\subset T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . Then, $\mathbf{C}=m|T_{x}\partial\Omega|$ for some positive $m\in\mathbb{R}$ in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ . If $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ , then $m\in\mathbb{N}$ .

#### Remark 3.20.

Note that some of the statements in this subsection hold in the more general setting of free boundary varifold with $H^{tan}_{V}\in L^{p}(U;\|V\|)$ for $p>n-1$ (see, for example, [20]).

### 3.3. Singular set and stratification

In order to analyse the fine properties of the singularities of an integral free boundary stationary (or more generally, $\|H^{tan}_{V}\|_{L^{\infty}(U)}\leq\Lambda$ ) varifold $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ , we need some further properties about the general structure of the singular set. In particular, we need to know that the singular set can be divided into different strata according to the maximal dimension of translation invariance for their tangent cones. We begin with a precise definition of the singular set.

#### Definition 3.21 (Regular and singular set).

Let $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ be an integral free boundary stationary varifold in $\Omega\cap U$ with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ . We define the regular set $\operatorname{reg}(V)$ of $V$ to be

$$ \operatorname{reg}(V):=\bigg\{x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|:\begin{array}[]{l}\textrm{there exists $r>0$ such that $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap B_{r}(x)$ is an embedded}\\
\textrm{$C^{\infty}$ hypersurface with (possibly empty) boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$}\end{array}\bigg\}. $$

Moreover, we define its complement to be the singular set $\operatorname{sing}(V)$ of $V$ by

$$ \operatorname{sing}(V):=\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\setminus\operatorname{reg}(V). $$

The singular set can be further subdivided into its boundary part

$$ \operatorname{sing}_{b}(V)\coloneqq\operatorname{sing}(V)\cap\partial\Omega, $$

and its interior part

$$ \operatorname{sing}_{i}(V)\coloneqq\operatorname{sing}(V)\cap\Omega. $$

#### Remark 3.22.

Note that by definition, $\operatorname{reg}(V)$ is a relatively open subset of $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ . Hence, $\operatorname{sing}(V)$ is a relatively closed subset of $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ . However, while $\operatorname{sing}_{b}(V)$ is also a relatively closed subset, $\operatorname{sing}_{i}(V)$ may not be. This simple but subtle observation is important in our analysis to follow.

The most fundamental result in the general varifold setting is Allard’s Regularity Theorem [4, Theorem 8.19]. Together with the free boundary version in [28, Theorem 4.13] (see also [52] and [1]) in the intrinsic Riemannian setting), we can state it for our purpose as the following $\epsilon$ -regularity result in terms of the reflected density defined in (3.19).

#### Proposition 3.23 (Consequence of Allard regularity - Density gap).

There exists a small constant $\epsilon=\epsilon(n)\in(0,1)$ such that the following holds: given any free boundary stationary integral varifold $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ , we have

$$ \{x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|:1\leq\overline{\Theta}_{V}(x)<1+\epsilon\}\subset\operatorname{reg}(V). $$

In other words, any singular point must have reflected density $\geq 1+\epsilon$ . As a consequence, $\operatorname{reg}(V)$ is an open and dense subset of $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ .

#### Remark 3.24.

In particular, if an interior point $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\Omega$ has a tangent cone which is a multiplicity one plane, then $\overline{\Theta}_{V}(x)=\Theta_{V}(x)=1$ and thus $B_{r}(x)\cap\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ is a smoothly embedded minimal hypersurface without boundary for some $r>0$ . On the other hand, if a boundary point $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\partial\Omega$ has a tangent cone which is a multiplicity one half-plane orthogonal to $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , then $\overline{\Theta}_{V}(x)=2\Theta_{V}(x)=1$ and thus $B_{r}(x)\cap\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ is a smoothly embedded minimal hypersurface with non-empty free boundary lying on $\partial\Omega\cap U$ for some $r>0$ .

Not much is known beyond the above $\epsilon$ -regularity without further assumptions (such as stability or multiplicity-one for certain tangent cones). However, there is also a very general result known as Almgren-Federer stratification, due to [24] and [7], that plays a key role in the singularity analysis of general stationary integral varifolds. The basic idea is to sub-divide the singular set into different stratum according to the order of symmetry (with respect to translations) for all possible tangent cones that can occur. We now describe this stratification procedure, paying special attention to the boundary behaviour. First, we recall some definitions and notation about varifold cones (not necessarily arising from tangent cones) inside Euclidean space.

#### Definition 3.25 (Spine of a cone).

Let $\mathbf{C}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ be an integer-rectifiable cone (in the sense that $(\eta_{0,r})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}$ for all $r>0$ ). We define the spine $S(\mathbf{C})$ of $\mathbf{C}$ to be the translation invariance set of $\mathbf{C}$ , namely

$$ S(\mathbf{C})\coloneqq\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:(\eta_{p,1})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}\}. $$

It is clear from the definition that the spine $S(\mathbf{C})$ is always a linear subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with dimension less than or equal to $n-1$ . In the case of free boundary cones contained inside the Euclidean half-space $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ (recall the paragraph containing (2.7)), we have the following useful characterization of the spine.

#### Lemma 3.26.

Let $\mathbf{C}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ be an integer-rectifiable cone with free boundary in $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . Then $S(\mathbf{C})$ is a linear subspace contained in $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . In particular,

$$ S(\mathbf{C})=\{p\in\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\;:\;(\eta_{p,1})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}\}. $$

Consequently, we have $(\eta_{p,1})_{\sharp}\|\delta\mathbf{C}\|_{sing}=\|\delta\mathbf{C}\|_{sing}$ for all $p\in S(\mathbf{C})$ .

#### Proof.

It suffices to show that $S(\mathbf{C})$ is actually contained inside the hyperplane $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . It follows from the simple observation $S(\mathbf{C})\subset\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|$ (as $0\in\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|$ since $\mathbf{C}$ is a cone) and the assumption that $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . Hence, being a subspace lying inside the half-space forces $S(\mathbf{C})\subset\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . The last assertion follows readily from Proposition 3.6. ∎

Let us now focus on the special situation of cones $\mathbf{C}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ that arise as tangent cones to a free boundary stationary integral varifold $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\Omega\cap U$ . Fix $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ . By Proposition 3.17 and Remark 3.18, $\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)\neq\emptyset$ , and any element $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ is an integral cone $\mathbf{C}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(T_{p}\widetilde{M})$ which is either stationary in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ when $x\in\Omega\cap U$ is an interior point; or free boundary stationary in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ with free boundary in $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\subset T^{+}_{x}\widetilde{M}$ when $x\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ is a boundary point. By Lemma 3.10, in the latter case, the doubled-cone $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ is a stationary cone in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ and its density function $\Theta_{\overline{\mathbf{C}}}$ coincides exactly with the reflected density function of $\mathbf{C}$ (recall (3.19)):

$$ \Theta_{\overline{\mathbf{C}}}=\overline{\Theta}_{\mathbf{C}}. $$

Moreover, the spine of the original tangent cone $\mathbf{C}$ and its doubled-cone $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ are related as follows:

$$ S(\mathbf{C})=S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\cap T_{x}\partial\Omega. $$

To see this, just note that the translation $\eta_{p,1}$ and the reflection $\theta_{-\nu}$ (recall (2.7)) commutes with each other when $p\in T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . This implies $S(\mathbf{C})\subset S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\cap T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . To see the other inclusion $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\cap T_{x}\partial\Omega\subset S(\mathbf{C})$ , take any $p\in S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\cap T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . By the definition of spine and commutativity of $\eta_{p,1}$ and $\theta_{-\nu}$ , we have

$$ \mathbf{C}+(\theta_{-\nu})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}=\overline{\mathbf{C}}=(\eta_{p,1})_{\sharp}\overline{\mathbf{C}}=(\eta_{p,1})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}+(\theta_{-\nu})_{\sharp}((\eta_{p,1})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}). $$

Note that $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\subset T_{x}^{+}\widetilde{M}$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|(\theta_{-\nu})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}\|\subset\theta_{-\nu}(T_{x}^{+}\widetilde{M})$ . If $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|$ is not contained in $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , then we must have $\mathbf{C}=(\eta_{p,1})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}$ , i.e. $p\in S(\mathbf{C})$ . If $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\subset T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , then $\mathbf{C}=m|T_{x}\partial\Omega|$ for some $m\in\mathbb{N}$ by Lemma 3.12 and thus $\mathbf{C}=(\eta_{p,1})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}$ as well. This verifies (3.47).

Next, we observe another useful dichotomy property of the spine with respect to $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ :

$$ \text{Either}\qquad S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\subset T_{x}\partial\Omega\qquad\text{ or }\qquad S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\perp T_{x}\partial\Omega. $$

If $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\subset T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , then (3.47) implies $S(\mathbf{C})=S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})$ . If $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\perp T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , then $\nu\in S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})$ and we have an orthogonal splitting $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})=S(\mathbf{C})\times\mathbb{R}\nu$ . To see why (3.49) is true, since by definition $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ is invariant under reflection, i.e. $(\theta_{-\nu})_{\sharp}\overline{\mathbf{C}}=\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ , we clearly have the spine $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})$ is also invariant under reflection.

It is well-known (see e.g. [62, Section 4]) that for a stationary integral cone $\mathbf{C}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , the spine can also be characterized as the set of points of maximal density which is equal to $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(0)$ (by the upper semi-continuity of density and that $\mathbf{C}$ is a cone), i.e.

$$ S(\mathbf{C})=\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\;:\;\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)=\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(0)\}. $$

For free boundary stationary integral cones $\mathbf{C}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ , we also have the same characterization (c.f. [20, Lemma 5.6]):

$$ S(\mathbf{C})=\{p\in\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\;:\;\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(p)=\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(0)\}. $$

In fact, the translation invariance along the spine gives a useful “dimension-reduction” argument known as cone splitting. In the case of a stationary integral cone $\mathbf{C}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , we know that up to a rotation the cone splits as follow:

$$ \mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}_{0}\times\mathbb{R}^{\dim(S(\mathbf{C}))} $$

where $\mathbf{C}_{0}$ is a stationary integral cone of dimension $n-1-\dim(S(\mathbf{C}))$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n-\dim(S(\mathbf{C}))}$ . In the case of a free boundary stationary integral cone $\mathbf{C}$ contained inside a half-space $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ , the same cone splitting applies to the doubled cone $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ . However, the dimension of the $\mathbb{R}$ -factor may be different as we have $\dim S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})=\dim S(\mathbf{C})+1$ in the second case of (3.49).

We now describe the Almgren-Federer stratification adapted to the free boundary setting. The key idea is again to sub-divide the singular set according to the maximal spine dimension of all possible tangent cones at a singular point. One has to be careful at a boundary singular point as the spine dimension could be different for the cone and its doubled cone. In order to give a unified statement that works for both interior and boundary singular points, we introduce the notion of modified cone in the definition below.

#### Definition 3.27.

Let $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ be a free boundary stationary varifold with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ . For each $j\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ , we define the $j$ -stratum $\mathcal{S}_{j}$ of the singular set as follows:

$$ \mathcal{S}_{j}:=\{x\in\operatorname{sing}(V)\;:\;\dim S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}})\leq j\text{ for all }\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)\} $$

where for each tangent cone $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ , the modified cone $\widehat{\mathbf{C}}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(T_{x}\widetilde{M})$ is defined as

$$ \widehat{\mathbf{C}}:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\mathbf{C}&\text{if $x\in\Omega$,}\\
\mathbf{C}+(\theta_{-\nu(x)})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}&\text{if $x\in\partial\Omega$.}\end{array}\right. $$

In other words, $\widehat{\mathbf{C}}$ is either the cone $\mathbf{C}$ itself or the doubled cone $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ depending on whether the cone is based at an interior or a boundary point $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ . Note that in either case $\widehat{\mathbf{C}}$ is stationary (without free boundary!) in $T_{p}\widetilde{M}$ and $\Theta_{\widehat{\mathbf{C}}}(0)=\overline{\Theta}_{V}(x)$ . From the definition we clearly have

$$ \mathcal{S}_{0}\subset\mathcal{S}_{1}\subset\dots\subset\mathcal{S}_{n-1}=\operatorname{sing}(V). $$

For each stratum $\mathcal{S}_{j}$ , it is useful to define the following subset of $\mathcal{S}_{j}$ :

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{j}:=\mathcal{S}_{j}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{j-1}=\left\{x\in\operatorname{sing}(V)\;:\;\max_{\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)}\dim(S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}}))=j\right\}. $$

#### Example 3.28 (Classical boundary tangent cones).

Consider the following union of two half-planes

$$ V_{1}=|\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\;:\;|x|=|y|\text{ and }y\geq 0\}|\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) $$

which is a free boundary stationary varifold contained in the half-space $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ , in this case we have

$$ \operatorname{sing}(V_{1})=\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{n-2}=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2}. $$

Perhaps a more interesting example is

$$ V_{2}=\left(2|\{(x,y):y=\sqrt{3}x,\;y\geq 0\}|+|\{(x,y):x\leq 0,\;y=0\}|\right)\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) $$

which is also a free boundary stationary varifold in the half-space $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ , in this case we still have

$$ \operatorname{sing}(V_{2})=\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{n-2}=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2}. $$

#### Remark 3.29.

Before we state the main result (Proposition 3.30) concerning estimates on the Hausdorff dimension of each stratum of the singular set, we first take a closer look at the $j$ -stratum for $j\geq n-3$ , which will be most relevant for use in our paper. In our discussions below, let $x\in\operatorname{sing}(V)$ and $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ . Recall that the modified cone $\widehat{\mathbf{C}}$ is always a stationary integral cone in $T_{p}\widetilde{M}$ by Proposition 3.17 and Lemma 3.10.

- (i) If $\dim(S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}}))=n-1$ (i.e. $x\in\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{n-1}$ ), then the classical constancy theorem says that $\widehat{\mathbf{C}}=m|P|$ for some hyperplane $P\in\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ and $m\in\mathbb{N}$ . In fact, $m\geq 2$ by Allard’s regularity (Proposition 3.23). If $x\in\operatorname{sing}_{i}(V)$ is an interior singular point, then clearly $\mathbf{C}=m|P|$ . If $x\in\operatorname{sing}_{b}(V)$ is a boundary singular point, then we have the following dichotomy: • either $P=T_{x}\partial\Omega$ and $\mathbf{C}=m|T_{x}\partial\Omega|$ for some $m\in\mathbb{N}$ (possibly $m=1$ ); • or $P\perp T_{x}\partial\Omega$ and $\mathbf{C}=m|P_{+}|$ for some $m\in\mathbb{N}$ with $m\geq 2$ and $P_{+}:=P\cap T^{+}_{x}\widetilde{M}$ .

- (ii) If $\dim(S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}}))=n-2$ , then by (3.52) we have up to rotations the splitting (3.57)

$$ \widehat{\mathbf{C}}=\widehat{\mathbf{C}}_{0}\times S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}})\cong\widehat{\mathbf{C}}_{0}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2}, $$

where $\widehat{\mathbf{C}}_{0}$ is a $1$ -dimensional stationary integral cone in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ . By [3], $\widehat{\mathbf{C}}_{0}$ consists of a finite union of rays emanating from the origin, each ray is counted with integer multiplicities satisfying the stationarity condition at the origin. Cones of the form (3.57) are often referred to in the literature (c.f. [63]) as (interior) classical tangent cones. If $x\in\operatorname{sing}_{i}(V)$ is an interior singular point, then $\widehat{\mathbf{C}}_{0}$ must consist of at least three rays. If $x\in\operatorname{sing}_{b}(V)$ is a boundary singular point, then we have the following dichotomy by (3.49): • either $S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}})=S(\mathbf{C})\subset T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , in which case (3.58)

$$ \mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}_{0}\times S(\mathbf{C}) $$

where $\mathbf{C}_{0}$ is a $1$ -dimensional free boundary stationary integral cone contained in the plane $\mathbb{R}^{2}\cong\operatorname{span}\{\nu(x),e\}$ with $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}_{0}\|\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}$ . Here, $e\in T_{x}\partial\Omega$ is a unit vector perpendicular to $S(\mathbf{C})$ and $\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}:=\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{2}:p\cdot\nu(x)\leq 0\}$ . We shall refer to cones of the form (3.58) as boundary classical tangent cone. • or $S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}})\perp T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , in which case $S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}})=S(\mathbf{C})\times\mathbb{R}\nu(x)$ so $\dim(S(\mathbf{C}))=n-3$ . In fact, (3.59)

$$ \mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}_{0}\times S(\mathbf{C})\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\nu(x) $$

where $\mathbb{R}_{+}\nu(x)$ denotes the ray $\{-r\nu(x):r\geq 0\}$ along $-\nu(x)$ that points into $\Omega$ , and $\mathbf{C}_{0}$ is a $1$ -dimensional stationary (without free boundary!) integral cone contained in a $2$ -dimensional subspace of $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . We shall refer to cones of the form (3.59) half classical tangent cone.

The usefulness of such stratification is due to the following fundamental result on the size of the $j$ -stratum of the singular set, which was first proved by Almgren [7] in the setting of area-minimizing currents.

#### Proposition 3.30.

Let $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ be a free boundary stationary integral varifold with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ . Then, for all $j\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$

$$ \dim_{\mathcal{H}}\mathcal{S}_{j}\leq j, $$

where $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}$ denotes the Hausdorff dimension.

#### Proof.

The proof is essentially the same as in the interior case (see e.g. [62, Theorem 4]). We shall follow the same structure as in [56, §3.4], where an analogous result is proved in the context of energy-minimizing harmonic maps.

The interior stratification theorem gives $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathcal{S}_{j}\cap\Omega\cap U)\leq j$ : indeed, $V$ is stationary in each ball compactly contained in $\Omega\cap U$ , and we can cover $\Omega\cap U$ by countably many such balls. It therefore remains to prove $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathcal{S}_{j}\cap\partial\Omega\cap U)\leq j$ .

Let us fix $j\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ and $\epsilon>0$ . We shall say that a subset $A\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ has the $\epsilon$ -approximation property if there exists some $\rho_{0}>0$ such that for all $y\in A$ and $\rho\in(0,\rho_{0}]$ , there is a $j$ -dimensional subspace $W_{y,\rho}$ of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ such that

$$ \eta_{y,\rho}(A\cap B_{\rho}(y))\subset U_{\epsilon}(W_{y,\rho}) $$

where $\eta_{y,\rho}$ denotes the homothety map in (2.6) and $U_{\epsilon}(W_{y,\rho})$ denotes the $\epsilon$ -open neighbourhood of $W_{y,\rho}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . By [56, §3.4, Lemma 3], there exists a positive function $\beta:(0,+\infty)\to(0,+\infty)$ such that $\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\beta(\epsilon)=0$ and $\mathcal{H}^{j+\beta(\epsilon)}(A)=0$ whenever $A\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfies the $\epsilon$ -approximation property.

Thus, it suffices to cover $\mathcal{S}_{j}\cap\partial\Omega\cap U$ , in local coordinates, by countably many sets with the $C\epsilon$ -approximation property, where $C$ is independent of $\epsilon$ . We use ambient geodesic normal coordinates throughout; the transfer to fixed coordinate charts is justified in Step 2. The main arguments can be divided into two steps.

Step 1: Show that the “good density” points accumulate around a $j$ -dimensional subspace.

Take any $x\in\mathcal{S}_{j}\cap\partial\Omega\cap U$ . We claim that there exists $\overline{\rho}=\overline{\rho}(x,\epsilon,V)\in(0,i_{0}/2)$ , with $B_{\overline{\rho}}(x)\subset U$ , such that for all $\rho\in(0,\overline{\rho}]$ there exists a $j$ -dimensional subspace $W_{x,\rho}\subset T_{x}\partial\Omega$ such that

$$ \eta_{0,\rho}\left(\exp_{x}^{-1}(\{y\in B_{\rho}(x)\cap\partial\Omega:\Theta_{V}(y)\geq\Theta_{V}(x)-\overline{\rho}\})\right)\subset U_{\epsilon}(W_{x,\rho}). $$

Here $U_{\epsilon}(W_{x,\rho})$ is the neighbourhood in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ , as above; the image of $\partial\Omega$ under $\exp_{x}^{-1}$ need not lie in $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ .

We will establish the claim by contradiction. Suppose the claim is false. Then there exist $x\in\mathcal{S}_{j}\cap\partial\Omega\cap U$ and sequences $\overline{\rho}_{i}\to 0$ and $\rho_{i}\in(0,\overline{\rho}_{i}]$ such that for each $i$

$$ \eta_{0,\rho_{i}}\left(\exp_{x}^{-1}(\{y\in B_{\rho_{i}}(x)\cap\partial\Omega:\Theta_{V}(y)\geq\Theta_{V}(x)-\overline{\rho}_{i}\})\right)\not\subset U_{\epsilon}(W) $$

for any $j$ -dimensional subspace $W\subset T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . Up to passing to a subsequence, we can assume that $V_{i}:=(\eta_{0,\rho_{i}})_{\sharp}(\exp_{x}^{-1})_{\sharp}V\to\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ as varifolds. Since $x\in\mathcal{S}_{j}$ , we know that $\dim S(\widehat{\mathbf{C}})\leq j$ , and hence $\dim S(\mathbf{C})\leq j$ by (3.47). Choose a $j$ -dimensional subspace $W\subset T_{x}\partial\Omega$ containing $S(\mathbf{C})$ . By (3.63), there exist $y_{i}\in B_{\rho_{i}}(x)\cap\partial\Omega$ such that, with $q_{i}:=\eta_{0,\rho_{i}}(\exp_{x}^{-1}(y_{i}))\in B^{\delta}_{1}(0)$ , we have

$$ \Theta_{V}(y_{i})\geq\Theta_{V}(x)-\overline{\rho}_{i}=\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(0)-\overline{\rho}_{i}, $$

but $q_{i}\notin U_{\epsilon}(W)$ . After passing to a subsequence, we can also assume

$$ q_{i}\to q\in\bigl(\overline{B^{\delta}_{1}(0)}\cap T_{x}\partial\Omega\bigr)\setminus U_{\epsilon}(W), $$

since the rescaled boundaries $\eta_{0,\rho_{i}}(\exp_{x}^{-1}(\partial\Omega))$ converge locally smoothly to $T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . By (3.64), $\liminf_{i\to\infty}\Theta_{V}(y_{i})\geq\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(0)$ . We claim that

$$ \Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(q)\geq\limsup_{i\to\infty}\Theta_{V}(y_{i}). $$

Once the claim is established, $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(q)\geq\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(0)$ . Conversely, exact boundary monotonicity for $\mathbf{C}$ at $q\in T_{x}\partial\Omega$ , together with conicality, gives $\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(q)\leq\Theta_{\mathbf{C}}(0)$ by letting the radius tend to infinity. Thus (3.51) implies $q\in S(\mathbf{C})\subset W$ , a contradiction.

It remains to verify (3.65). Fix $s>0$ and $a>0$ . Since $q_{i}\to q$ , the differential estimate (3.26) gives, for all sufficiently large $i$ ,

$$ \eta_{0,\rho_{i}}\bigl(\exp_{x}^{-1}(B_{\rho_{i}s}(y_{i}))\bigr)\subset\overline{B^{\delta}_{(1+a)s}(q)}. $$

The balls $B_{\rho_{i}s}(y_{i})$ are compactly contained in $U$ for large $i$ . Applying Lemma 3.14 at the boundary point $y_{i}$ and using (3.27), we obtain

$$ \Theta_{V}(y_{i})\leq e^{C_{5}\rho_{i}s}\frac{\|V\|(B_{\rho_{i}s}(y_{i}))}{\omega_{n-1}(\rho_{i}s)^{n-1}}\leq e^{C_{5}\rho_{i}s}(1+o_{i}(1))\frac{\|V_{i}\|(\overline{B^{\delta}_{(1+a)s}(q)})}{\omega_{n-1}s^{n-1}}, $$

where $o_{i}(1)\to 0$ for fixed $s,a$ . Weak convergence on the compact closed ball therefore yields

$$ \limsup_{i\to\infty}\Theta_{V}(y_{i})\leq\frac{\|\mathbf{C}\|(\overline{B^{\delta}_{(1+a)s}(q)})}{\omega_{n-1}s^{n-1}}. $$

Letting first $s\downarrow 0$ and then $a\downarrow 0$ proves (3.65), since open and closed balls give the same density limit.

Step 2: Decompose $\mathcal{S}_{j}\cap\partial\Omega\cap U$ into a countable union of sets satisfying the approximation property.

This step is exactly the same as in the interior case. We provide the proof here for readers’ convenience. First, for each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ we let

$$ \mathcal{S}_{j}^{k}:=\left\{x\in\mathcal{S}_{j}\cap\partial\Omega\cap U:\text{ \eqref{E:stratification-proof-key-claim} holds with $\overline{\rho}=\frac{1}{k}$}\right\}, $$

and for each $k,\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ we define

$$ \mathcal{S}_{j}^{k,\ell}:=\left\{x\in\mathcal{S}_{j}^{k}:\Theta_{V}(x)\in\left[\frac{\ell-1}{k},\frac{\ell}{k}\right)\right\}. $$

Clearly, $\mathcal{S}_{j}\cap\partial\Omega\cap U=\bigcup_{k,\ell=1}^{\infty}\mathcal{S}_{j}^{k,\ell}$ . For any $x\in\mathcal{S}_{j}^{k,\ell}\subset\mathcal{S}_{j}^{k}$ , the definitions give

$$ \mathcal{S}_{j}^{k,\ell}\subset\left\{y\in\mathcal{S}_{j}\cap\partial\Omega\cap U:\Theta_{V}(y)\geq\Theta_{V}(x)-\frac{1}{k}\right\}, $$

and for every $\rho\in(0,\frac{1}{k}]$ , there exists a $j$ -dimensional subspace $W_{x,\rho}\subset T_{x}\partial\Omega$ such that

$$ \eta_{0,\rho}\left(\exp_{x}^{-1}\left(\left\{y\in B_{\rho}(x)\cap\partial\Omega:\Theta_{V}(y)\geq\Theta_{V}(x)-\frac{1}{k}\right\}\right)\right)\subset U_{\epsilon}(W_{x,\rho}). $$

Therefore,

$$ \eta_{0,\rho}(\exp_{x}^{-1}(\mathcal{S}_{j}^{k,\ell}\cap B_{\rho}(x)))\subset U_{\epsilon}(W_{x,\rho}). $$

To pass to a fixed normal coordinate chart, let $f=\exp_{p}^{-1}$ and restrict to a relatively compact smaller chart on which $f$ and $f^{-1}$ have Lipschitz constants at most $L\geq 1$ . Smoothness gives

$$ f(y)-f(x)=df_{x}\bigl(\exp_{x}^{-1}(y)\bigr)+o(r) $$

uniformly for $x,y$ in this smaller chart with $|f(y)-f(x)|<r$ . Apply the preceding inclusion with $\rho=Lr\leq 1/k$ , and use $\|df_{x}\|\leq L$ . For all sufficiently small $r$ , depending also on $\epsilon$ , the distance from $f(y)-f(x)$ to the $j$ -dimensional subspace $df_{x}(W_{x,Lr})$ is strictly less than $2L^{2}\epsilon r$ whenever $x,y\in\mathcal{S}_{j}^{k,\ell}$ and $|f(y)-f(x)|<r$ . Thus the coordinate image of each such local piece has the $2L^{2}\epsilon$ -approximation property. The charts can be chosen with a common bound for $L$ by (3.25) and (3.26). A countable chart cover and the approximation lemma give

$$ \mathcal{H}^{j+\beta(2L^{2}\epsilon)}(\mathcal{S}_{j}\cap\partial\Omega\cap U)=0. $$

Letting $\epsilon\downarrow 0$ completes the proof.

∎

### 3.4. Curvature varifolds with boundary

In this subsection, we recall the notion of curvature varifolds with boundary first introduced by Hutchinson [34] in the boundaryless setting and later extended by Mantegazza [45] to encompass the notion of boundary. Both [34] and [45] work in the Euclidean setting (or submanifolds inside Euclidean space). We shall adapt it to the intrinsic Riemannian setting avoiding the use of isometric embedding. The main idea is to define a generalized second fundamental form and impose the validity of integration by parts of such curvature varifolds at the Grassmannian level. It turns out that this sub-class of integral varifolds enjoys some nice compactness and a-priori regularity properties and is a natural object that arises in stable limit-interface of Allen-Cahn equation (c.f. [60]).

#### Remark 3.31.

We point out that one needs to work within the class of integral varifolds to yield some useful geometric properties of curvature varifolds (with or without boundary). This is the setting considered in [34] and [45]. One fundamental reason is that any integral varifolds with locally bounded first variation must have its generalized mean curvature vector perpendicular almost everywhere to the approximate tangent space (which exists a.e. by rectifiability). This result, known as Brakke’s Perpendicularity Theorem, was first proved in the Euclidean setting by Brakke in his monumental monograph [10, Chapter 5]. We shall extend this fundamental result to the intrinsic Riemannian setting. Note that this result is just about the properties of the generalized mean curvature vector but provides no information about the singular part $\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ of the first variation.

#### Theorem 3.32 (Brakke’s Perpendicularity Theorem).

Let $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ be an integral varifold with locally bounded first variation. Then, we have

$$ V\Big(\{(x,S)\in G(U):S(H_{V}(x))\neq 0\}\Big)=0 $$

where $H_{V}$ is the generalized mean curvature vector as defined in (3.2). Moreover, the following “flattening properties” hold: for $\|V\|$ -a.e. $x\in U$ ,

$$ \lim_{r\to 0}\frac{1}{r^{n}}\int_{B_{r}(x)}\|P_{y,x}(T_{y}V)-T_{x}V\|^{2}\;d\|V\|(y)=0 $$

where $P_{y,x}:\mathbf{G}_{y}(n,n-1)\to\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ is the map obtained by parallel transport from $y$ to $x$ along the unique minimizing geodesic between $y$ and $x$ .

Since we are only interested in codimension one varifolds, we can give a simpler description of curvature varifolds compared to the ones in [34] and [45]. First, recall that $\pi:G(U):=\cup_{x\in U}\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)\to U$ is a smooth $\mathbb{RP}^{n-1}$ -bundle over $U\subset\widetilde{M}$ by the identification $S\cong\pm N_{S}$ . At each $(x,S)\in G(U)$ , there is a natural splitting (which is orthogonal with respect to a Sasaki-type Riemannian metric $\tilde{g}$ on $G(U)$ naturally induced from $(\widetilde{M},g)$ c.f. [37, Section 2]) of the tangent space

$$ T_{(x,S)}G(U)=\mathcal{H}_{(x,S)}\oplus\ker d\pi_{(x,S)} $$

for some “horizontal” subspace $\mathcal{H}_{(x,S)}$ such that $d\pi_{(x,S)}:\mathcal{H}_{(x,S)}\to T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ is a linear isomorphism. On the other hand, the “vertical” subspace $\ker d\pi_{(x,S)}$ is tangential to the fiber $G_{x}(n,n-1)$ which can be identified with $S$ itself (since $T_{\pm N_{S}}\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\cong S$ ). We shall use $\widetilde{\nabla}$ to denote the Levi-Civita connection on $G(U)$ with respect to the Sasaki-type metric above. In what follows, we call any map $X:G(U)\to T\widetilde{M}$ such that $X(x,S)\in T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ for all $(x,S)\in G(U)$ a vector field on $G(U)$ with values in $T\widetilde{M}$ .

#### Definition 3.33 (Curvature varifolds with boundary).

A varifold $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ is said to be a curvature varifold with boundary if there exist on the Grassmannian $G(U)$

- • a tensor-valued $\mathbf{B}_{V}\in L^{1}_{loc}(G(U);V)$ with values in $T^{*}\widetilde{M}\otimes T^{*}\widetilde{M}\otimes T\widetilde{M}$ , i.e. for any continuous vector fields $X,Y$ on $G(U)$ with values in $T\widetilde{M}$ ,

$$ \mathbf{B}_{V}(X,Y)\text{ is a locally $V$-integrable vector field with values in $T\widetilde{M}$} $$

satisfying (3.69)

$$ V\left(\left\{(x,S)\in G(U):S(\mathbf{B}_{V}(S^{\perp}(X),S^{\perp}(Y))\neq 0\text{ for some $X,Y$}\right\}\right)=0; $$

- • and a vector-valued Radon measure $\partial V$ on $G(U)$ with values in $T\widetilde{M}$ , i.e.

$$ \partial V=\textbf{n}_{V}\|\partial V\| $$

where $\|\partial V\|$ is the total variation Radon measure of $\partial V$ and $\textbf{n}_{V}$ is a $\|\partial V\|$ -measurable vector field on $G(U)$ with values in $T\widetilde{M}$ and $|\textbf{n}_{V}|=1$ $\|\partial V\|$ -a.e., satisfying (3.70)

$$ \|\partial V\|\left(\left\{(x,S)\in G(U):S(\textbf{n}_{V})\neq\textbf{n}_{V}\right\}\right)=0; $$

such that for any $\varphi\in C^{1}_{c}(G(U))$ and any $C^{1}$ vector field $X:U\to T\widetilde{M}$ , we have

$$ \int_{G(U)}\varphi(x,S)\,X(x)\cdot\textbf{n}_{V}(x,S)d\|\partial V\|=\int_{G(U)}S(\nabla^{hor}\varphi(x,S))\cdot X(x)+\varphi(x,S)\operatorname{div}_{S}X(x)\;dV(x,S) $$

$$ +\int_{G(U)}\mathbf{B}_{V}(\nabla^{ver}\varphi(x,S),X(x))\cdot N_{S}-\varphi(x,S)\,\mathbf{H}_{V}(x,S)\cdot X(x)\;dV(x,S) $$

where $\mathbf{H}_{V}:=\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{B}_{V}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{B}_{V}(e_{i},e_{i})\in L^{1}_{loc}(G(U);V)$ with values in $T\widetilde{M}$ . Here, $\{e_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ is any orthonormal basis for $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ and $\nabla\varphi=\nabla^{hor}\varphi+\nabla^{ver}\varphi$ is the $\tilde{g}$ -gradient of $\varphi$ written with respect to the orthogonal splitting (3.68). We call $\mathbf{B}_{V}$ the generalized second fundamental form, $\textbf{n}_{V}$ the varifold outward co-normal and $\|\partial V\|$ the varifold boundary measure of $V$ . Here, we adopt the convention to identify $T\widetilde{M}$ and $T^{*}\widetilde{M}$ using the metric $g$ whenever necessary. We shall use $\mathbf{CV}^{\partial}_{n-1}(U)$ to denote the space of all $(n-1)$ -dimensional curvature varifolds with boundary in $U$ .

#### Remark 3.34.

Note that $\nabla^{ver}\varphi(x,S)\in\ker d\pi_{(x,S)}$ , when regarded as a vector in $S$ is only well-defined up to the anti-podal isomorphism $p\mapsto-p$ on $S$ . This reflects the choice of a unit normal $\pm N_{S}$ to the un-oriented subspace $S$ . Nonetheless, the term $\mathbf{B}_{V}(\nabla^{ver}\varphi(x,S),X(x))\cdot N_{S}$ in (3.71) is well-defined independent of the choice of $N_{S}$ .

#### Remark 3.35.

Condition (3.69) says that $\mathbf{B}_{V}$ at $V$ -a.e. $(x,S)\in G(U)$ is essentially a bi-linear map $S\times S\to S^{\perp}$ (however, we do not assume that $\mathbf{B}_{V}(X,Y)=\mathbf{B}_{V}(Y,X)$ in general). Similarly, condition (3.70) says that $\textbf{n}_{V}$ at $\|\partial V\|$ -a.e. $(x,S)$ is essentially tangential to $S$ . These conditions are necessary in order for $\mathbf{B}_{V}$ and $\textbf{n}_{V}$ to be uniquely defined by (3.71). Note that no such conditions are required in [34] and [45] as they regard $\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ as a subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}}$ , the space of all $n\times n$ real matrices, and they allow the test functions $\varphi\in C^{1}_{c}(U\times\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}})$ instead of the smaller subspace $C^{1}_{c}(G(U))$ considered here in (3.71). As a result, (3.69) and (3.70) together imply all the formal and tangential properties in [45, Proposition 3.6 and 3.7].

#### Remark 3.36.

When $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ , our definition generalizes the notion of curvature varifolds with boundary in [45] to the case of general varifolds in the Riemannian setting. If $U\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , then the Grassmannian splits globally as a product $G(U)\subset U\times\mathfrak{gl}(n,\mathbb{R})$ if we regard $S\in\mathfrak{gl}(n,\mathbb{R})\cong\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}}$ as the orthogonal projection matrix. Taking $X=\partial_{i}$ to be parallel coordinate vector fields in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , it is straightforward to check that (3.71) reduces to [45, Definition 3.1]. In general, we can always locally trivialize the Grassmannian bundle $G(B_{r}(x))=B_{r}(x)\times\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ , say within a small geodesic ball $B_{r}(x)\subset U$ and use parallel transport along minimizing geodesics from $x$ to identify $\mathbf{G}_{y}(n,n-1)$ with $\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ for all $y\in B_{r}(x)$ , to reduce the situation to the Euclidean setting (modulo some extra terms coming from the ambient geometry). Notice that under such local trivialization, we can express any $\varphi\in C^{1}_{c}(G(B_{r}(x)))$ as $\varphi(y,S)$ where $y\in B_{r}(x)$ and $S\in\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ and the orthogonal splitting 3.68 at the base point $x\in\widetilde{M}$ becomes

$$ \nabla\varphi(x,S)=\nabla^{\widetilde{M}}\varphi(x,S)+\nabla^{\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)}\varphi(x,S). $$

Note that the extra term $\operatorname{div}_{S}X$ appearing in (3.71) (that was not present in [45]), when $X=\partial_{i}$ is a (non-parallel!) coordinate vector field in geodesic normal coordinates, involves up to first order derivatives of $g_{ij}$ and can be estimated using (3.25).

#### Remark 3.37.

Note that the notion of curvature varifold with boundary is essentially a local property in the sense that one only needs to check (3.71) for $\varphi\in C^{1}_{c}(G(U_{\alpha}))$ where $\{U_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha}$ is any locally finite open cover of $U$ . This follows from the linearity of $\varphi$ in (3.71) and a standard partition of unity argument. We will mainly apply this observation to any locally finite open cover of $U$ by small enough geodesic balls.

We first note several elementary consequences by choosing suitable test functions $\varphi$ in (3.71), in case $V$ is also a rectifiable (resp. integral) varifold.

#### Lemma 3.38.

Let $V\in\mathbf{CV}^{\partial}_{n-1}(U)\cap\mathbf{RV}_{n-1}(U)$ .

- (i) $\mathbf{B}_{V}$ and $\partial V$ are uniquely determined by (3.71) and $\operatorname{spt}\|\partial V\|\subset\operatorname{spt}V$ .

- (ii) If $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ , then $\pi_{*}\|\partial V\|$ is singular with respect to $\|V\|$ , i.e.

$$ \pi_{*}\|\partial V\|\perp\|V\|. $$

Moreover, $V$ has locally bounded first variation in $U$ and the generalized mean curvature $H_{V}$ and the generalized vector-valued boundary measure $\eta_{V}\,\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ defined in (3.2) are given by (3.72)

$$ H_{V}(x)=\mathbf{H}_{V}(x,T_{x}V)\text{ and }\eta_{V}\|\delta V\|_{sing}=\pi_{*}(\partial V) $$

where $T_{x}V$ is the approximate tangent space of $V$ which exists for $\|V\|$ -a.e. $x\in U$ .

#### Proof.

For (i), the proof in [45, Proposition 3.4] carries over once we fix a local trivialization as in Remark 3.36 and choose $\varphi(y,S)=\phi(y)\psi(S)$ and $X=\partial_{i}$ . It is clear from (3.71) that $\operatorname{spt}\|\partial V\|\subset\operatorname{spt}V$ . Note that the proof in [45] only requires rectifiability of $V$ . For (ii), if we take $\varphi=\varphi(x)\in C^{1}_{c}(U)$ (or more precisely, the lift of such a function to $G(U)$ ), using Theorem 3.32 and (3.70), we see that $V$ has locally bounded first variation and (3.72) holds (c.f. [45, p.827–829]). ∎

#### Remark 3.39.

If $V\in\mathbf{RV}_{n-1}(U)$ is not integral, then $\pi_{*}\|\partial V\|$ is not necessarily singular with respect to $\|V\|$ since $\partial V$ will also contain information about the tangential derivative of the density $\Theta_{V}$ . See Example 3.41.

#### Example 3.40 (Triple junction as curvature varifold with boundary).

Consider the unit-density varifold $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ given by three rays from the origin $\ell^{+}_{1},\ell^{+}_{2},\ell^{+}_{3}$ meeting at equal angle of $2\pi/3$ . Denote by $\vec{n}_{i}$ the unit vector centred at the origin pointing towards $\ell_{i}$ . Due to the balancing of $\vec{n}_{i}$ at the origin, $V$ is a stationary varifold in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , hence $H_{V}\equiv 0$ and $\|\delta V\|_{sing}=0$ . One can check from the definition that $V$ is a curvature varifold with boundary with $\mathbf{B}_{V}\equiv 0$ and

$$ \partial V=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\vec{n}_{i}\delta_{(0,\ell_{i})}\neq 0 $$

where $\ell_{i}\in\mathbf{G}_{0}(2,1)$ is the unique line containing the ray $\ell^{+}_{i}$ . Note that $\pi_{*}(\partial V)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{3}\vec{n}_{i}\right)\delta_{0}=0$ . On the other hand, $\|\partial V\|=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\delta_{(0,\ell_{i})}$ is a sum of three delta measures on the Grassmannian $G(\mathbb{R}^{2})$ and the pushforward measure $\pi_{*}\|\partial V\|=3\delta_{0}$ is singular with respect to $\|V\|$ . This example shows that in general we only have $\|\delta V\|_{sing}\leq\pi_{*}\|\partial V\|$ as Radon measures on $U$ .

#### Example 3.41 (Weighted smoothly embedded hypersurfaces).

Let $\Sigma\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a properly embedded smooth hypersurface with boundary and $f:\Sigma\to\mathbb{R}$ be a smooth function. Suppose $\Sigma$ is two-sided and oriented by the global unit normal vector field $N_{\Sigma}$ . Consider the rectifiable varifold $V\in\mathbf{RV}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ with weight measure given by

$$ \|V\|=e^{f}d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\Sigma, $$

then a direct computation shows that $V$ is a curvature varifold with boundary with $\mathbf{B}_{V}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}$ supported on $T\Sigma$ given by the classical second fundamental form1313 13 We denote $w=w^{T}+w^{N}$ for the orthogonal decomposition $T_{x}\mathbb{R}^{n}=T_{x}\Sigma\oplus N_{x}\Sigma$ :

$$ \mathbf{B}_{V}|_{(x,T_{x}\Sigma)}(u,v):=(D_{u^{T}}v^{T})^{N}, $$

and the vector-valued Radon measure $\partial V$ is given by

$$ \partial V(x,T_{x}\Sigma)=-e^{f}\nabla^{\Sigma}f(x)\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\Sigma(x)\otimes\delta_{T_{x}\Sigma}+e^{f}\eta(x)\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-2}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\partial\Sigma(x)\otimes\delta_{T_{x}\Sigma} $$

where $\eta(x)\in T_{x}\Sigma$ is the outward unit co-normal of $\partial\Sigma$ . Note that $\partial V$ contains a non-trivial part which is absolutely continuous with respect to $V$ unless $f$ is constant on $\Sigma$ . On the other hand, $V$ has locally bounded first variation with $H_{V}(x)=\mathbf{H}_{V}(x,T_{x}\Sigma)$ and

$$ \|\delta V\|_{sing}=e^{f}d\mathcal{H}^{n-2}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\partial\Sigma\leq e^{f}|\nabla^{\Sigma}f|\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\Sigma+e^{f}d\mathcal{H}^{n-2}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\partial\Sigma=\pi_{*}\|\partial V\|. $$

More generally, one can also consider $f\in BV(\Sigma)$ and replace $\nabla^{\Sigma}f\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\Sigma$ with the vector-valued Radon measure $Df$ on $\Sigma$ .

Finally, we recall the following boundary rectifiability theorem [45, Theorem 7.1] in the context of integral curvature varifold with boundary.

#### Theorem 3.42 (Boundary Rectifiability Theorem).

Let $V\in\mathbf{CV}^{\partial}_{n-1}(U)\cap\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ . Then, $\pi_{*}\|\partial V\|$ is an $(n-2)$ -rectifiable measure on $U$ , i.e. there exists a countably $(n-2)$ -rectifiable subset $\Gamma\subset U$ and a positive Borel function $\tau:\Gamma\to(0,\infty)$ such that

$$ \pi_{*}\|\partial V\|=\tau\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-2}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}\Gamma. $$

## 4. The Allen-Cahn equation on Riemannian manifolds

In this section, we will study the geometric properties of limit-interfaces arising in stationary or stable solutions to the Allen-Cahn equation on Riemannian manifolds with boundary. Let $\Omega$ be a domain in $(\widetilde{M},g)$ as in Section 2.1 and fix an open set $U\subset\widetilde{M}$ . For any $\epsilon>0$ , we consider the Allen-Cahn energy for any $u\in W^{1,2}(\Omega\cap U)$ ,

$$ E_{\epsilon}(u):=\int_{\Omega\cap U}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|\nabla u|^{2}+\frac{W(u)}{\varepsilon}\right)\;d\mathrm{vol}_{g} $$

where $W:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a “double-well potential” which is a non-negative smooth function satisfying the following (a common choice is $W(s)=\frac{1}{4}(1-s^{2})^{2}$ with the unique local maximum at $\gamma=0$ ):

- • $W(\pm 1)=W^{\prime}(\pm 1)=0$ ,

- • $W$ has a unique local non-degenerate maxima at $\gamma\in(-1,1)$ ,

- • there exist some $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $\kappa\in(0,1)$ such that $W^{\prime\prime}(t)\geq\kappa$ for all $|t|\geq\alpha$ .

We shall denote the energy constant1414 14 Note that our definition of the constant $h_{0}$ is the same as in our previous paper [39], but differs by a factor of 2 from [33, 29]. with respect to $W$ by

$$ h_{0}:=\int_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{2W(s)}\;ds. $$

For easy reference, we will also denote the (normalized) energy density $e_{\epsilon}(u)$ and the discrepancy function $\xi_{\epsilon}(u)$ for any $u\in C^{1}(\Omega\cap U)$ respectively by

$$ e_{\epsilon}(u):=\frac{1}{h_{0}}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|\nabla u|^{2}+\frac{W(u)}{\varepsilon}\right)\quad\text{ and }\quad\xi_{\epsilon}(u):=\frac{1}{h_{0}}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|\nabla u|^{2}-\frac{W(u)}{\varepsilon}\right). $$

Note that $e_{\epsilon}(u)\geq 0$ and $\xi_{\epsilon}(u)\leq e_{\epsilon}(u)$ everywhere.

For any $u_{\varepsilon}\in W^{1,2}(\Omega\cap U)$ with $\varepsilon>0$ , we can associate a Radon measure $\mu_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ on $U$ by

$$ \mu_{u_{\varepsilon}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{h_{0}}\varepsilon|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}\ d\mathrm{vol}_{g}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}{\Omega\cap U}, $$

and a varifold $V^{u_{\varepsilon}}\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ by

$$ V^{u_{\varepsilon}}(\phi):=\int_{\{x\in\Omega\cap U:|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}(x)|\neq 0\}}\phi\left(x,S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)\right)\ d\mu_{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)\qquad\forall\phi\in C_{c}(G(U)) $$

where $S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)\in\mathbf{G}_{x}(n,n-1)$ is the hyperplane orthogonal to $\nabla u_{\varepsilon}(x)\neq 0$ . Note that $\mu_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the ambient volume measure $d\mathrm{vol}_{g}$ and is supported on the closure of $\{x\in\Omega\cap U:|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}(x)|\neq 0\}$ in $U$ which is in general not an $(n-1)$ -rectifiable subset. Therefore, although the varifold $V^{u_{\varepsilon}}$ is concentrated on $S^{u_{\varepsilon}}$ along the Grassmannian factor, the spatial support of $\|V^{u_{\varepsilon}}\|=\mu_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ is diffused.

#### Remark 4.1.

Our definition of the varifold $V^{u_{\varepsilon}}$ in (4.5) is consistent with [30, 18, 46], but slightly different from the one in [39]. Nonetheless, whenever equi-partition of energy holds (i.e. $\xi_{\varepsilon}\to 0$ in $L^{1}(U)$ ), it will give rise to the same varifold limit $V^{u_{\varepsilon}}\to V$ if it exists as $\varepsilon\to 0$ .

### 4.1. General critical points to the Allen–Cahn energy

We first recall the key properties of general critical points to the Allen-Cahn energy functional, which study was pioneered by Hutchinson and Tonegawa in [33] for the Euclidean setting; the Riemannian setting (c.f. [29, Appendix B]) together with the boundary behaviour was studied in our previous paper [39]. The Euler-Lagrange equation for (4.1) is given by the following elliptic semi-linear Allen-Cahn equation with homogeneous Neumann boundary condition:

$$ \left\{\begin{array}[]{rl}-\varepsilon^{2}\Delta u+W^{\prime}(u)&=0\quad\text{in $\Omega\cap U$}\\
\partial u/\partial\nu&=0\quad\text{on $\partial\Omega\cap U$.}\end{array}\right. $$

By standard elliptic regularity, any weak solution $u\in W^{1,2}(\Omega\cap U)$ to (4.6) is in fact a classical solution $u\in C^{3}(\overline{\Omega}\cap U)$ .

#### Assumptions 4.2.

We will consider solutions $u_{\varepsilon}$ to (4.6) under the following additional assumptions:

- (A1) (Uniform energy bound) There exists some $E_{0}>0$ such that

$$ E_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})\leq E_{0}. $$

- (A2) (Uniform $L^{\infty}$ bound on $u_{\varepsilon}$ ) There exists some $C_{0}>0$ such that

$$ \|u_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega\cap U)}\leq C_{0}. $$

The theorem below summarizes the key properties of the limit-interface arising from general critical points to the Allen-Cahn energy. Note that the main theorem [39, Theorem 3.3] there actually holds with trivial modifications of the proof to the situation of varying metrics and domains as well.

#### Theorem 4.3.

[39, Theorem 3.3] Let $\{\varepsilon_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of positive real numbers such that $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ , and let $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of solutions to (4.6) satisfying (A1)-(A2) in Assumptions 4.2 with respect to a sequence of Riemannian metrics $g_{i}$ on $U$ and a sequence of domains $\Omega_{i}\subset\widetilde{M}$ such that

$$ g_{i}\to g\quad\text{ and }\quad\Omega_{i}\to\Omega $$

in the $C^{2}$ -sense to some Riemannian metric $g$ and some $C^{2}$ domain $\Omega\subset\widetilde{M}$ satisfying all the assumptions in 2.1. Then, after passing to a subsequence, there exist some $u\in BV(\Omega\cap U)$ and $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ such that

- • $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\to u$ strongly in $L^{1}(\Omega\cap U;d\mathrm{vol}_{g})$ ;

- • $V^{u_{\epsilon_{i}}}\to V$ as varifolds in $U$ (recall (4.5)).

Moreover, the following statements are true for any such $u$ and $V$ obtained above:

- (1) (Discrepancy estimates and equi-partition of energy) The discrepancy function $\xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})$ as defined in (4.3) satisfies the pointwise upper bound locally away from $\partial U$ : (4.7)

$$ \xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})\leq\varepsilon_{i}^{-4/5}\qquad\text{ for all large $i$}; $$

moreover the discrepancy function converges to zero strongly in $L^{1}$ , i.e. (4.8)

$$ \xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})\to 0\quad\text{ in }L^{1}(\Omega\cap U;d\mathrm{vol}_{g}). $$

As a result, we have for each $\phi\in C_{c}(U)$ , (4.9)

$$ \|V\|(\phi)=\lim_{i\to\infty}\mu_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}(\phi)=\lim_{i\to\infty}\frac{2}{h_{0}}\int_{\overline{\Omega}\cap U}\frac{W(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})}{\varepsilon_{i}}\phi\;d\mathrm{vol}_{g}. $$

- (2) (Hausdorff convergence of level sets) The phase boundary is contained in the support of the limit-interface, i.e.

$$ \partial^{*}\{u=1\}\subset\operatorname{spt}\|V\| $$

where $\partial^{*}\{u=1\}\subset\Omega\cap U$ is the reduced boundary1515 15 See, for example, [38] for a precise definition in the local Riemannian setting. of $u\in BV(\Omega\cap U)$ . Moreover, as $i\to\infty$ ,

$$ u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\to\pm 1\quad\text{ locally uniformly on $(\Omega\cap U)\setminus\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$} $$

and for each $b\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ \{x\in\overline{\Omega}\cap U:|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(x)|\leq 1-b\}\to\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\quad\text{ locally in Hausdorff topology.} $$

- (3) (Integer-rectifiability of limit-interface) The limit-interface is integer-rectifiable, i.e. $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ , with density

$$ \Theta_{V}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\text{odd}&\text{for $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$-a.e. $x\in\partial^{*}\{u=1\}$},\\ \text{even}&\text{for $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$-a.e. $x\in(\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\Omega)\setminus\partial^{*}\{u=1\}$}.\end{array}\right. $$

- (4) (Variational property of limit-interface) The limit-interface $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ is free boundary stationary, with respect to the metric $g$ , with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ .

#### Remark 4.4.

The assumptions (A1) and (A2) are really the minimal assumptions one has to make to expect the conclusions in Theorem 4.3. Condition (A2) typically follows from a maximum principle argument on the global Allen-Cahn equation (1.1). Condition (A1) is necessary in order to guarantee a uniform bound on the BV-norm of $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ and the mass of $V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}$ so that standard compactness theorems can be applied to extract a convergent subsequence. In particular, there are no assumptions on the stability (or Morse index) of $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ with respect to the Allen-Cahn energy functional $E_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ . We emphasize that Theorem 4.3 allows higher multiplicity convergence and boundary concentration phenomena as constructed by Malchiodi-Ni-Wei [44] and Malchiodi-Wei [43]. As these examples show, in general the limit-interface $V$ may not be stationary in $U$ if there is a part of $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ leaning onto the boundary $\partial\Omega$ . Nonetheless, the first variation of $V$ is given by (3.7) but it is a difficult question to infer further regularity (e.g. whether $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\operatorname{sing}V)=0$ ) as a-priori the touching part can interact with $\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ in highly complicated manners.

#### Remark 4.5.

Note that we have only established in [39] Hausdorff convergence of the transition level sets to the support of the limit-interface locally away from $\partial\Omega$ . This is due to the technical arguments that in [39] we only make use of monotonicity formula on balls that are either centred at a boundary point or disjoint from $\partial\Omega$ . The last assertion of (2) in Theorem 4.3 essentially relies on a uniform density-ratio bounds which have to be also valid for balls that intersect $\partial\Omega$ but are not centred at a boundary point. This can be achieved by a reflected ball argument as in [28] and [59]. For the sake of completeness, we provide the proof in Appendix A.

As highlighted in Remark 4.4, Theorem 4.3 is likely to be sharp in such generality. However, as the examples in [44, 43] show, a free boundary stationary integral varifold can be quite far from a genuine free boundary minimal hypersurface. In order to obtain better regularity properties for the limit interface, it is necessary to impose stronger assumptions on $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ . Since $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ are critical points to a variational problem, a natural assumption is that of stability (or more generally, finite Morse index), which is going to be studied in the following sections.

### 4.2. Stable critical points to Allen-Cahn equation

We now study further properties of the limit-interface $V$ arising from Theorem 4.3 under the additional assumption that each $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ is stable.

#### Assumptions 4.6.

From this section onwards, we will consider solutions $u_{\varepsilon}$ to (4.6) under the following additional assumption:

- (A3) (Stability) Each $u_{\varepsilon}$ is a stable critical point in the sense that the second variation of $E_{\varepsilon}$ is non-negative-definite at $u_{\varepsilon}$ , i.e. (4.10)

$$ \left.\frac{d^{2}}{dt^{2}}\right|_{t=0}E_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon}+t\psi)\geq 0\qquad\forall\psi\in C_{c}^{1}(U). $$

Note that the test function $\psi$ in (4.10) is allowed to be non-zero along $\partial\Omega\cap U$ , and therefore $u_{\varepsilon}$ is stable as a “free boundary problem” (in the sense that the boundary values of $u_{\varepsilon}$ are allowed to change freely on $\partial\Omega\cap U$ in the variational problem). Recall that $u\in C^{3}(\overline{\Omega}\cap U)$ for any solution to (4.6) and thus we can define two Radon measures $\mu^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ and $\hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ supported on $\partial\Omega\cap U$ by

$$ \mu^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}\coloneqq\frac{1}{h_{0}}\varepsilon|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}{\partial\Omega\cap U} $$

and

$$ \hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}\coloneqq e_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}{\partial\Omega\cap U}. $$

Clearly, we have $\mu^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}\leq 2\hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ as measures but in general we do not have $\hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}\leq C\mu^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ unless we have pointwise lower bound of the discrepancy function $\xi_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})$ up to the boundary $\partial\Omega$ .

We shall also denote the unit normal $N_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ to the (regular part of) level sets of $u_{\varepsilon}$ , which is a $C^{2}$ vector field on $\overline{\Omega}\cap U\cap\{\nabla u_{\varepsilon}\neq 0\}$ , defined by

$$ N_{u_{\varepsilon}}:=\frac{\nabla u_{\varepsilon}}{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|} $$

We also recall the definition of the enhanced second fundamental form $\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ , which is a $(1,1)$ -tensor of class $C^{1}$ in $\overline{\Omega}\cap U\cap\{\nabla u_{\varepsilon}\neq 0\}$ defined by

$$ \mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon}}:=\nabla N_{u_{\varepsilon}}. $$

By convention, we shall just let $N_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ and $\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ vanish on $\{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|=0\}$ 1616 16 Using this convention, $N_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ and $\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ will be discontinuous across the exceptional set $\{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|=0\}$ . However, as we will see, we will always pair $N_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ and $\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ with the Radon measures such as $\mu_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ and $\mu^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ that vanish on this exceptional set so that we will only be integrating over the set $\{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|\neq 0\}$ .. The pointwise Hilbert-Schmidt norm of $\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ on $\{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|\neq 0\}$ is given by

$$ |\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon}}|^{2}=\frac{|\operatorname{Hess}u|^{2}-|\nabla|\nabla u||^{2}}{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}}. $$

We first derive an $\varepsilon$ -stability inequality for stable solutions to the Allen-Cahn equation (4.6). The same inequality was first established in the interior Euclidean setting by Padilla-Tonegawa [51] (c.f. [60]) and then the Riemannian setting by Hiesmayr [30]. We extend this to the Riemannian setting including the boundary terms.

#### Proposition 4.7 ( $\varepsilon$ -stability inequality).

Suppose $u_{\varepsilon}$ is a stable solution to (4.6) satisfying (A3) in Assumption 4.6. Then the following inequality holds: for any $\psi\in C^{1}_{c}(U)$ ,

$$ \int|\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon}}|^{2}\psi^{2}\;d\mu_{u_{\varepsilon}}\leq\int|\nabla\psi|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}(N_{u_{\varepsilon}},N_{u_{\varepsilon}})\psi^{2}\;d\mu_{u_{\varepsilon}}+\int\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial\Omega}(N_{u_{\varepsilon}},N_{u_{\varepsilon}})\psi^{2}\;d\mu^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}} $$

where $\operatorname{Ric}$ is the Ricci curvature of $(\widetilde{M},g)$ and $\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial\Omega}$ is the second fundamental form1717 17 Our sign convention here is that $\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial\Omega}$ is positive definite for a convex domain $\Omega\subset(\widetilde{M},g)$ . of $\partial\Omega$ with respect to the outward unit normal $\nu$ .

#### Proof.

A direct calculation as in [51] and integrating by parts gives for any $\phi\in C^{1}_{c}(U)$ ,

$$ \begin{split}0\leq\left.\frac{d^{2}}{dt^{2}}\right|_{t=0}E_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon}+t\phi)&=\int_{\Omega\cap U}\left(\varepsilon|\nabla\phi|^{2}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}W^{\prime\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})\phi^{2}\right)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g},\\
&=\int_{\Omega\cap U}\phi\left(-\varepsilon\Delta\phi+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}W^{\prime\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})\phi\right)d\mathrm{vol}_{g}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}\frac{\partial\phi^{2}}{\partial\nu}\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\\
\end{split} $$

To rewrite the above in the form of (4.15), first recall by the Bochner formula that

$$ \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\Delta|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}=\varepsilon|\operatorname{Hess}u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon}W^{\prime\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}+\varepsilon\operatorname{Ric}(\nabla u_{\varepsilon},\nabla u_{\varepsilon}) $$

and also the boundary analogue of Bochner formula (c.f. [59, Lemma 3.1])

$$ \frac{\partial|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}}{\partial\nu}=-2\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial\Omega}(\nabla u_{\varepsilon},\nabla u_{\varepsilon}). $$

We can then1818 18 Although (4.16) was derived for $C^{1}$ test functions $\phi$ , it is standard to see by an approximation argument that our choice $\psi|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|$ is a valid test function even though $|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|$ is in general not $C^{1}$ across the exceptional set $\{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|=0\}$ . The interested readers can refer to [51, Proposition 2.6] for more details. Also, technically $\psi|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|$ is only defined on $\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ but we can extend it suitably across $\partial\Omega\cap U$ which does not affect the integrals in (4.16). plug $\phi=\psi|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|$ into (4.16) to obtain (4.15). ∎

We now move on to the main result of this section concerning the properties of limit-interfaces arising from stable solutions to the Allen-Cahn equation.

#### Theorem 4.8.

Let $\{\varepsilon_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of positive real numbers such that $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ , and let $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of solutions to (4.6) satisfying (A1)-(A2) in Assumptions 4.2. Suppose, furthermore, that each $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ is stable, i.e. (A3) in Assumption 4.6 is satisfied, with respect to the metric $g_{i}$ . Then, for any limit-interface $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ obtained from Theorem 4.3, the following holds:

- (1) $V$ is a curvature varifold with boundary (recall Definition 3.33), i.e.

$$ V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)\cap\mathbf{CV}^{\partial}_{n-1}(U). $$

- (2) (Ambient stability inequality) For any $\psi\in C^{1}_{c}(U)$ , we have (4.19)

$$ \int|\mathbf{B}_{V}|^{2}\psi^{2}\,d\|V\|\leq\int|\nabla\psi|^{2}\,d\|V\|+(n-1)k_{0}\int\psi^{2}\,d\|V\|+2\kappa_{0}\int\psi^{2}\,d\|\delta V\|_{sing}, $$

where $|\mathbf{B}_{V}|^{2}(x)=|\mathbf{B}_{V}(x,T_{x}V)|^{2}$ with $T_{x}V$ being the approximate tangent plane of $\|V\|$ that exists at $\|V\|$ -a.e. $x\in U$ .

- (3) (Stationarity across touching set) The first variation of $V$ is given by (4.20)

$$ \delta V(X)=\int X\cdot\nu\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing}\qquad\forall X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U). $$

#### Remark 4.9.

By (1) and Theorem 3.42, $\pi_{*}\|\partial V\|$ is an $(n-2)$ -rectifiable measure on $U$ .

#### Remark 4.10.

Note that if $V=|\Sigma|$ is a unit-density varifold for some smoothly embedded, two-sided, stable free boundary minimal hypersurface $\Sigma\subset\Omega$ with $\partial\Sigma\subset\partial\Omega$ , the classical intrinsic stability inequality for $\Sigma$ reads (recall the notation as in Example 3.41):

$$ \int_{\Sigma}|B_{\Sigma}|^{2}\psi^{2}\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\leq\int_{\Sigma}|\nabla^{\Sigma}\psi|^{2}\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}-\int_{\Sigma}\operatorname{Ric}(N_{\Sigma},N_{\Sigma})\psi^{2}\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}-\int_{\partial\Sigma}\mathrm{I\!I}_{\partial\Omega}(N_{\Sigma},N_{\Sigma})\psi^{2}\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-2} $$

where $B_{\Sigma}$ is the classical second fundamental form of $\Sigma$ . Comparing this with (4.19), note that the term involving the extrinsic gradient $\nabla\psi$ is replaced by the intrinsic gradient $\nabla^{\Sigma}\psi$ and the boundary term differs by a factor of two.

#### Remark 4.11.

Since $V$ is a free boundary stationary varifold with free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ , combining (4.20) with (3.7), we conclude that

$$ H_{\partial\Omega}(x)=0\qquad\text{for $\|V\|$-a.e. $x\in\partial\Omega\cap U$.} $$

In other words, the part that $V$ leans on to the boundary must be a minimal portion of $\partial\Omega$ .

#### Proof.

First of all, we show that that the first variation of the diffused varifold $V^{u_{\varepsilon}}\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ (recall (4.5)) associated to a solution $u_{\varepsilon}$ to (4.6) is given by: for any $\tilde{X}\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ ,

$$ \delta V^{u_{\varepsilon}}(\tilde{X})=\int_{\Omega\cap U}\xi_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})\operatorname{div}_{g}\tilde{X}\;d\mathrm{vol}_{g}+\int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}e_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})(\tilde{X}\cdot\nu)\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}. $$

To prove (4.22), we first recall the following Pohozaev identity (see [39, Lemma 4.1], note that we are using the normalized energy density as in (4.3))

$$ \int_{\Omega\cap U}\left(h_{0}e_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})\operatorname{div}_{g}\tilde{X}-\varepsilon\nabla\tilde{X}(\nabla u_{\varepsilon},\nabla u_{\varepsilon})\right)\;d\mathrm{vol}_{g}=\int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}h_{0}e_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})(\tilde{X}\cdot\nu)\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}. $$

Observe that $\operatorname{div}_{S^{u_{\varepsilon}}}\tilde{X}=\operatorname{div}_{g}\tilde{X}-\nabla\tilde{X}(N_{u_{\varepsilon}},N_{u_{\varepsilon}})$ and $\varepsilon|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}=h_{0}(e_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})+\xi_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon}))$ , the integrand in the left hand side of (4.23) can be written as

$$ h_{0}e_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})\operatorname{div}_{g}\tilde{X}-\varepsilon\nabla\tilde{X}(\nabla u_{\varepsilon},\nabla u_{\varepsilon})=-h_{0}\xi_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})\operatorname{div}_{g}\tilde{X}+\varepsilon|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}\operatorname{div}_{S^{u_{\varepsilon}}}\tilde{X} $$

from which (4.22) follows (recall (4.5)).

Next, we test (4.22) with a vector field1919 19 Strictly speaking, in order to deal with the singularities of $N_{\varepsilon}$ across $\{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|=0\}$ , we should first consider $\varphi\left(x,Id-\frac{\nabla u_{\varepsilon}\otimes\nabla u_{\varepsilon}}{s+|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}}\right)$ for $s>0$ and then let $s\to 0$ . For more details on this technical aspect, see [60]. For simplicity of presentation, we will pretend $|\nabla u|\neq 0$ everywhere.

$$ \tilde{X}(x)=\varphi(x,S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x))S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)(X(x)) $$

for any $C^{1}$ vector field $X:U\to T\widetilde{M}$ and any $\varphi\in C^{1}_{c}(G(B_{r}(x_{0})))$ where $x_{0}\in U$ and $r<\frac{1}{4}\min\{\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x_{0},\partial U),i_{0}\}$ . A direct computation shows that

$$ \operatorname{div}_{S^{u_{\varepsilon}}}\tilde{X}=S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(\nabla^{hor}\varphi)\cdot X+\varphi\operatorname{div}_{S^{u_{\varepsilon}}}X+B_{u_{\varepsilon}}(\nabla^{ver}\varphi,S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(X))\cdot N_{u_{\varepsilon}}-\varphi H_{u_{\varepsilon}}\cdot X $$

where everything is evaluated at either $x$ or $(x,S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x))$ ; here $B_{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)$ and $H_{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)$ are respectively the second fundamental form (as a $(1,2)$ -tensor) and the mean curvature vector (see Example 3.41) of the level set $\{u_{\varepsilon}=u_{\varepsilon}(x)\}$ of $u_{\varepsilon}$ through the point $x\in\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ . Note that the free boundary condition $\frac{\partial u_{\varepsilon}}{\partial\nu}=0$ means that

$$ S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)(\nu(x))=\nu(x)\quad\text{for all $x\in\partial\Omega$.} $$

Plugging these back into (4.22), we obtain

$$ \int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}\varphi(x,S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x))X(x)\cdot\nu(x)e_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})(x)\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}+\int_{\Omega\cap U}\xi_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})(x)\operatorname{div}_{g}\tilde{X}(x)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g} $$

$$ =\int_{\Omega\cap U}S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)\left(\nabla^{hor}\varphi(x,S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x))\right)\cdot X(x)+\varphi(x,S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x))\operatorname{div}_{S^{u_{\varepsilon}}}X(x)\,dV^{u_{\varepsilon}} $$

$$ +\int_{\Omega\cap U}B_{u_{\varepsilon}}\left(\nabla^{ver}\varphi(x,S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)),S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)X(x)\right)\cdot N_{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)-\varphi(x,S^{u_{\varepsilon}}(x))H_{u_{\varepsilon}}(x)\cdot X(x)\,dV^{u_{\varepsilon}}. $$

We will pass $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ in (4.24) to deduce that $V=\lim_{i\to\infty}V^{\varepsilon_{i}}$ is in fact a curvature varifold with boundary. Moreover, we only present below the proof in the case $g_{i}=g$ and $\Omega_{i}=\Omega$ for all $i$ and leave the trivial modifications to the readers. In order to do this, we shall prove that all terms in (4.24) can be suitably bounded as measure-function pairs (see Appendix C, or [34, 60]) and appeal to the compactness result of measure-function pairs as in Proposition C.3. With this goal in mind, we define a tensor-valued $\mathbf{B}_{V^{u_{\varepsilon}}}\in L^{1}_{loc}(G(U);V^{u_{\varepsilon}})$ with values in $T^{*}\widetilde{M}\otimes T^{*}\widetilde{M}\otimes T\widetilde{M}$ by

$$ \mathbf{B}_{V^{u_{\varepsilon}}}(X,Y)=B_{u_{\varepsilon}}(S(X),S(Y)) $$

and a vector-valued Radon measure $\partial V^{u_{\varepsilon}}$ on $G(U)$ with values in $T\widetilde{M}$ by (recall (4.12))

$$ \partial V^{u_{\varepsilon}}=S(\nu(x))\,d\hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}\otimes\delta_{S^{u_{\varepsilon}}} $$

which clearly fulfil (3.69) and (3.70). By the well-known formula for the second fundamental form of a level set (see e.g. [30, Lemma 3.3]),

$$ |\mathbf{B}_{V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}}|^{2}(x,S)\leq|B_{u_{\varepsilon}}|^{2}(x)\leq\frac{|\operatorname{Hess}u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}-\big|\nabla|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|\big|^{2}}{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|^{2}}=|\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon}}|^{2}(x), $$

where $\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ denotes the enhanced second fundamental form as defined in (4.14).

In order to apply the compactness theorem (Proposition C.3), we need to show that $\mathbf{B}_{V^{u_{\varepsilon}}}$ is locally uniformly bounded in $L^{2}(B_{r}(x_{0});V^{u_{\varepsilon}})$ independent of $\varepsilon$ . Set (recall (2.8)) $\psi(x)=\chi(\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,x_{0}))$ in the $\varepsilon$ -stability inequality (4.15), we see that (recall that $\mu^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}\leq 2\hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ by definitions (4.11) and (4.12))

$$ \displaystyle\int_{G(B_{r/2}(x_{0}))}|\mathbf{B}_{V^{u_{\varepsilon}}}|^{2}(x,S)\,dV^{u_{\varepsilon}} \displaystyle\leq\int_{B_{r/2}(x_{0})}|\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon}}|^{2}\;d\|V^{u_{\varepsilon}}\| \displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{4}{r^{2}}+(n-1)k_{0}\right)\|V^{u_{\varepsilon}}\|(B_{r}(x_{0}))+2\kappa_{0}\hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}(B_{r}(x_{0})) $$

By Assumptions (A1) in 4.2, we have a uniform bound on the first term of (4.26) since

$$ \|V^{u_{\varepsilon}}\|(B_{r}(x_{0}))\leq\frac{2}{h_{0}}E_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})\leq\frac{2E_{0}}{h_{0}}. $$

On the other hand, by [39, Lemma 3.2] (with $\Lambda_{0}=0$ in our case), we also have a uniform bound on the second term of (4.26):

$$ \hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}(B_{r}(x_{0}))\leq C(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0},r)\frac{E_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})}{h_{0}}\leq C(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0},r)\frac{E_{0}}{h_{0}}. $$

Putting these back into (4.26), we have the following local uniform $L^{2}$ -bounds:

$$ \int_{G(B_{r/2}(x_{0}))}|\mathbf{B}_{V^{u_{\varepsilon}}}|^{2}(x,S)\,dV^{u_{\varepsilon}}\leq C(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0},r)\frac{E_{0}}{h_{0}}. $$

We consider now a sequence of positive numbers $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ and a sequence of solutions $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ to (4.6) as in Theorem 4.3. By (4.28), we can apply Proposition C.3 in Appendix C2020 20 The result there is applicable since no metric structure is required (except the fact that $X=G(B_{r}(x_{0}))$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space) and hence is independent of the Riemannian metric. to extract a subsequence such that

$$ (\mathbf{B}_{V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}},V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})\rightharpoonup(\mathbf{B}_{V},V) $$

where $\mathbf{B}_{V}\in L^{1}_{loc}(G(B_{r}(x_{0}));V)$ is a tensor-valued map with values in $T^{*}\widetilde{M}\otimes T^{*}\widetilde{M}\otimes T\widetilde{M}$ , and

$$ \int\mathbf{B}_{V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}}(X,Y)\cdot Z\;dV^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\to\int\mathbf{B}_{V}(X,Y)\cdot Z\;dV $$

for any continuous vector fields $X,Y,Z$ on $G(B_{r}(x_{0}))$ with values in $T\widetilde{M}$ . This clearly implies $\mathbf{B}_{V}$ satisfies (3.69). On the other hand, the uniform bound (4.27) implies that, after passing to a subsequence,

$$ \partial V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\rightharpoonup\partial V=\textbf{n}_{V}\|\partial V\| $$

for some vector-valued Radon measure $\partial V$ on $G(B_{r}(x_{0}))$ with values in $T\widetilde{M}$ . From the definition of $\partial V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}$ , it is clear that $\partial V$ satisfies (3.70). Passing $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ in (4.24), using that $\xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})\to 0$ in $L^{1}(\Omega\cap U;d\mathrm{vol}_{g})$ by Theorem 4.3 (1), we obtain

$$ \int\varphi(x,S)X(x)\cdot\textbf{n}_{V}(x,S)\;d\|\partial V\|=\int S\left(\nabla^{hor}\varphi(x,S)\right)\cdot X(x)+\varphi(x,S)\operatorname{div}_{S}X(x)\;dV $$

$$ +\int\mathbf{B}_{V}\left(\nabla^{ver}\varphi(x,S),S(X(x))\right)\cdot N_{S}-\varphi(x,S)\mathbf{H}_{V}(x,S)\cdot X(x)\;dV $$

where $\mathbf{H}_{V}=\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{B}_{V}\in L^{1}_{loc}(G(B_{r}(x_{0}));V)$ with values in $T\widetilde{M}$ . This shows that $V$ is a curvature varifold with boundary in any geodesic ball $B_{r}(x_{0})$ according to Definition 3.33. Using a locally finite open covering of $U$ by such balls, (1) follows by Remark 3.37.

We now proceed to prove the stability type inequality (4.19) in (2). First of all, since $\partial V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\rightharpoonup\partial V$ , combined with the fact that $V$ is a free boundary varifold with $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ by Theorem 4.3 (4) and using Proposition 3.6 together with (3.72), we have

$$ \nu\,\hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}=\pi_{*}(\partial V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})\rightharpoonup\pi_{*}(\partial V)=\nu\|\delta V\|_{sing}. $$

Therefore, $\hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\rightharpoonup\|\delta V\|_{sing}$ . By the lower semi-continuity property (C.5) in Proposition C.3, (4.25) and the $\varepsilon$ -stability inequality (4.15), since $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ by Theorem 4.3 (3), for any $\psi\in C^{1}(U)$ we have (recall again that $\mu^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}\leq 2\hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon}}$ )

$$ \int|\mathbf{B}_{V}(x,T_{x}V)|^{2}\psi^{2}(x)\;d\|V\|(x)\leq\liminf_{i\to\infty}\int|B_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}(x)|^{2}\psi^{2}(x)\;d\mu_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}(x) $$

$$ \leq\int|\nabla\psi|^{2}\;d\|V\|+(n-1)k_{0}\int\psi^{2}\;d\|V\|+2\kappa_{0}\int\psi^{2}\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing} $$

which is the desired inequality (4.19).

Finally, we prove assertion (3). Let $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ in (4.22), by the continuity of first variation with respect to varifold convergence, together with Theorem 4.3 (1) and (4.31), we obtain for any $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ ,

$$ \delta V(X)=\lim_{i\to\infty}\delta V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}(X)=\int X\cdot\nu\;d\|\delta V\|_{sing}. $$
