#### Remark 4.12 (Test functions supported inside the regular set).

Let $W\subset\subset U\setminus\mathrm{sing}(V)$ be an open set such that $W\cap\mathrm{reg}(V)\neq\emptyset$ , and let $\phi\in C^{1}_{c}(W)$ . In this case, we can get a more precise stability inequality as follows. First, note that, by (4.5),

$$ \int_{U}\operatorname{Ric}(x)(N_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(x)},N_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}(x))\phi^{2}(x)\,d\|V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\|(x)=\int_{G(U)}\operatorname{Ric}(x)(N_{S},N_{S})\phi^{2}(x)\,dV^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}(x,S). $$

Letting $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ and denoting $\Sigma=\operatorname{reg}V$ , we have

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\int_{U}\operatorname{Ric}(x)(N_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(x)},N_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}(x))\phi^{2}(x)\,d\|V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\|(x)=\int_{U}\operatorname{Ric}(N_{\Sigma},N_{\Sigma})\phi^{2}\,d\|V\|. $$

Therefore, when $\phi\in C^{1}_{c}(W)$ with $W\cap\mathrm{reg}(V)\neq\emptyset$ , the stability inequality (4.19) becomes

$$ \int_{U}\left(|B_{\Sigma}|^{2}+\operatorname{Ric}(N_{\Sigma},N_{\Sigma})\right)\phi^{2}\,d\|V\|\leq\int_{U}|\nabla\phi|^{2}\,d\|V\|+2\kappa_{0}\int_{U}\phi^{2}\,d\|\delta V\|_{sing}. $$

However, it is unclear whether one can recover the boundary term as in the classical case even when $\phi$ is supported inside $\operatorname{reg}V$ because we do not know the convergence of the Radon measures $\mu^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}$ instead of $\hat{\mu}^{\partial}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}$ .

#### Remark 4.13.

By the trace inequality in Lemma 3.8, (4.19) implies for any $\delta>0$

$$ \int|\mathbf{B}_{V}|^{2}\psi^{2}\,d\|V\|\leq(1+\delta)\int|\nabla\psi|^{2}\,d\|V\|+C(n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\delta)\int\psi^{2}\,d\|V\| $$

which is expressed entirely in interior terms resembling the concept of $\delta$ -stability as studied in [31], for example.

### 4.3. Excluding Classical Tangent Cones

As a first step towards the optimal regularity of limit-interface $V$ arising from stable solutions to the Allen-Cahn equation as in Theorem 4.8, we will show in this section that one can rule out classical tangent cones both in the interior and at the boundary for a generic set of singular points in $\operatorname{sing}V$ . Our method mostly follows the work of [58] but extending to the Riemannian setting with boundary. Besides our previous work [39], the conclusions in Theorem 4.8 will also play a major role in the arguments below.

We first recall the notion of classical tangent cones based at an interior point.

#### Definition 4.14 (Interior classical tangent cones).

Let $\mathbf{C}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ be a stationary integral varifold cone (i.e. $(\eta_{0,r})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}$ for all $r>0$ ). We say that $\mathbf{C}$ is an interior classical tangent cone if

$$ \operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|=\bigcup_{j=1}^{N}P_{j} $$

for some $N\geq 3$ , and each $P_{j}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is a distinct half-hyperplane meeting along a common $(n-2)$ -dimensional subspace.

#### Remark 4.15.

By the stationarity and integrality of $\mathbf{C}$ , in fact we have as varifolds

$$ \mathbf{C}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Theta_{j}|P_{j}|\quad\text{ for some constants $\Theta_{j}\in\mathbb{N}$.} $$

Moreover, if we denote $\eta_{j}$ to be the outward unit co-normal of $\partial P_{j}$ with respect to the half-hyperplane $P_{j}$ , then stationarity implies the balancing condition

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{N}\Theta_{j}\eta_{j}=0 $$

is satisfied along the spine $S(\mathbf{C})=\cap_{j=1}^{N}P_{j}$ (recall Definition 3.25).

Next, we introduce an analogous notion of classical tangent cones based at a boundary point.

#### Definition 4.16 (Boundary classical tangent cones).

Let $\mathbf{C}\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ be a free boundary stationary integral varifold cone (i.e. $(\eta_{0,r})_{\sharp}\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{C}$ for all $r>0$ ) with free boundary on $\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . We say that $\mathbf{C}$ is a boundary classical tangent cone if

$$ \operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|=\bigcup_{j=1}^{N}P_{j}\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+} $$

for some $N\geq 2$ , and each $P_{j}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is a distinct half-hyperplane meeting along a common $(n-2)$ -dimensional subspace. We further divide the case according to the dichotomy (3.49) on the spine of the doubled cone $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ (as defined in Lemma 3.10). We say that $\mathbf{C}$ is of

- • Type I: if $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\subset\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ , $N\geq 2$ , and each $P_{j}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ but $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\neq\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ ;

- • Type II: if $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\perp\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ and $N\geq 3$ .

#### Remark 4.17.

By the free boundary stationarity and integrality of $\mathbf{C}$ , in fact we have as varifolds

$$ \mathbf{C}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Theta_{j}|P_{j}|\quad\text{ for some constants $\Theta_{j}\in\mathbb{N}$} $$

if $\mathbf{C}$ is of type I (c.f. Example 3.28). Moreover, if we denote $\eta_{j}$ to be the outward unit co-normal of $\partial P_{j}$ with respect to the half-hyperplane $P_{j}$ , then free boundary stationarity implies the free boundary balancing condition

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{N}\Theta_{j}\eta_{j}\perp\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+} $$

is satisfied along the spine $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})=\cap_{j=1}^{N}P_{j}\subset\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . If $\mathbf{C}$ is of type II, then the doubled cone $\overline{\mathbf{C}}$ is in fact an interior classical tangent cone with $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\perp\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ .

The main result of this section is the following:

#### Theorem 4.18 (Exclusion of classical tangent cones).

Let $\{\varepsilon_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of positive real numbers such that $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ , and let $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of solutions to (4.6) satisfying (A1)-(A2) in Assumptions 4.2. Assume, furthermore, that each $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ is stable, i.e. (A3) in Assumption 4.6 is satisfied. Then, for any limit-interface $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ obtained from Theorem 4.3,

$$ \mathcal{Z}\subset\operatorname{spt}\|V\| \mathcal{H}^{n-2}(\mathcal{Z})=0 $$

such that for any $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\setminus\mathcal{Z}$ , there does not exist $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ which is an interior classical tangent cone in $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ when $x\in\Omega$ ; or a boundary classical tangent cone in $T^{+}_{x}\widetilde{M}$ when $x\in\partial\Omega$ .

#### Proof.

Our proof follows the main strategy of [58, Proposition 3.2] which treats the interior case in the Euclidean setting. First of all, the $\varepsilon$ -stability inequality (4.15) implies that after passing to a subsequence, we have

$$ |\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}|^{2}\;d\mu_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\rightharpoonup\mu $$

as Radon measures on $U$ . Now, we define

$$ \mathcal{Z}:=\left\{x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\;:\;\limsup_{r\to 0}\frac{\mu(B_{r}(x))}{r^{n-3}}>0\right\}, $$

which is a Borel set since $\mu$ is a Radon measure on $U$ . Moreover, we have $\mathcal{H}^{n-3+\gamma}(\mathcal{Z})=0$ for every $\gamma>0$ (c.f. [55, Remark 3.1 and Theorem 3.2]).

We now show that such $\mathcal{Z}$ satisfies the assertion in the theorem by a contradiction argument as in [58]. Suppose on the contrary that there exists $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\setminus\mathcal{Z}$ such that some tangent cone of $V$ at $x$ is a classical tangent cone. We will focus on the case $x\in\partial\Omega$ is a boundary point (as the interior case is similar and has been treated in the Euclidean setting in [58]). Therefore, we would obtain a tangent cone $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ at $x\in\partial\Omega$ which is a boundary classical tangent cone in $T^{+}_{x}\widetilde{M}$ . There are two cases to consider according to whether $\mathbf{C}$ is of type I or type II as described in Definition 4.16.

We first look at the case where $\mathbf{C}$ is of type I, i.e.

$$ T_{x}\partial\Omega\neq\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|=\bigcup_{j=1}^{N}P_{j} $$

for some $N\geq 2$ , and each $P_{j}\subset T^{+}_{x}\widetilde{M}$ is a distinct half-hyperplane meeting along the $(n-2)$ -dimensional spine $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})\subset T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . After a rotation, we may assume that $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ and the half-hyperplanes $P_{j}$ can be expressed as

$$ P_{j}=\{t\textbf{p}_{j}\;:\;t\geq 0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2} $$

for some distinct vectors $\textbf{p}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}$ with $|\textbf{p}_{j}|=1/2$ .

Step 1: Passing the analysis back to the $\varepsilon$ -level.

Since $\mathbf{C}\in\operatorname{VarTan}(V,x)$ is a tangent cone at $x$ , we have $\lim_{i\to\infty}(\eta_{0,r_{i}})_{\sharp}(\exp_{x}^{-1})_{\sharp}V=\mathbf{C}$ for some $r_{i}\to 0$ . On the other hand, $V=\lim_{i\to\infty}V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}$ for some $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ , where each $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ is a stable solution to (4.6) with $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{i}$ satisfying (A1)-(A2) in Assumptions 4.2. After passing to a subsequence, we can assume without loss of generality that

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}(\eta_{0,r_{i}})_{\sharp}(\exp_{x}^{-1})_{\sharp}V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}=\mathbf{C}\quad\text{ and }\quad\lim_{i\to\infty}\frac{\varepsilon_{i}}{r_{i}}=0. $$

Setting

$$ \tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}:=\frac{\varepsilon_{i}}{r_{i}}\to 0\quad\text{ and }\quad\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}:=u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\circ\exp_{x}\circ\eta_{0,r_{i}^{-1}}. $$

If we let $\Phi_{x,r_{i}}:=\exp_{x}\circ\eta_{0,r_{i}^{-1}}:B^{\delta}_{i_{0}/2}(0)\to B^{g}_{r_{i}i_{0}/2}(x)$ which is a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism taking $\Omega_{i}\cap B^{\delta}_{R}(0)$ to $\Omega\cap B^{g}_{Rr_{i}}(x)$ for any fixed $R<\min\{\frac{i_{0}}{2},\frac{1}{2\kappa_{0}}\}$ where $\Omega_{i}\subset T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ are $C^{2}$ domains satisfying

$$ \Omega_{i}\cap B^{\delta}_{R}(0)\text{ converges locally in $C^{2}$ to }T^{+}_{x}\widetilde{M}\cap B^{\delta}_{R}(0), $$

Therefore, $\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}\in C^{2}(\overline{\Omega}_{i}\cap B^{\delta}_{R}(0))$ are stable solutions to the homogeneous Allen-Cahn equation

$$ -\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}^{2}\Delta_{\tilde{g}_{i}}\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}+W^{\prime}(\tilde{u}_{\varepsilon_{i}})=0\qquad\text{in $\Omega_{i}\cap B^{\delta}_{R}(0)$} $$

where $\tilde{g}_{i}:=r_{i}^{-2}\Phi^{*}_{x,r_{i}}g$ is a Riemannian metric on $B^{\delta}_{R}(0)$ , together with the homogeneous Neumann boundary condition

$$ \frac{\partial\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}}{\partial\tilde{\nu}_{i}}=0\qquad\text{ along $\partial\Omega_{i}\cap B^{\delta}_{R}(0)$} $$

where $\tilde{\nu}_{i}$ is the outward unit normal of $\partial\Omega_{i}$ with respect to the metric $\tilde{g}_{i}$ . Note that the Riemannian metrics $\tilde{g}_{i}$ converge uniformly on $B^{\delta}_{R}(0)$ in $C^{2}$ to the flat metric $\delta$ on $T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ and $\Omega_{i}$ converges in $C^{2}$ -sense to $T_{x}^{+}\widetilde{M}$ by (4.37).

We now check that $\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}$ satisfies uniform bounds (A1)-(A2) with $U=B^{\delta}_{R}(0)\subset T_{x}\widetilde{M}$ with respect to the metric $\tilde{g}_{i}$ in Assumptions 4.2. It is clear from the definition that (A2) is satisfied by $\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}$ with the same $C_{0}$ . On the other hand, the uniform energy bound (A1), with a different $\tilde{E}_{0}$ , can be seen from the almost-monotonicity formula applied to $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ (c.f. [39, Proposition 4.15]). Therefore, Theorem 4.3 can be applied to the varifolds $V^{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}}\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(B^{\delta}_{R}(0))$ defined by

$$ V^{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}}(\phi):=\int_{\{y\in\Omega_{i}\cap B^{\delta}_{R}(0):|\nabla^{\tilde{g}_{i}}\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}(y)|\neq 0\}}\phi\left(y,S^{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}}(y)\right)\ d\mu_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}}(y)\qquad\forall\phi\in C_{c}(G(B^{\delta}_{R}(0))). $$

It is straightforward from (4.36) and the definitions that

$$ V^{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}}\to\mathbf{C}\quad\text{as varifolds in $\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(B^{\delta}_{R}(0))$}. $$

Recall that $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\setminus\mathcal{Z}$ , after passing to a subsequence of $\{\varepsilon_{i}\}$ , we can further assume that

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\int_{B^{\delta}_{2}(0)}|\tilde{\mathcal{A}}_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}}|^{2}\;d\tilde{\mu}_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}}=\lim_{i\to\infty}\frac{1}{(2r_{i})^{n-3}}\int_{B^{g}_{2r_{i}}(x)}|\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}|^{2}d\mu_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}=0 $$

where the first integral is computed with respect to the metric $\tilde{g}_{i}$ .

Therefore, after suitably passing to subsequences, we can reduce our problem to the following situation (we are omitting the tildes for simplicity): let $U=B_{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ denote the Euclidean ball of radius $2$ centred at the origin, there exists a sequence of positive real numbers $\{\varepsilon_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ such that

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\varepsilon_{i}=0 $$

and a sequence $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ of $C^{2}$ solutions to the homogeneous Allen-Cahn equation

$$ -\varepsilon_{i}^{2}\Delta_{g_{i}}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}+W^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})=0\qquad\text{ in $\Omega_{i}\cap B_{2}$} $$

with homogeneous Neumann boundary condition

$$ \frac{\partial u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}{\partial\nu_{i}}=0\qquad\text{ along $\partial\Omega_{i}\cap B_{2}$} $$

where $\{g_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ is a sequence of $C^{2}$ Riemannian metrics on $B_{2}$ and $\{\Omega_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ is a sequence of Euclidean $C^{2}$ domains in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with outward unit normal $\nu_{i}$ (with respect to $g_{i}$ ) such that

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}g_{i}=\delta\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\lim_{i\to\infty}\Omega_{i}=\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+} $$

in the $C^{2}$ -sense. Moreover, $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ satisfies the uniform bounds (A1)-(A2) in Assumptions 4.2; $\{g_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty}$ and are stable in the sense of (4.10) in (A3), Assumptions 4.6. Moreover, we have in addition

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}=\mathbf{C}\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\lim_{i\to\infty}\int_{B_{2}}|\mathcal{A}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}|^{2}\;d\mu_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}=0. $$

Moreover, we set up our coordinates $(y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ so that

$$ S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})=\{(0,z)\;:\;z\in\mathbb{R}^{n-2}\}=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2}. $$

Step 2: Show that, in the limit sense as $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ , for $\mathcal{L}^{n-2}$ -a.e. point on the spine $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})$ , the $y$ -cross sections of all the intermediate level sets of $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ are uniformly regular.

More precisely, we claim that there exists some $c=c(W)>0$ such that if we denote the set of irregular cross sections by

$$ \mathcal{I}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}:=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{n-2}\;:\;\begin{array}[]{l}\textrm{$|z|<1$ and for any $r>0$, there exists some $z^{\prime}\in B_{r}(z)$ such that }\\
\textrm{$|\nabla^{g_{i}}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(y^{\prime},z^{\prime})|_{g_{i}}<\frac{c}{\varepsilon_{i}}$ for some $|y^{\prime}|<1$ and $|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(y^{\prime},z^{\prime})|\leq\frac{1}{2}$}\end{array}\right\}, $$

then

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{L}^{n-2}(\mathcal{I}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})=0. $$

#### Remark 4.19.

Note that by standard elliptic estimates (c.f. [39, Lemma 4.7]), we have the uniform gradient estimate $\varepsilon_{i}|\nabla^{g_{i}}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(y^{\prime},z^{\prime})|_{g_{i}}\leq C$ for some large enough $C>0$ . Therefore, (4.43) amounts to showing that in a limiting measure-theoretic sense, inside the transition layer $\{|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|\leq\frac{1}{2}\}$ , the gradient of $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ is indeed of order $\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{i}}$ .

The proof first involves an estimate of the left hand side of (4.43) by a combination of covering arguments, standard elliptic estimates and the two-dimensional Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality. Then, by the vanishing of the discrepancy function in the $L^{1}$ -limit (Theorem 4.3(1)) and the simplifying assumption (4.42) from Step 1, we can obtain (4.43) verbatim from the proof of [58, Lemma 4.1].

Step 3: Show that, in the limit sense as $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ , for $\mathcal{L}^{n-2}$ -a.e. point on the spine $S(\overline{\mathbf{C}})$ , we have at a fixed distance from the spine the cross sections of all the intermediate level sets of $u_{\varepsilon}$ concentrate near every $P_{j}$ .

Recall that

$$ \operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|=\bigcup_{j=1}^{N}\{t\textbf{p}_{j}\;:\;t\geq 0\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2} $$

for some $N\geq 2$ and distinct vectors $\textbf{p}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}$ with $|\textbf{p}_{j}|=1/2$ . Define the non-concentration set along the spine by

$$ \mathcal{N}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}:=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{n-2}\;:\;\begin{array}[]{l}\textrm{$|z|<1$, and there exists some $t^{\prime}\in[-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}]$ and $j^{\prime}=1,\cdots,N$ }\\
\textrm{such that $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(y,z)\neq t^{\prime}$ for all $y$ with $|y-\textbf{p}_{j^{\prime}}|<\sigma$}\end{array}\right\}, $$

then we claim that

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{L}^{n-2}(\mathcal{N}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})=0. $$

To prove (4.44), it suffices to establish $\lim_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{L}^{n-2}(\mathcal{N}^{j}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})=0$ for each $j=1,\cdots,N$ , where

$$ \mathcal{N}^{j}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}:=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{n-2}\;:\;\begin{array}[]{l}\textrm{$|z|<1$, and there exists some $t^{\prime}\in[-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}]$ }\\
\textrm{such that $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(y,z)\neq t^{\prime}$ for all $y$ with $|y-\textbf{p}_{j}|<\sigma$}\end{array}\right\}. $$

For notational simplicity, we will fix $j$ and write the vector $\textbf{p}=\textbf{p}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}$ and the $(n-1)$ -dimensional half-hyperplane $P=P_{j}$ . There are two cases to consider: either $\textbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}\setminus\partial\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}$ or $\textbf{p}\in\partial\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}$ . We will focus only on the latter case as the former case is similar and resembles the interior theory treated in [58, Lemma 4.2]. From now on, we take

and we will denote, for any $z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ , the half-cylinder of size $\frac{\sigma}{2}$ centred at $(\textbf{p},z^{\prime})$ by

$$ \limsup_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{L}^{n-2}(B_{\frac{\sigma}{4}}(z^{\prime})\cap\mathcal{N}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})>0. $$

For any $z^{\prime\prime}\in B_{\frac{\sigma}{4}}(z^{\prime})\cap\mathcal{N}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}$ , by the definition of $\mathcal{N}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}$ and $S_{i}(\textbf{p},z^{\prime})$ , we must have

and thus $\limsup_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{L}^{n-1}(S_{i}(\textbf{p},z^{\prime}))>0$ by the choice of $z^{\prime}$ . This will immediately lead to a contradiction once we show that

$$ u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\to 1 B_{\sigma}(\textbf{p},z^{\prime})\setminus P $$

$$ \mu_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}(\mathfrak{B}_{\ell})\leq 2\Theta(P)\eta^{-1}\int_{\mathfrak{B}_{\ell}\cap\Omega_{i}}|\xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})|\;dv_{g_{i}}+\big(1-g_{i}(N_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}},\nabla^{g_{i}}d_{g_{i}}^{P})^{2}\big)\;d\mu_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}} $$

which goes to zero as $i\to\infty$ by Theorem 4.3 (1) and (4.42) again. This shows that

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\mu_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}(\mathcal{B}^{b}_{i}(\textbf{p},z^{\prime}))\leq N(n)\lim_{i\to\infty}\mu_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}(\mathfrak{B}_{\ell})=0. $$

#### Lemma 4.21.

$\lim_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{L}^{n-1}(S^{II}_{i}(\textbf{p},z^{\prime};b))=0$ .

#### Lemma 4.22.

There exists $s_{0}=s_{0}(\Theta(P))\in(0,1)$ small enough such that for any $s\in(0,s_{0})$ , we have

The last inequality is due to the observation (c.f. Combining the above with (4.55), and taking limsup on both sides of (4.54), we obtain

$$ \limsup_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{L}^{n-1}(S^{I}_{i}(\textbf{p},z^{\prime};b))\leq\left(\omega_{n-1}\left(\frac{\sigma}{2}\right)^{n-1}+\frac{1}{\Theta(P)}\right)s, $$

which proves the assertion in the lemma. ∎

By Lemma 4.21 and 4.22, together with (4.49), we have

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{L}^{n-1}(S_{i}(\textbf{p},z^{\prime}))\leq C(n)s\qquad\text{for all $s\in(0,s_{0})$,} $$

hence we obtain the desired conclusion (4.46).

In what follows, we will use $B^{k}_{r}$ to denote the Euclidean ball of radius $r>0$ centred at the origin. Let $\pi_{S(\mathbf{C})}$ be the orthogonal projection map (with respect to the flat metric) onto the spine $S(\mathbf{C})\cong\mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ . We first establish a lemma saying that generic level sets of $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ satisfy some nice properties.

$$ |\nabla u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|\geq\frac{c}{\varepsilon_{i}}\qquad\text{ on $B^{2}_{1}\times B^{n-2}_{r_{z}}(z)\cap\left\{|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|\leq\frac{1}{2}\right\}$.} $$

Applying an elementary geometric lemma [58, Lemma 4.3]2525 25 The proof there works verbatim in the Riemannian setting with boundary., Lemma 4.23 with another use of Fatou’s lemma implies that for $\mathcal{L}^{1}$ -a.e. $t\in(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ such that (1) and (2) in Lemma 4.23 holds,

$$ \liminf_{i\to\infty}\int_{\ell_{z}}|\kappa^{i}_{z}|\;ds_{g_{i}}=0 $$

for $\mathcal{L}^{n-2}$ -a.e. $z\in B^{n-2}_{1}\setminus(\mathcal{I}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\cup\mathcal{N}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})$ which is also a regular value of $\pi_{S(\mathbf{C})}$ restricted on the level hypersurface $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}=t\}$ in $B^{2}_{1}\times(B^{n-2}_{1}\setminus\mathcal{I}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})$ . Here, $\ell^{i}_{z}:=\pi_{S(\mathbf{C})}^{-1}(z)\cap\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}=t\}$ is a $C^{3}$ planar curve contained in $B^{2}_{1}\times\{z\}$ , and $\kappa^{i}_{z}$ is the geodesic curvature of the planar curve $\ell^{i}_{z}$ with respect to $g_{i}$ . Since $\lim_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{L}^{n-2}(\mathcal{I}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\cup\mathcal{N}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})=0$ by (4.43) and (4.44), we can choose a sequence of $z_{i}\in B^{n-2}_{1}\setminus(\mathcal{I}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\cup\mathcal{N}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})$ which is a regular value of $\pi_{S(\mathbf{C})}$ restricted on the level hypersurface $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}=t\}$ in $B^{2}_{1}\times(B^{n-2}_{1}\setminus\mathcal{I}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})$ and, possibly after passing to a subsequence,

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\int_{\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}}|\kappa^{i}_{z_{i}}|\;ds_{g_{i}}=0. $$

Finally, we describe the contradiction arguments. Note that each $\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}$ is a non-empty union of disjoint, connected, properly embedded planar curves in $\Omega_{i}\cap(B^{2}_{1}\times\{z_{i}\})$ with (possibly empty) free boundary in $\partial\Omega_{i}\cap(B^{2}_{1}\times\{z_{i}\})$ . Moreover, by the definition of $\mathcal{N}_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}$ , $\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}$ must intersect every one of the disjoint disks $B^{2}_{\sigma}(\textbf{p}_{j})\times\{z_{i}\}$ for all $j=1,\cdots,N$ . Since $N\geq 2$ and $\operatorname{spt}\|\mathbf{C}\|\neq\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ , for all sufficiently large $i$ (recall (4.41)), we have one of the following cases to consider: (in what follows, we call a component “unbounded” if it is not contained in a compact subset of $B^{2}_{1}\times\{z_{i}\}$ )

- • there exists a closed (i.e. without boundary) component of $\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}$ , which would result in $\int_{\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}}|\kappa^{i}_{z_{i}}|\;ds_{g_{i}}\geq 1.99\pi$ .

- • there exists a component of $\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}$ with two free boundary points at $\partial\Omega_{i}\cap(B^{2}_{1}\times\{z_{i}\})$ , which would result in $\int_{\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}}|\kappa^{i}_{z_{i}}|\;ds_{g_{i}}\geq 0.99\pi$ .

- • there exists a component of $\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}$ that intersects both $B^{2}_{\sigma}(\textbf{p}_{j_{1}})\times\{z_{i}\}$ and $B^{2}_{\sigma}(\textbf{p}_{j_{2}})\times\{z_{i}\}$ for some $j_{1}\neq j_{2}$ such that one of the $\textbf{p}_{j_{1}}$ or $\textbf{p}_{j_{2}}$ does not lie on $\partial\mathbb{R}^{2}_{+}$ , by the Hausdorff convergence of the level sets in Theorem 4.3 (2), we must have

$$ \int_{\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}}|\kappa^{i}_{z_{i}}|\;ds_{g_{i}}\geq c(\textbf{p}_{j_{1}},\textbf{p}_{j_{2}},\sigma)>0. $$

- • there exists an unbounded component of $\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}$ that intersects only one $B^{2}_{\sigma}(\textbf{p}_{j})\times\{z_{i}\}$ for some $\textbf{p}_{j}\neq(0,\frac{1}{2})$ which has exactly one free boundary point at $\partial\Omega_{i}\cap(B^{2}_{1}\times\{z_{i}\})$ , in this case we must have

$$ \int_{\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}}|\kappa^{i}_{z_{i}}|\;ds_{g_{i}}\geq c(\textbf{p}_{j},\sigma)>0. $$

- • there exists an unbounded component of $\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}$ that intersects only one $B^{2}_{\sigma}(\textbf{p}_{j})\times\{z_{i}\}$ without boundary points, which would again result in $\int_{\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}}|\kappa^{i}_{z_{i}}|\;ds_{g_{i}}\geq 0.99\pi$ .

Therefore, in all of the above cases, we always have (recall that $\sigma$ only depends on $\mathbf{C}$ as well)

$$ \int_{\ell^{i}_{z_{i}}}|\kappa^{i}_{z_{i}}|\;ds_{g_{i}}\geq c(\mathbf{C})>0 $$

which clearly contradicts (4.59). This finishes the proof of excluding boundary classical tangent cones of Type I. The proof for Type II is very similar and the details are left to the reader. ∎

## Appendix A Monotonicity of reflected density

In this appendix, we use the reflected ball arguments as in [59] to establish a monotonicity-type formula for the “reflected” rescaled energy up to the boundary. Besides giving an alternative approach to the monotonicity formula in [39], the reflected ball arguments have the advantage that the balls can intersect the boundary without being centred at a boundary point. This yields up-to-the-boundary Hausdorff convergence of the intermediate level sets $\{|u_{\varepsilon}|\leq 1-b\}$ to the support of the limit-interface (see Theorem 4.3 (2) and Remark 4.5).

Throughout this appendix, we assume that $u_{\varepsilon}\in C^{3}(\overline{\Omega}\cap U)$ solves the following inhomogeneous Allen-Cahn equation as in [39]:

$$ \begin{cases}-\varepsilon\Delta_{g}u_{\varepsilon}+\dfrac{W^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})}{\varepsilon}=\lambda_{\varepsilon}&\text{in }\Omega\cap U,\\[4.0pt]
\partial u_{\varepsilon}/\partial\nu=0&\text{on }\partial\Omega\cap U,\end{cases} $$

where $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ , with (A1)-(A2) in Assumptions 4.2 and

$$ |\lambda_{\varepsilon}|\leq\Lambda_{0}. $$

#### Remark A.1.

We will mainly focus on the homogeneous case $\Lambda_{0}=0$ . When $\Lambda_{0}\neq 0$ , we can consider as in [39] the following modified (non-negative) potential

$$ \widetilde{W}_{\varepsilon}(s)=W(s)-\varepsilon\lambda_{\varepsilon}s+\varepsilon C_{0}\Lambda_{0}. $$

and the following modified normalized energy density and discrepancy function (recall (4.3)):

$$ \widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon}):=e_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})+f_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon}),\qquad\widetilde{\xi}_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon}):=\xi_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon})-f_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon}). $$

where $f_{\varepsilon}(u_{\varepsilon}):=h_{0}^{-1}(-\lambda_{\varepsilon}u_{\varepsilon}+C_{0}\Lambda_{0})$ satisfies $0\leq f_{\varepsilon}\leq 2h_{0}^{-1}C_{0}\Lambda_{0}$ . Thus the same computations below apply to $\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}$ and $\widetilde{\xi}_{\varepsilon}$ in place of $e_{\varepsilon}$ and $\xi_{\varepsilon}$ . Note that the associated varifold $V^{u_{\varepsilon}}$ defined in (4.5) is independent of the potential term and hence the limit-interface $V$ would be the same even if we consider the modified quantities as above.

In what follows, we let $V=\lim_{i\to\infty}V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}$ be a limit-interface as obtained in Theorem 4.3 for some $\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ . We will write $u_{i}=u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ for simplicity. The goal of this appendix is to establish the following (c.f. Theorem 4.3 (2) and Remark 4.5):

#### Proposition A.2.

For any $b\in(0,1)$ , the subsets $\{|u_{i}|\leq 1-b\}$ locally converge in the Hausdorff sense to $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ in $\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ .

To proceed with the reflected balls argument, we recall the Fermi coordinates with respect to $\partial\Omega$ . Fix $p\in\partial\Omega$ , and let $(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n-1})$ be geodesic normal coordinates on a neighbourhood $\mathcal{O}$ of $p$ in $\partial\Omega$ . We parametrise an open subset of the two-sided tubular neighbourhood $U_{\frac{1}{2\kappa_{0}}}(\partial\Omega)$ by

$$ \Phi:\mathcal{O}\times\left(-\frac{1}{2\kappa_{0}},\frac{1}{2\kappa_{0}}\right)\longrightarrow\widetilde{M},\qquad\Phi(y,t):=\exp_{y}(-t\nu(y)). $$

Here $t$ is geometrically the signed boundary distance function (recall (2.4)), and $t>0$ corresponds to the interior of $\Omega$ . In these coordinates, the metric takes the form $g=dt^{2}+g_{t}$ , with $g_{t}=g_{0}+2t\mathrm{I\!I}_{0}+O(t^{2}),$ where $\mathrm{I\!I}_{0}$ is the second fundamental form with respect to the inward unit normal $\partial_{t}=\nabla d$ . We define reflection across $\partial\Omega$ by

$$ \mathcal{R}(y,t):=(y,-t). $$

Then $\mathcal{R}|_{\partial\Omega}=\mathrm{Id}$ and $\mathcal{R}^{2}=\mathrm{Id}$ (i.e. $\mathcal{R}$ is an involution). Its differential is exactly $\operatorname{diag}(I_{n-1},-1)$ , but reflection is not generally an isometry. More precisely,

$$ (D\mathcal{R}_{x})^{*}D\mathcal{R}_{x}=\mathrm{Id}+O(|t|), $$

where the adjoint is taken with respect to the metrics at $x$ and $\mathcal{R}(x)$ .

Fix a point $a\in\overline{\Omega}\cap U_{\frac{1}{4\kappa_{0}}}(\partial\Omega)$ which will be our centre, and set

$$ r(x):=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,a),\qquad\widetilde{r}(x):=r(\mathcal{R}(x)),\qquad\widetilde{B}_{\rho}(a):=\Omega\cap U_{\frac{1}{4\kappa_{0}}}(\partial\Omega)\cap\{\widetilde{r}(x)<\rho\} $$

where $\rho\in(0,\frac{1}{4\kappa_{0}})$ will be taken small enough so that all the functions and vector fields are well-defined and their cutoffs are compactly supported in $U$ . Introduce

$$ \zeta(x):=\frac{1}{2}\nabla r^{2}=r\nabla r=-\exp_{x}^{-1}(a),\qquad A(x):=(D\mathcal{R}_{x})^{-1},\qquad Y(x):=A(x)\zeta(\mathcal{R}(x)). $$

Fix $\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}([0,\infty))$ with $0\leq\varphi\leq 1$ , $\varphi^{\prime}\leq 0$ , $\varphi\equiv 1$ on $[0,1]$ , and $\varphi\equiv 0$ on $[2,\infty)$ . For a small scale $\rho>0$ , define

$$ X(x):=\varphi(r(x)/\rho)\zeta(x)+\varphi(\widetilde{r}(x)/\rho)Y(x)=X_{1}(x)+X_{2}(x). $$

This vector field is compactly supported in $U$ , and $|X|\leq C\rho$ . Along $\partial\Omega$ , the map $D\mathcal{R}$ is orthogonal reflection across $T\partial\Omega$ . Since $r=\widetilde{r}$ there, the normal components of $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ cancel, so that $X\cdot\nu=0$ .

As in [39, Section 4], standard computations give $\nabla\zeta=\mathrm{Id}+O(r)$ and $\operatorname{div}\zeta=n+O(r)$ . Hence

$$ \operatorname{div}X_{1}=n\varphi(r/\rho)+\frac{r}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(r/\rho)+O(r)\varphi(r/\rho), $$

and, writing $\nabla X(v,v)=\langle\nabla_{v}X,v\rangle$ , we obtain

$$ \nabla X_{1}(\nabla u,\nabla u)=\varphi(r/\rho)|\nabla u|^{2}+\frac{r}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(r/\rho)(\partial_{r}u)^{2}+O(r)\varphi(r/\rho)|\nabla u|^{2}. $$

For the reflected term, differentiating $Y=A(\zeta\circ\mathcal{R})$ gives

$$ \nabla Y=(\nabla A)(\zeta\circ\mathcal{R})+A\circ(\nabla\zeta)_{\mathcal{R}(x)}\circ D\mathcal{R}_{x}=\mathrm{Id}+O(\widetilde{r}+t). $$

Here $\nabla A=O(1)$ on the fixed tubular neighbourhood, while the second term is $\mathrm{Id}+O(\widetilde{r})$ . Moreover, from $d\widetilde{r}(Y)=\widetilde{r}$ we deduce

$$ \operatorname{div}X_{2}=n\varphi(\widetilde{r}/\rho)+\frac{\widetilde{r}}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(\widetilde{r}/\rho)+O(\widetilde{r}+t)\varphi(\widetilde{r}/\rho). $$

Set $\eta=Y/\widetilde{r}$ away from $\widetilde{r}=0$ . The cutoff term in $\nabla X_{2}(\nabla u,\nabla u)$ is

$$ \frac{\widetilde{r}}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(\widetilde{r}/\rho)\langle\nabla\widetilde{r},\nabla u\rangle\langle\eta,\nabla u\rangle. $$

By (A.3),

$$ \nabla\widetilde{r}=(D\mathcal{R}_{x})^{*}D\mathcal{R}_{x}\eta=\eta+O(t). $$

Consequently, replacing this product by $\langle\eta,\nabla u\rangle^{2}$ introduces an error bounded by

$$ Ct\frac{\widetilde{r}}{\rho}|\varphi^{\prime}(\widetilde{r}/\rho)|\,|\nabla u|^{2}. $$

Write

$$ S_{\rho}:=\varphi(r/\rho)+\varphi(\widetilde{r}/\rho),\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_{\rho}:=-\frac{\widetilde{r}}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(\widetilde{r}/\rho)\geq 0. $$

On the support of the first cutoff, $r\leq 2\rho$ ; on the support of the reflected cutoff, $0\leq t\leq\widetilde{r}\leq 2\rho$ . Thus there exist a function $q_{1}$ and a tensor $Q_{2}$ , depending on $\rho$ and $\varphi$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{div}X \displaystyle=nS_{\rho}+\frac{r}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(r/\rho)+\frac{\widetilde{r}}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(\widetilde{r}/\rho)+q_{1}, \displaystyle\nabla X(\nabla u,\nabla u) \displaystyle=S_{\rho}|\nabla u|^{2}+\frac{r}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(r/\rho)(\partial_{r}u)^{2}+\frac{\widetilde{r}}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(\widetilde{r}/\rho)\langle\eta,\nabla u\rangle^{2}+Q_{2}(\nabla u,\nabla u), $$

with the cutoff-independent bounds

$$ |q_{1}|\leq C\rho S_{\rho},\qquad|Q_{2}|\leq C\rho(S_{\rho}+T_{\rho}). $$

Recall now the Pohozaev identity from [39, Section 4] (note that we have a different normalization constant in (4.3)). Since $X\cdot\nu=0$ and $\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=0$ , for $\lambda_{\varepsilon}=0$ it reads

$$ \int_{\Omega\cap U}\bigl(e_{\varepsilon}\operatorname{div}X-\varepsilon h_{0}^{-1}\nabla X(\nabla u,\nabla u)\bigr)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}=0. $$

Using $ne_{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon h_{0}^{-1}|\nabla u|^{2}=(n-1)e_{\varepsilon}-\xi_{\varepsilon}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\bigl((n-1)e_{\varepsilon}-\xi_{\varepsilon}\bigr)S_{\rho}\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}+\int_{\Omega}e_{\varepsilon}\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(r/\rho)+\frac{\widetilde{r}}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(\widetilde{r}/\rho)\right)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g} \displaystyle\quad-h_{0}^{-1}\int_{\Omega}\varepsilon\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(r/\rho)(\partial_{r}u)^{2}+\frac{\widetilde{r}}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}(\widetilde{r}/\rho)\langle\eta,\nabla u\rangle^{2}\right)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}+h_{0}^{-1}\int_{\Omega}\bigl(q_{1}e_{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon Q_{2}(\nabla u,\nabla u)\bigr)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}. $$

All integrands here and below are supported in $U$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle I(\rho) \displaystyle:=\int_{\Omega}e_{\varepsilon}S_{\rho}\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g},\qquad J_{1}(\rho):=\int_{\Omega}(-\xi_{\varepsilon})S_{\rho}\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}, \displaystyle J_{2}(\rho) \displaystyle:=h_{0}^{-1}\int_{\Omega}\varepsilon\left[\varphi(r/\rho)(\partial_{r}u)^{2}+\varphi(\widetilde{r}/\rho)\langle\eta,\nabla u\rangle^{2}\right]\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}, \displaystyle J_{3}(\rho) \displaystyle:=h_{0}^{-1}\int_{\Omega}\bigl(q_{1}e_{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon Q_{2}(\nabla u,\nabla u)\bigr)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}. $$

Using $\rho\,\partial_{\rho}\varphi(s/\rho)=-(s/\rho)\varphi^{\prime}(s/\rho)$ , the Pohozaev identity becomes

$$ (n-1)I(\rho)-\rho I^{\prime}(\rho)=-J_{1}(\rho)-\rho J_{2}^{\prime}(\rho)-J_{3}(\rho). $$

This is the argument of [59]; the error term $J_{3}$ accounts for curvature and the fact that $\mathcal{R}$ is not an isometry. Since $\varphi^{\prime}\leq 0$ , we have $I^{\prime}\geq 0$ and $J_{2}^{\prime}\geq 0$ . Moreover, $|J_{1}|\leq I$ , and (A.4) gives $|J_{3}(\rho)|\leq C\rho I(\rho)+C\rho^{2}I^{\prime}(\rho).$ Indeed, $\varepsilon h_{0}^{-1}|\nabla u|^{2}\leq 2e_{\varepsilon}$ and $\int_{\Omega}e_{\varepsilon}T_{\rho}\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}\leq\rho I^{\prime}(\rho)$ . It follows from (A.5) that $(1+C\rho)\rho I^{\prime}(\rho)\geq(n-1)I(\rho)+J_{1}(\rho)-C\rho I(\rho).$ Dividing by $1+C\rho$ and using $|J_{1}|\leq I$ , we may enlarge $C$ to obtain $\rho I^{\prime}(\rho)\geq(n-1)I(\rho)+J_{1}(\rho)-C\rho I(\rho).$ Consequently,

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\bigl(e^{C\rho}\rho^{1-n}I(\rho)\bigr)\geq e^{C\rho}\rho^{-n}J_{1}(\rho). $$

Choose such cutoffs $\varphi_{j}$ decreasing pointwise to the characteristic function $\mathbf{1}_{[0,1]}$ . By dominated convergence,

$$ \displaystyle I_{j}(\rho) \displaystyle\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}(\rho,a):=\int_{B_{\rho}(a)\cap\Omega}e_{\varepsilon}\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}+\int_{\widetilde{B}_{\rho}(a)}e_{\varepsilon}\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}, \displaystyle J_{1,j}(\rho) \displaystyle\rightarrow D_{\varepsilon}(\rho,a):=\int_{B_{\rho}(a)\cap\Omega}(-\xi_{\varepsilon})\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}+\int_{\widetilde{B}_{\rho}(a)}(-\xi_{\varepsilon})\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}. $$

We first integrate (A.6) over a compact interval of admissible positive radii and then pass to the limit. This yields the integrated inequality for $\mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}$ and $D_{\varepsilon}$ . Since the ball integrals are locally absolutely continuous in the radius, the corresponding differential inequality holds for almost every radius.

We have thus proved the following monotonicity-type formula (the interior case follows from [39, Section 4.1]).

#### Proposition A.3 (Reflected monotonicity formula).

There exists $C=C(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0},\Lambda_{0})\geq 0$ such that the following holds: for every $a\in\overline{\Omega}\cap U_{\frac{1}{4\kappa_{0}}}(\partial\Omega)$ and almost every $\rho\in(0,\frac{1}{4\kappa_{0}})$ ,

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\left(e^{C\rho}\rho^{1-n}\mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}(\rho,a)\right)\geq e^{C\rho}\rho^{-n}D_{\varepsilon}(\rho,a). $$

On the other hand, for any $a\in\Omega\cap U_{\frac{1}{4\kappa_{0}}}(\partial\Omega)$ and almost every $0<\rho<\min\{\frac{1}{4\kappa_{0}},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(a,\partial\Omega)\}$ , we have

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\left(e^{C\rho}\rho^{1-n}\int_{B_{\rho}(a)}e_{\varepsilon}\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}\right)\geq e^{C\rho}\rho^{-n}\int_{B_{\rho}(a)}(-\xi_{\varepsilon})\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}. $$

#### Remark A.4.

The monotonicity formulas above are stated for the homogeneous case, i.e. $\Lambda_{0}=0$ . When $\Lambda_{0}\neq 0$ , they hold with $e_{\varepsilon}$ and $\xi_{\varepsilon}$ replaced by $\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}$ and $\widetilde{\xi}_{\varepsilon}$ from (A.2).

With Proposition A.3, we can now proceed to the proof of Proposition A.2.

#### Proof of Proposition A.2.

Let $\mu_{i}=\mu_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}=\|V^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\|$ be the Radon measures as defined in (4.4). Note that $\mu_{i}\to\|V\|$ as Radon measures on $U$ . By [39, Theorem 3.3(2)], we already have the required Hausdorff convergence away from the boundary $\partial\Omega$ . Therefore, we now focus on the additional arguments needed to conclude the Hausdorff convergence up to the boundary using Proposition A.3.

Fix $b\in(0,1)$ and work on a relatively compact subset of $U$ , shrinking the admissible radii if needed. The local gradient estimate and the discrepancy and energy estimates in [39, Section 4.2 and Propositions 4.10, 4.13, 4.15] give

$$ \varepsilon|\nabla u_{\varepsilon}|\leq C,\qquad\xi_{\varepsilon}^{+}\leq C\varepsilon^{-4/5},\qquad\int_{B_{r}(a)\cap\Omega}e_{\varepsilon}\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}\leq Cr^{n-1} $$

for $\varepsilon\leq r\leq r_{0}$ and all centres under consideration. To obtain the last estimate for a ball meeting the boundary whose centre is interior, include it in $B_{2r}(\pi(a))\cap\Omega$ ; balls disjoint from the boundary are covered by the interior estimate. The integral discrepancy estimate then yields

$$ r^{-n}\int_{B_{r}(a)\cap\Omega}\xi_{\varepsilon}^{+}\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}\leq Cr^{-7/8}\qquad\text{for any $c\varepsilon^{4/5}\leq r\leq r_{0}$}. $$

Here $c>0$ can be any fixed constant, cf. [39, Proposition 4.13].

For the reflected sets, $t\leq\widetilde{r}$ and $\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\mathcal{R}(x))=2t$ imply

$$ \widetilde{B}_{r}(a)\subset B_{3r}(a)\cap\Omega. $$

Thus the same upper bounds apply to the reflected energy and positive discrepancy, after changing the constants.

Suppose now that $|u_{\varepsilon}(a)|\leq 1-b$ . The gradient bound in (A.9), positivity of $W$ away from its wells, and the local volume lower bound give $\varepsilon^{1-n}\mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon,a)\geq\theta_{b}>0.$ Apply Proposition A.3 from $\varepsilon$ to $s_{\varepsilon}=c\varepsilon^{4/5}$ . Choosing $c$ sufficiently small preserves a positive lower bound at $s_{\varepsilon}$ . From $s_{\varepsilon}$ to a fixed small radius, use (A.10). Its integral is bounded by $Cr^{1/8}$ , so, after decreasing $r_{0}$ , we obtain $\mathcal{E}_{\varepsilon}(r,a)\geq\theta r^{n-1}$ for $\varepsilon\leq r\leq r_{0}.$ Finally, (A.11) gives the lower bound for the original energy measure:

$$ \mu_{i}(B_{r}(a))\geq\theta_{0}r^{n-1}\quad\text{if }|u_{i}(a)|\leq 1-b,\qquad 3\varepsilon_{i}\leq r\leq r_{0}. $$

The constants are locally uniform in $a$ and independent of $i$ for all sufficiently large $i$ .

Consequently, if $a_{i}\in\{|u_{i}|\leq 1-b\}$ and $a_{i}\to x\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ , then $x\in\operatorname{spt}\mu$ . Indeed, for each fixed sufficiently small $r>0$ and all large $i$ , $B_{r/4}(a_{i})\subset\overline{B}_{r/2}(x)$ . By (A.12) and weak convergence,

$$ \mu(\overline{B}_{r/2}(x))\geq\limsup_{i\to\infty}\mu_{i}(\overline{B}_{r/2}(x))\geq\theta_{0}(r/4)^{n-1}>0. $$

For completeness, we also justify the converse approximation for every $b\in(0,1)$ . Suppose that $x\in\operatorname{spt}\mu$ and, along a subsequence, a connected neighbourhood $B\cap\overline{\Omega}$ of $x$ contains no point with $|u_{i}|\leq 1-b$ . Passing to a further subsequence, assume $u_{i}>1-b$ there. The energy bound implies $u_{i}\to 1$ in measure and in $L^{1}$ on this neighbourhood. Choose a $C^{1}$ function $h$ on $[1-b,C_{0}]$ , with bounded derivative, satisfying

$$ h(1)=0,\qquad 2Wh^{\prime}+W^{\prime}h=2W. $$

Such a function extends regularly across $1$ : writing $W(s)=(s-1)^{2}w(s)$ , with $w>0$ , it is given by

$$ h(s)=\frac{\displaystyle\int_{1}^{s}(q-1)\sqrt{w(q)}\,dq}{(s-1)\sqrt{w(s)}},\qquad h(1)=0. $$

For a nonnegative smooth cutoff $\psi$ supported in $B$ , test (A.1) with $\psi h(u_{i})$ to obtain

$$ \int_{\Omega}\psi\left(\frac{2W(u_{i})}{\varepsilon_{i}}+2h_{0}h^{\prime}(u_{i})\xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{i})\right)\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}=\lambda_{i}\int_{\Omega}\psi h(u_{i})\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}-\varepsilon_{i}\int_{\Omega}h(u_{i})\nabla u_{i}\cdot\nabla\psi\,d\mathrm{vol}_{g}. $$

The right-hand side tends to zero: its first term does so by $h(u_{i})\to 0$ in $L^{1}$ , and its second is $O(\sqrt{\varepsilon_{i}})$ by the energy bound. By [39, Theorem 5.4], $\xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{i})\to 0$ in $L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\overline{\Omega}\cap U)$ . It follows that $\int\psi W(u_{i})/\varepsilon_{i}\to 0$ , and hence $\int\psi e_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{i})\to 0$ . Taking $\psi=1$ near $x$ contradicts $x\in\operatorname{spt}\mu$ . The negative phase is treated in the same way, using a function $h$ vanishing at $-1$ . This proves the converse approximation. Together with the preceding argument and local compactness, it proves Proposition A.2. ∎

## Appendix B Revisiting rectifiability and integrality

In this appendix, we give an alternative proof of the rectifiability and integrality for stable limit-interfaces of the Allen–Cahn equation with Neumann boundary conditions, following the approach of De Rosa–Pigati [21, Sections 6–7]. We retain the vanishing-discrepancy theorem of [39], but do not use its rectifiability or integrality conclusions. The argument therefore revisits these two steps in light of stability, rather than providing an independent proof of the entire convergence result in Theorem 4.3 in the setting of general critical points. Set-up and notation are as in the previous sections (c.f. Section 4). We start with the following lemma.

#### Lemma B.1.

There is a constant $C$ , independent of $i$ , such that

$$ \int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}e_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\leq CE_{0},\qquad\int|B_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}|^{2}\,d\mu_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\leq CE_{0},\qquad\|\delta\widetilde{V}_{i}\|(\widetilde{M})\leq CE_{0}. $$

where $\widetilde{V}^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ is defined by (c.f. Remark 4.1)

$$ \widetilde{V}^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}(\phi)=\int_{\{\nabla u_{\varepsilon_{i}}\neq 0\}}\sqrt{2W(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})}|\nabla u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|\phi(x,S^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}})\,dv_{g}. $$

#### Proof.

The stress-energy tensor $T_{i}:=e_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})g-\varepsilon_{i}\,du_{i}\otimes du_{i}$ satisfies $\operatorname{div}_{g}T_{i}=0,$ and $T_{i}(\nu,\cdot)=e_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})\,g(\nu,\cdot)$ on $\partial\Omega\cap U$ . Consequently, for every $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ ,

$$ \int_{\Omega\cap U}T_{i}:\nabla X\,dv_{g}=\int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}e_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})\langle X,\nu\rangle\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}. $$

Choosing a fixed $X$ with $X=\nu$ on $\partial\Omega\cap U$ , since $|T_{i}|\leq Ce_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})$ , there holds (cf. [39, Lemma 3.2])

$$ \int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}e_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}=\int_{\Omega\cap U}T_{i}:\nabla X\,dv_{g}\leq CE_{0}. $$

We next give the isotropic boundary counterpart of [21, Theorem 6.4]. Set $w_{i}=|\nabla u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|$ . Arguing as in the proof of Proposition 4.7, yields

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Omega\cap U}\varepsilon_{i}\bigl(|\nabla^{2}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|^{2}-|\nabla w_{i}|^{2}\bigr)\,dv_{g}\leq CE_{0}, $$

where the boundary term is controlled by (B.2); note that no sign assumption on the second fundamental form of $\partial\Omega$ is required. On $\{w_{i}>0\}$ ,

$$ |\nabla^{2}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|^{2}-|\nabla w_{i}|^{2}=w_{i}^{2}|B_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}|^{2}+|\nabla^{T}w_{i}|^{2}, $$

where $\nabla^{T}$ denotes the tangential gradient along the level sets of $u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ , which proves the curvature estimate.

For almost every $s$ , the regular level set $\{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}=s\}$ meets $\partial\Omega$ orthogonally, with outward conormal $\nu$ , or it does not meet it at all, in which case part of the argument below simplifies. Its first variation is bounded as follows

$$ \displaystyle h_{0} \displaystyle\|\delta\widetilde{V}^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\|(U) \displaystyle\leq\sqrt{n-1}\left(\int_{\Omega\cap U}\varepsilon_{i}|B_{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}|^{2}w_{i}^{2}\,dv_{g}\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{\Omega\cap U}\frac{2W(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})}{\varepsilon_{i}}\,dv_{g}\right)^{1/2}+\int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}\sqrt{2W(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})}\,w_{i}\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-1} \displaystyle\leq CE_{0}. $$

This is the analogue of [21, Corollary 6.6], with the additional boundary contribution. In particular, the estimate concerns the full ambient first variation, not only vector fields tangent to the boundary. ∎

#### Proposition B.2.

The varifold $V$ is rectifiable and stationary with free boundary:

$$ \delta V(X)=0\quad\text{for every }X\in\mathfrak{X}^{tan}_{c}(U). $$

#### Proof.

We adapt the positive-density argument of [21, Theorem 6.7]. First, the boundary version of [21, Lemma 6.2] gives, for each sufficiently small $b>0$ , constants $R,c_{b}>0$ such that

$$ |u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(x)|\leq 1-b\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\|\widetilde{V}^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\|(B_{R\varepsilon_{i}}(x))\geq c_{b}\varepsilon_{i}^{n-1} $$

for all large $i$ . To see this, suppose that the normalised masses on the left tend to zero and rescale by $\varepsilon_{i}$ about the corresponding points. Elliptic estimates give a limit on $B_{R}(0)$ intersected with a full space or a half-space containing the origin. This limit is then a constant. Its value lies in $[-1+b,1-b]$ , and the equation forces it to equal $\gamma$ (the unique local non-degenerate maxima of $W$ ). Stability would then imply

$$ -W^{\prime\prime}(\gamma)\int\zeta^{2}\leq\int|\nabla\zeta|^{2} $$

for every test function supported away from the curved boundary, with no restriction on its trace on the flat boundary. A radial cutoff contradicts this inequality when $R$ is sufficiently large.

Multiplying (4.6) with $\gamma-u_{\varepsilon_{i}}$ gives

$$ \int_{\Omega\cap U}\frac{(\gamma-u_{\varepsilon_{i}})W^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})}{\varepsilon_{i}}\,dv_{g}=\int_{\Omega\cap U}\varepsilon_{i}|\nabla u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|^{2}\,dv_{g}\leq 2E_{0}. $$

The integrand on the left is nonnegative, and $W(s)\leq Cb(\gamma-s)W^{\prime}(s)$ for $|s|>1-b$ . Using $h_{0}e_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})=2W(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})/\varepsilon_{i}+h_{0}\xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})$ therefore gives

$$ \int_{\{|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|>1-b\}}e_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})\,dv_{g}\leq Cb+\int_{\Omega\cap U}|\xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})|\,dv_{g}. $$

Compare [21, equation (6.12)].

Fix a sufficiently small $r_{0}>0$ and define

$$ G_{i,b}:=\left\{x\in\Omega\cap U:\begin{array}[]{l}|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(x)|\leq 1-b,\\
\|\delta\widetilde{V}^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\|(B_{r}(x))\leq b^{-1}\|\widetilde{V}^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\|(B_{r}(x))\quad\text{for every }0<r<r_{0}\end{array}\right\}. $$

Besicovitch’s covering theorem, Lemma B.1, and (B.5) imply

$$ \|\widetilde{V}^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\|(M\setminus G_{i,b})\leq Cb+o_{i}(1). $$

This is the good-set construction in [21, equation (6.11) and the proof of Theorem 6.7]. At a point of $G_{i,b}$ , the first-variation bound in its definition and the varifold monotonicity inequality propagate (B.4) to

$$ \|\widetilde{V}^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\|(B_{r}(x))\geq c_{b}r^{n-1}\qquad(R\varepsilon_{i}\leq r<r_{0}). $$

The exponential factor absorbs both $b^{-1}$ and the ambient geometric error. Since we have bounded the full first variation in $U$ , this applies also when the ball intersects $\partial\Omega$ .

For fixed $b$ , take a weak limit $\sigma_{b}$ of $\|\widetilde{V}^{u_{\varepsilon_{i}}}\|\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}G_{i,b}$ . Then $\sigma_{b}\leq\mu$ and $(\mu-\sigma_{b})(U)\leq Cb$ . Every point of $\operatorname{spt}\sigma_{b}$ is a limit of points in $G_{i,b}$ , so (B.7), applied first on slightly smaller balls, gives $\mu(B_{r}(x))\geq c_{b}r^{n-1}$ there. Letting $b$ tend to zero along a countable sequence proves positive upper $(n-1)$ -density at $\mu$ -almost every point. Lemma B.1 and Allard’s rectifiability theorem [4, Section 5] now show that $V$ is rectifiable.

Finally, $h_{0}e_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})-\sqrt{2W(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})}|\nabla u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|\leq h_{0}|\xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})|$ combined with $|\varepsilon_{i}|\nabla u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|^{2}-\sqrt{2W(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})}|\nabla u_{\varepsilon_{i}}||\leq 2h_{0}|\xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})|$ imply that $h_{0}^{-1}T_{i}\,dv_{g}$ converges. For $X\in\mathfrak{X}^{tan}_{c}(U)$ , the right-hand side of (B.1) vanishes. Passing to the limit proves $\delta V(X)=0$ . ∎

#### Proposition B.3.

The varifold $V$ is integral, including its restriction to $\partial\Omega$ (compare with [39, Proposition 6.1]).

#### Proof.

We follow [21, Lemmas 7.7–7.8 and Theorem 7.10]. The fact that $\xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})\rightarrow 0$ in $L^{1}$ simplifies the proof.

Fix a point $x$ at which $V$ has density $\theta\in(0,\infty)$ and a unique tangent varifold $\theta|P|$ . At $\mu$ -almost every such point in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ , arguing as in [39, Proposition 6.1] it is enough to consider $P=T_{x}\partial\Omega$ . Using normal coordinates in the interior and Fermi coordinates at the boundary, choose a diagonal blow-up sequence with $\varepsilon_{i}/r_{i}\to 0$ . The resulting metrics $g_{i}$ converge smoothly to the Euclidean metric, and the domains are either a full space or the half-space $\{t\geq 0\}$ . Write $z=(y,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}$ , with $P=\{t=0\}$ , and set

$$ I_{r}:=(-r,r)\quad\text{or}\quad I_{r}:=[0,r),\qquad Q_{r}:=B_{r}^{n-1}\times I_{r}, $$

respectively. In the boundary case $\partial_{t}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}=0$ at $t=0$ . From now on, write

$$ \bar{e}_{i}:=\frac{\varepsilon_{i}}{2}|Du_{\varepsilon_{i}}|^{2}+\frac{W(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})}{\varepsilon_{i}},\qquad\bar{\xi}_{i}:=\frac{\varepsilon_{i}}{2}|Du_{\varepsilon_{i}}|^{2}-\frac{W(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})}{\varepsilon_{i}} $$

for the Euclidean energy and discrepancy in these coordinates. The metric errors vanish, and varifold convergence together with vanishing of the discrepancy in $L^{1}$ yields

$$ h_{0}^{-1}\bar{e}_{i}\,dz\rightharpoonup\theta\,\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}P,\qquad\int_{Q_{3}}\bigl(|\bar{\xi}_{i}|+\varepsilon_{i}|D_{y}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|^{2}\bigr)\,dz\longrightarrow 0. $$

The second assertion is the isotropic counterpart of [21, equation (7.12)], with the discrepancy included.

Choose $0\leq\chi\in C_{c}^{\infty}((-1,1))$ with $\chi=1$ on $[-1/2,1/2]$ , and define

$$ f_{i}(y):=\frac{1}{h_{0}}\int_{I_{1}}\chi(t)\bar{e}_{i}(y,t)\,dt. $$

As in [21, Lemma 7.7], test the stress-energy identity with $X=\chi(t)\varphi(y)\partial_{y_{a}}$ . The resulting distributional identity on $B_{2}^{n-1}$ has the form

$$ Df_{i}=\operatorname{div}R_{i}+r_{i},\qquad\|R_{i}\|_{L^{1}(B_{2}^{n-1})}+\|r_{i}\|_{L^{1}(B_{2}^{n-1})}\rightarrow 0. $$

In the Euclidean metric, the terms are explicit

$$ R_{i}^{ab}=\frac{1}{h_{0}}\int_{I_{1}}\chi\varepsilon_{i}\partial_{y_{a}}u_{i}\partial_{y_{b}}u_{i}\,dt,\qquad r_{i}^{a}=-\frac{1}{h_{0}}\int_{I_{1}}\chi^{\prime}\varepsilon_{i}\partial_{y_{a}}u_{i}\partial_{t}u_{i}\,dt. $$

Their $L^{1}$ norms tend to zero by (B.8) and Cauchy–Schwarz. The additional tensor and zeroth-order terms are bounded by $C\|g_{i}-\delta\|_{C^{1}}\int_{Q_{3}}\bar{e}_{i}$ . Since $f_{i}\geq 0$ and $f_{i}\,dy\rightharpoonup\theta\,dy$ , Allard’s strong constancy lemma [5, Theorem 1.(4)] gives

$$ f_{i}\rightarrow\theta\quad\text{in }L^{1}(B_{1}^{n-1}). $$

There holds

$$ \int_{Q_{2}\cap\{|u_{i}|>1-b\}}\bar{e}_{i}\,dz\leq Cb+o_{i}(1). $$

Put

$$ d_{i}(y):=\int_{I_{2}}\bigl(|\bar{\xi}_{i}|+\varepsilon_{i}|D_{y}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|^{2}\bigr)(y,t)\,dt. $$

The weak- $(1,1)$ estimate for the local Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator $\mathcal{M}$ and (B.8) show that $\mathcal{M}d_{i}\to 0$ in measure on $B_{1}^{n-1}$ . For fixed $b>0$ , we can therefore choose Lebesgue points $y_{i}\in B_{1}^{n-1}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle f_{i}(y_{i}) \displaystyle\rightarrow\theta, \displaystyle\mathcal{M}d_{i}(y_{i}) \displaystyle\rightarrow 0, \displaystyle\int_{I_{2}\cap\{|t|\geq 1/4\}}\bar{e}_{i}(y_{i},t)\,dt \displaystyle\rightarrow 0, \displaystyle\int_{I_{2}\cap\{|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(y_{i},\cdot)|>1-b\}}\bar{e}_{i}(y_{i},t)\,dt \displaystyle\leq Cb+o_{i}(1). $$

For the third condition use the concentration of the limit measure on $P$ . For the last one use (B.11) and Markov’s inequality, increasing $C$ so that its exceptional set occupies at most half of $B_{1}^{n-1}$ . The exceptional sets for the other conditions have vanishing measure. This makes explicit the selection used in [21, proof of Theorem 7.10]. In particular,

$$ \int_{I_{1}}\bar{e}_{i}(y_{i},t)\,dt\rightarrow h_{0}\theta,\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{i}(y_{i})\rightarrow 0. $$

Consider any sequence $t_{i}\in I_{1}$ such that $|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(y_{i},t_{i})|\leq 1-b$ , and rescale about $(y_{i},t_{i})$ by $\varepsilon_{i}$ . For each fixed $R$ , the definition of the maximal operator gives

$$ \varepsilon_{i}^{-(n-1)}\int_{B_{R\varepsilon_{i}}(y_{i},t_{i})\cap Q_{2}}\bigl(|\bar{\xi}_{i}|+\varepsilon_{i}|D_{y}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|^{2}\bigr)\,dz\leq CR^{n-1}\mathcal{M}d_{i}(y_{i})\rightarrow 0. $$

Compactness therefore gives a one-dimensional limit $q=q(t)$ satisfying (cf. [21, Lemma 7.8 and Remark 7.9])

$$ q^{\prime\prime}=W^{\prime}(q),\qquad\frac{1}{2}(q^{\prime})^{2}=W(q),\qquad|q(0)|\leq 1-b. $$

In the boundary case, if $t_{i}/\varepsilon_{i}$ remained bounded, the limit would be defined on a half-line $[-b,\infty)$ and satisfy $q^{\prime}(-b)=0$ . Equation (B.15) would force $q(-b)=\pm 1$ , and uniqueness for the ordinary differential equation would make $q$ constant, a contradiction. Moreover, another contradiction argument using (B.15) gives

$$ \varepsilon_{i}|\partial_{t}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(y_{i},t)|\geq c_{b}>0\quad\text{whenever }t\in I_{1},\quad|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(y_{i},t)|\leq 1-b, $$

for all large $i$ .

The uniform estimate $\varepsilon_{i}|Du_{\varepsilon_{i}}|\leq C$ on $Q_{2}$ and the third condition in (B.12) exclude transition points near the artificial endpoints of $I_{1}$ . Together with the preceding boundary argument, this shows that every component of

$$ \{t\in I_{1}:|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(y_{i},t)|<1-b\} $$

has both endpoints in the interior of $I_{1}$ . By (B.16), the restriction of $u_{i}$ to each component is strictly monotone, and its endpoint values are $-1+b$ and $1-b$ , in either order.

We can now prove integrality. Let $N_{i}$ be the number of these components and set

$$ h_{b}:=\int_{-1+b}^{1-b}\sqrt{2W(s)}\,ds. $$

The elementary inequality

$$ 0\leq\bar{e}_{i}-\sqrt{2W(u_{\varepsilon_{i}})}\,|\partial_{t}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|\leq|\bar{\xi}_{i}|+\varepsilon_{i}|D_{y}u_{\varepsilon_{i}}|^{2} $$

shows, by change of variables on each monotone component and (B.13), that

$$ \int_{I_{1}\cap\{|u_{\varepsilon_{i}}(y_{i},\cdot)|<1-b\}}\bar{e}_{i}(y_{i},t)\,dt=N_{i}h_{b}+o_{i}(1). $$

In particular, $N_{i}$ is bounded independently of $i$ and of sufficiently small $b$ . The remaining energy is bounded by the last condition in (B.12). Since $h_{b}=h_{0}+O(b^{2})$ , we obtain $\operatorname{dist}(\theta,\mathbb{N})\leq Cb.$ Letting $b\downarrow 0$ proves $\theta\in\mathbb{N}$ and completes the argument. ∎

## Appendix C Measure-function convergence

In this appendix we shall summarise some basic notions and results from the theory of measure-function pairs, which are used in the proof of Theorem 4.8. See [34, 60] or [30] for more details.

#### Definition C.1.

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space and $N\in\mathbb{N}$ . Let $\mu$ be a Radon measure on $X$ and $f:X\to\mathbb{R}^{N}$ a Borel-measurable vector-valued function which is in $L^{1}_{loc}(X;\mu)$ . We shall call such a pair $(\mu,f)$ a measure-function pair over $X$ .

#### Definition C.2.

Let $(\mu_{i},f_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of measure-function pairs over $X$ . We say $(\mu_{i},f_{i})$ converges to a measure function pair $(\mu,f)$ over $X$ in the weak sense (or, more simply, weakly) if the following conditions hold:

- (i) $\mu_{i}\to\mu$ as Radon measures on $X$ ; and

- (ii) for any $\phi\in C_{c}(X,\mathbb{R}^{N})$ , we have (C.1)

$$ \int_{X}\langle f_{i},\phi\rangle\,d\mu_{i}\to\int_{X}\langle f,\phi\rangle\,d\mu. $$

We shall denote this convergence by $(\mu_{i},f_{i})\rightharpoonup(\mu,f)$ .

The main result we shall need in the proof of Theorem 4.8 is the following compactness result.

#### Proposition C.3 ([34]).

Let $(\mu_{i},f_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of measure-function pairs over $X$ . Suppose that

$$ \sup_{i}\mu_{i}(X)<+\infty, $$

and

$$ \sup_{i}\int_{X}|f_{i}|^{2}\,d\mu_{i}<+\infty. $$

Then, there is a subsequence $(\mu_{i^{\prime}},f_{i^{\prime}})$ and a measure-function pair $(\mu,f)$ over $X$ such that

$$ (\mu_{i^{\prime}},f_{i^{\prime}})\rightharpoonup(\mu,f). $$

Moreover, the weak limit $(\mu,f)$ satisfies

$$ \int_{X}|f|^{2}\,d\mu\leq\liminf_{i}\int_{X}|f_{i}|^{2}\,d\mu_{i}. $$
